Fix $n\ge1$ and a point $p\in\mathbb C^n$, and write
$\mathcal O_{\mathbb C^n,p}$ for the ring of holomorphic germs at $p$, with
addition and multiplication of germs defined by representatives on a common
neighbourhood ([[def-holomorphic-germ-ring-and-its-maximal-ideal]]). Recall
that a germ is a unit exactly when its value at $p$ is nonzero
([[prop-units-in-the-holomorphic-germ-ring]]).

A germ $f\in\mathcal O_{\mathbb C^n,p}$ is a **hypersurface equation germ** at
$p$ when $f$ is nonzero and not a unit.

Such an equation germ $f$ is **reduced** when no irreducible element of
$\mathcal O_{\mathbb C^n,p}$ divides $f$ twice: there is no irreducible
$q\in\mathcal O_{\mathbb C^n,p}$ with $q^2\mid f$ in
$\mathcal O_{\mathbb C^n,p}$. In other words, a reduced equation germ is a
nonzero nonunit that is not divisible by the square of an irreducible germ.

The zero germ and the unit germs are excluded from hypersurface equations, so
reducedness is only defined for nonzero nonunits.

**Convention for a general centre.** The published germ ring is defined at the
origin, and on this page $\mathcal O_{\mathbb C^n,p}$ is read through the
translation convention: the biholomorphism $z\mapsto z+p$ of $\mathbb C^n$
pulls germs at $p$ back to germs at $0$, so $\mathcal O_{\mathbb C^n,p}$ denotes
the isomorphic ring of holomorphic germs at $p$, a germ at $p$ corresponds to
its translate $z\mapsto f(z+p)$ at $0$, and the maximal ideal is the translate
of $\mathfrak m_{n,0}$; the dimension lemma proved below identifies it with the
ideal generated by the coordinate differences $z_i-p_i$. Every definition and
result on this page is transported along this identification, which only
relabels the base point. At $p=0$ the convention is the identity.

By the unique factorisation property of the holomorphic germ ring
([[thm-holomorphic-germ-ring-is-a-ufd]]) a nonzero nonunit $f$ has a
factorisation

$$f=u\,q_1^{e_1}\cdots q_r^{e_r}$$

with $u$ a unit, $r\ge1$, the $q_i$ pairwise nonassociate irreducible germs,
and exponents $e_i\ge1$; the $r$-tuple of associate classes of the $q_i$ and
the exponents $e_i$ are determined by $f$. Comparing two such factorisations
shows that $f$ is reduced exactly when every $e_i=1$: if some $e_i\ge2$ then
$q_i^2\mid f$, and conversely a divisor $q^2\mid f$ with $q$ irreducible makes
$q$ associate to one of the $q_i$ with $e_i\ge2$, by uniqueness of the
factorisation applied to a factorisation of the quotient.

Reducedness is a property of the equation germ, not of its zero set. The germs
$z_1$ and $z_1^2$ at the origin of $\mathbb C^2$ are both nonzero nonunits and
have the same zero set near the origin, but only $z_1$ is reduced. The
geometric identification of equations that cut out the same zero set germ is
the subject of the later definition of a hypersurface germ on this page.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, inherited from the published block theory
([[thm-central-character-summands-split-into-linkage-blocks]],
[[def-standard-and-costandard-objects-in-category-o]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

Work in category $\mathcal O$ of a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie
algebra $\mathfrak g$ with the conventions of [[def-bgg-category-o]]: a Cartan
subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, a positive system with simple roots $\alpha_i$, the
Weyl group $W$ of [[def-root-reflections-and-the-weyl-group-action]], the Weyl
vector $\rho$, and the dot action $w\cdot\lambda=w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho$. Write
$Q^+=\sum_i\mathbb Z_{\geq0}\alpha_i$ and $\mu\le\lambda$ when
$\lambda-\mu\in Q^+$.

**The fixed weight.** Fix a weight $\lambda$ which is **integral**,
**dot-regular** and **dominant**: $\langle\lambda+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle\in\mathbb Z$
for every root $\alpha$ (so the integral Weyl group $W_\lambda$ of
[[def-integral-weyl-group-of-a-weight]] is all of $W$), and
$\langle\lambda+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle\neq0$, respectively $>0$, for every
root, respectively every positive root ([[def-dot-action-facets-and-single-wall-translation-data]]).
The set $\Phi_\lambda$ of [[def-integral-weyl-group-of-a-weight]] is therefore
the full root system and $W_\lambda=W$.

**The block.** The regular point $\lambda+\rho$ lies in an open chamber. An element fixing
it preserves that chamber, so [[thm-the-weyl-group-acts-simply-transitively-on-weyl-chambers]]
makes its stabilizer trivial; hence the linkage class
$$C=W_\lambda\cdot\lambda=W\cdot\lambda$$
has exactly $|W|$ elements. The **regular integral block** is the full
subcategory
$$\mathcal O_\lambda:=\mathcal O_C$$
of objects of $\mathcal O$ whose simple composition factors have labels in
$C$, as in [[thm-central-character-summands-split-into-linkage-blocks]]; it is
nonzero, abelian and extension-closed as a block, and
$K_0(\mathcal O_\lambda)$ is the subgroup of $K_0(\mathcal O)$ of
[[def-grothendieck-group-and-character-of-category-o]] spanned by the classes
of objects of the block.

**Its labelled objects.** For $w\in W$ define the standard and costandard
objects and the simple object by
$$\Delta(w\cdot\lambda):=M(w\cdot\lambda),\qquad \nabla(w\cdot\lambda):=D(M(w\cdot\lambda)),\qquad L(w\cdot\lambda):=M(w\cdot\lambda)/J(w\cdot\lambda),$$
where $M$ is the Verma module of [[def-verma-module]], $D$ the restricted dual
of [[def-standard-and-costandard-objects-in-category-o]], and $J(w\cdot\lambda)$
the sum of all proper submodules, so that $L(w\cdot\lambda)$ is the unique
simple quotient of $\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)$ by
[[thm-verma-module-has-a-unique-simple-quotient]]. By
[[thm-simple-objects-of-category-o-are-highest-weight-modules]] the simple
objects of $\mathcal O_\lambda$ are exactly the $L(w\cdot\lambda)$ for
$w\in W$, pairwise non-isomorphic. Let $P(w\cdot\lambda)$ denote a projective
cover of $L(w\cdot\lambda)$, which may be chosen inside the linkage class of
$w\cdot\lambda$ and is unique up to isomorphism and indecomposable
([[thm-category-o-has-enough-projectives]]); every such $P(w\cdot\lambda)$
carries a finite Verma flag
([[thm-projectives-in-category-o-have-verma-flags]],
[[def-verma-flag-and-its-multiplicities]]).

**Triangularity of the Verma-flag matrix.** For all $v,w\in W$,
$$[\Delta(w\cdot\lambda):L(v\cdot\lambda)]\neq0\ \Longrightarrow\ v\cdot\lambda\le w\cdot\lambda,\qquad [\Delta(w\cdot\lambda):L(w\cdot\lambda)]=1,$$
where the multiplicity is the composition multiplicity of
[[def-standard-and-costandard-objects-in-category-o]]. Indeed
$(P(v\cdot\lambda):\Delta(w\cdot\lambda))=[\Delta(w\cdot\lambda):L(v\cdot\lambda)]$
by [[thm-bgg-reciprocity]] and
$(P(v\cdot\lambda):\Delta(w\cdot\lambda))\neq0$ forces
$w\cdot\lambda-v\cdot\lambda\in Q^+$ while
$(P(v\cdot\lambda):\Delta(v\cdot\lambda))=1$ by
[[cor-projective-standard-labels-lie-above-the-head]].

**The antidominant weight.** Let $w_0\in W$ be the longest element. Since
$\langle w_0\cdot\lambda+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle
=\langle\lambda+\rho,w_0^{-1}\alpha^\vee\rangle<0$ for every positive root
$\alpha$, the antidominant Verma module $\Delta(w_0\cdot\lambda)$ is simple
([[cor-antidominant-verma-modules-are-simple]]), so
$$\Delta(w_0\cdot\lambda)=L(w_0\cdot\lambda)$$
and this is the unique standard object of the block that is simple: for
$w\neq w_0$ the regular weight $w\cdot\lambda$ is not antidominant, so some
positive root $\alpha$ has
$\langle w\cdot\lambda+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle\in\mathbb Z_{>0}$, and
[[thm-verma-embedding-for-an-arbitrary-positive-root]] embeds
$M(s_\alpha\cdot(w\cdot\lambda))$ as a proper submodule of
$\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)$. The weight $w_0\cdot\lambda$ is called the
**antidominant weight** of the block and $\Delta(w_0\cdot\lambda)$ its
antidominant Verma module.

**Grothendieck group.** By [[prop-the-grothendieck-group-of-o-has-simple-and-standard-bases]]
applied to the finite label set $C=W\cdot\lambda$, both the classes
$[\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)]$ and the classes $[L(w\cdot\lambda)]$, $w\in W$,
form $\mathbb Z$-bases of $K_0(\mathcal O_\lambda)$, and the transition matrix
between them is unitriangular for any linear order of $W$ extending the order
on the dot orbit induced by $\le$.

Every statement above uses the published block, Verma, duality and
projective-cover theory named in the citations, and that theory assumes the
Axiom of Choice; the definition itself selects nothing further.

$A_{n-1}$ with Cartan $\mathfrak h$, positive system $\Phi^+$, Weyl vector
$\rho$, Weyl group $W$ (identified with $S_n$) and dot action
$w\cdot\lambda=w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho$. Fix a dominant regular integral weight
$\lambda$, i.e. $\langle\lambda+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle\neq0$ for every root and
$\lambda$ integral, and let $\mathcal O_\lambda$ be the corresponding regular
integral block in the conventions of
[[def-regular-integral-category-o-block-and-its-antidominant-weight]]: standard
objects $\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)=M(w\cdot\lambda)$, simples $L(w\cdot\lambda)$,
indecomposable projectives $P(w\cdot\lambda)$ for $w\in W$, with
$\lambda=e\cdot\lambda$ the unique dominant and $w_0\cdot\lambda$ the unique
antidominant element and $\Delta(w_0\cdot\lambda)=L(w_0\cdot\lambda)$.

This item freezes the following conventions, each inherited from the cited
suppliers and used verbatim below.

(i) **Multiplicity conventions.** $(P(w\cdot\lambda):\Delta(y\cdot\lambda))$ is
the Verma-flag multiplicity of [[def-verma-flag-and-its-multiplicities]] and
$[M(y\cdot\lambda):L(w\cdot\lambda)]$ the composition multiplicity, and
$$(P(w\cdot\lambda):\Delta(y\cdot\lambda))=[M(y\cdot\lambda):L(w\cdot\lambda)]$$
by BGG reciprocity ([[thm-bgg-reciprocity]]).

(ii) **Bruhat reversal convention.** Along the bijection
$W\ni w\mapsto w\cdot\lambda$ the Bruhat order runs opposite to the dominance
order, in the two exact senses used on this page: $y\le w$ implies
$w\cdot\lambda\le y\cdot\lambda$ in the dominance order, and every nonzero
multiplicity forces the index direction, i.e.
$[M(y\cdot\lambda):L(w\cdot\lambda)]\neq0$ implies $y\le w$ in the Bruhat
order. The first sense is the inclusion direction of
[[lem-dominant-integral-dot-translates-embed-in-the-verma-module]] (for
$w\ge y$ one has $M(w\cdot\lambda)\subseteq M(y\cdot\lambda)$, so the highest
weight of the submodule is the lower one), and the second is
[[lem-jordan-holder-factors-of-verma-modules-lie-above-the-head]], which
confines every composition factor of $M(y\cdot\lambda)$ to labels
$w\ge y$. The full statement that the two orders are isomorphic as posets is
not needed here and is not asserted; only these two directions, together with
the finiteness of intervals of the Bruhat order
([[lem-bruhat-order-basic-properties-for-permutations]]), are used.

(iii) **Hecke and Kazhdan–Lusztig normalization.** The Kazhdan–Lusztig basis
$\underline H_w=\sum_{y\le w}p_{y,w}H_y$ of the normalized type-$A$ Hecke
algebra ([[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-the-kazhdan-lusztig-basis]]), with
$$p_{y,w}=v^{\ell(w)-\ell(y)}P_{y,w}(v^{-2})$$
in the classical $q=v^{-2}$ normalization
([[def-kazhdan-lusztig-polynomials-in-the-classical-q-normalization]]), support
$p_{y,w}=0$ unless $y\le w$, diagonal $p_{w,w}=1$, and simultaneous inversion
symmetry $p_{y^{-1},w^{-1}}=p_{y,w}$.

(iv) **Soergel label and character dictionary.** Write $R_x$ for the
polynomial standard graph bimodule supported at $x$, and $B_x$ for the
normalized indecomposable polynomial Soergel bimodule, which is generally not a
standard graph bimodule. With right reduction $\bar B=B\otimes_S\mathbb C$
and left coinvariant-module values of $V$, the projective dictionary is
$$V(P(w\cdot\lambda))\cong\bar B_{w^{-1}}$$
([[thm-indecomposable-projectives-correspond-to-indecomposable-soergel-modules]]).
The graph label $x$ corresponds to the standard
$\Delta(x^{-1}\cdot\lambda)$. The individual support ranks are measured on the
polynomial lift before reduction, as in
[[prop-verma-flag-multiplicities-are-standard-filtration-ranks-under-v]];
no separated graph-support filtration of the reduced module is asserted.

For degree bookkeeping use precisely the standard-generator normalization of
[[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]]:
$\Delta_x(d)=R_x(d-\ell(x))$, and $r_{x,d}(B)$ counts these normalized polynomial
standard layers. Thus the coefficient polynomial is
$$m_x(B;v):=\sum_d r_{x,d}(B)v^d,\qquad h_\Delta(B)=\sum_xm_x(B;v)\widetilde T_x,\qquad\widetilde T_x=v^{\ell(x)}T_x.$$
Here $\widetilde T_x$ is the normalized **standard** Hecke element $H_x$ used
in clause (iii) and
[[def-normalized-type-a-hecke-algebra-and-its-bar-involution]]. The published
Soergel split-Grothendieck-ring convention instead names its simple
Kazhdan--Lusztig generators $H_i=v(T_i+1)=\widetilde T_{s_i}+v$; these must not
be confused with the standard element $H_{s_i}=vT_i$
([[thm-split-grothendieck-group-of-the-soergel-category-is-the-type-a-hecke-algebra]]).
The standard-character supplier
[[lem-the-type-a-standard-character-is-multiplicative]] identifies $h_\Delta$
with that split-Grothendieck-ring isomorphism. This records the coefficient
normalization, and does not infer the image of a general indecomposable $B_x$
by multiplying simple generators. In particular the character theorem must be
used to identify $h_\Delta(B_x)$ with $\underline H_x$; a product of simple
Soergel classes is a Bott--Samelson class and need not be $[B_x]$.
The inverse labels and all rank comparisons above use auxiliary polynomial
gradings only; forgetting them gives the ordinary projective dictionary.

rows.consumer_statement_or_definition:
Fix $n\ge1$ and a complex-analytic hypersurface germ $X$ at a point
$p\in\mathbb C^n$, and fix a defining equation $f$ of $X$ together with a
representative of $f$ on a connected open neighbourhood $U$ of $p$
([[def-complex-analytic-hypersurface-germ-and-reduced-equation]]). We keep the
symbol $X$ for the corresponding representative zero set in $U$. Since the
defining germ is nonzero, $f$ is not identically zero on $U$. The identity
theorem implies that its germ at every $q\in U$ is nonzero
([[thm-identity-theorem-in-several-complex-variables]]); at $q\in X$ it is
also a nonunit. Thus $(X,q)$ is a hypersurface germ at every point under
consideration.

For a point $q\in X$, write $I_q(X)$ for the vanishing ideal of $X$ at $q$:
the ideal of germs $g\in\mathcal O_{\mathbb C^n,q}$ vanishing on $X$ near $q$.
A **local reduced equation** of $X$ at $q$ is a germ
$f_q\in\mathcal O_{\mathbb C^n,q}$ such that

$$(f_q)=I_q(X)\qquad\text{and}\qquad f_q\ \text{is reduced at }q .$$

Such equations exist and are well defined by the following two observations.
First, taking the square-free reduction of the germ of any defining equation
of $(X,q)$ produces a reduced germ generating $I_q(X)$, by the principal
vanishing-ideal lemma applied with base point $q$ and by the square-free
reduction lemma
([[lem-vanishing-ideal-of-a-reduced-hypersurface-germ]],
[[lem-square-free-reduction-of-holomorphic-germ]]). Second, if $f_q$ and
$f'_q$ both generate the nonzero principal ideal $I_q(X)$ in the germ ring,
then $f_q=uf'_q$ and $f'_q=vf_q$ for germs $u,v$, so $uv=1$ by cancellation in
the integral domain $\mathcal O_{\mathbb C^n,q}$
([[thm-holomorphic-germ-ring-is-a-ufd]]); thus $u$ and $v$ are units and
any two local reduced equations differ by a unit
([[prop-units-in-the-holomorphic-germ-ring]]).

A point $q\in X$ is a **regular point** of $X$ when

$$df_q(q)\ne0$$

for one — equivalently, by the unit relation just noted, for every — local
reduced equation $f_q$ of $X$ at $q$; here $df_q(q)$ is the complex
differential of the germ $f_q$ at its own base point $q$. A point that is not
regular is a **singular point** of $X$. The **regular locus** $\operatorname{Reg}(X)$
and the **singular locus** $\operatorname{Sing}(X)$ are the subsets of $X$
consisting of its regular and of its singular points.

rows.consumer_statement_or_definition:
Let $G$ be a topological group and let $H\le G$ be any subgroup
([[def-subgroup]]), not assumed normal or closed. The pair $(G,H)$ has
**relative property (T)** if every strongly continuous unitary representation
of $G$ ([[def-strongly-continuous-unitary-representation]]) with almost
invariant vectors ([[def-almost-invariant-vectors-for-a-unitary-representation]])
has a nonzero vector fixed by every $\pi(h)$ for $h\in H$.

A pair $(Q,\varepsilon)$ with $Q\subseteq G$ and $\varepsilon>0$ is a
**relative Kazhdan pair** for $(G,H)$ if every strongly continuous unitary
representation of $G$ having a $(Q,\varepsilon)$-invariant unit vector has a
nonzero $H$-invariant vector. A subset $Q\subseteq G$ is a **relative Kazhdan
set** if $(Q,\varepsilon)$ is a relative Kazhdan pair for some
$\varepsilon>0$.

When $H=G$, these are respectively Kazhdan's property (T), Kazhdan pairs, and
Kazhdan sets ([[def-kazhdans-property-t]],
[[def-kazhdan-pair-and-kazhdan-constant]]).

rows.consumer_statement_or_definition:
Let $f$ have an isolated singularity at $a$. By
[[thm-laurent-expansion-annulus]], on every sufficiently small punctured disc
about $a$ it has a Laurent expansion

$$f(z)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}c_n(z-a)^n.$$

By [[thm-laurent-coefficient-formula-and-uniqueness]], the coefficient $c_{-1}$
is uniquely determined on that disc, and
[[cor-laurent-coefficients-independent-of-radius]] shows that shrinking the
disc does not change it. It is the **residue** of $f$ at $a$, written

$$\operatorname{Res}(f,a):=c_{-1}.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) and work with the finite
classical $\mathfrak{gl}_n$ tableau blocks of
[[def-integral-parabolic-category-o-block-for-higher-level-schur-weyl-duality]],
and with the general translation machinery of
[[def-translation-functor-between-o-blocks]] and
[[prop-translation-functors-are-exact-and-biadjoint-across-a-wall]].

Let $V$ be the natural $\mathfrak{gl}_n$-module and $V^{*}$ its dual. For a
residue $i$ define the **residue translation functor** $f_i$ on
$\mathcal O^\Lambda$ by tensoring with $V$ and projecting onto the entry-multiset
central character in which exactly one entry $i$ is replaced by $i+1$; define
$e_i$ by tensoring with $V^{*}$ and the reverse character change ($i+1\mapsto i$,
with the signs of the natural form). Concretely, on a block
$\mathcal O^\Lambda_\alpha$ the functor is the exact block projection
$\operatorname{pr}_{\alpha+\alpha_i}(-\otimes V)$ for $f_i$ and
$\operatorname{pr}_{\alpha-\alpha_i}(-\otimes V^{*})$ for $e_i$, where
$\alpha_i$ is the Fock root label of the dictionary item
([[def-the-fock-convention-dictionary-for-finite-type-a-quantum-modules]]).

On the direct sum $\mathcal O^\Lambda$ of the blocks these functors are exact
and biadjoint, preserve projective and injective objects, and commute with the
restricted transpose duality
([[prop-restricted-duality-is-an-exact-involution-on-category-o]]).
Equivalently, $f_i$ is the generalized $i$-eigencomponent of the tensor
Casimir (including the place factors), and $e_i$ is the generalized
$-n-i$-eigencomponent on the dual tensor product.

The functors are **special residue translations**, not automatically ordinary
regular-wall translations; the Fock root label shifts by $\pm\alpha_i$, and
that label is not the classical $\mathfrak{gl}_n$ highest weight.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) and work with the finite
classical $\mathfrak{gl}_n$ tableau blocks of
[[def-integral-parabolic-category-o-block-for-higher-level-schur-weyl-duality]],
and with the general translation machinery of
[[def-translation-functor-between-o-blocks]] and
[[prop-translation-functors-are-exact-and-biadjoint-across-a-wall]].

[F4] Block dictionary ([[def-integral-parabolic-category-o-block-for-higher-level-schur-weyl-duality]]): the central characters are labelled by entry multisets and the Fock root label $\alpha_i$ shifts one entry; its Verification constructs the fixed-centre $\mathfrak{gl}_n$ reduction to $\mathfrak{sl}_n$.
proof_uses: 1.1 **Definition of the functors.** Tensoring with $V$ or $V^{*}$ preserves $\mathcal O$ and parabolic local finiteness: tensor a finite parabolic span of a vector with the finite tensor factor. By the fixed-centre equivalence in [F4], the exact semisimple central-character projections in [F1] extend to $\mathfrak{gl}_n$: first project to an $I_n$ eigenvalue and then to the corresponding $\mathfrak{sl}_n$ central character. Tensoring with $V$ shifts the centre scalar by $1$, and tensoring with $V^*$ shifts it by $-1$. Thus these projections define the stated functors. Replacing $i$ by $i+1$ changes the Fock weight by $-\alpha_i$, so a source weight $\Lambda-\alpha$ becomes $\Lambda-(\alpha+\alpha_i)$; the reverse move gives $\alpha-\alpha_i$. A target with no admitted tableau is the zero category and its projection is zero. [F1, F4, construct, algebra]

2.1 **Exactness and biadjunction.** Tensoring with a finite-dimensional module is exact, and the fixed-centre block projections of step 1.1 are exact, hence so are $f_i,e_i$. For $W=V$ or $V^*$, evaluation and coevaluation give both adjunctions between $-\otimes W$ and $-\otimes W^*$; $W^{**}=W$ supplies the second direction. These maps are $\mathfrak{gl}_n$-linear, preserve the Cartan-semisimple and locally parabolic-finite categories, and respect the scalar-centre shifts. For a source block $\alpha$ and target block $\beta=\alpha+\alpha_i$, no maps connect distinct central-character components. Therefore projection restricts both adjunctions to $\operatorname{Hom}(f_iM,N)\cong\operatorname{Hom}(M,e_iN)$ and $\operatorname{Hom}(N,f_iM)\cong\operatorname{Hom}(e_iN,M)$, with the evaluation/coevaluation units and counits. This proves biadjunction without a regular-wall hypothesis, including zero target blocks. [F1, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 **The Casimir description.** The well-definedness supplier [F6] computes the tensor-Casimir scalars on generalized-standard flag sections: a valid $\lambda\mapsto\lambda+\varepsilon_j$ section has scalar $a_j$, and a valid $\lambda\mapsto\lambda-\varepsilon_j$ section has scalar $-a_j-n+1$. In particular the reverse move from entry $i+1$ has scalar $-n-i$. Its extension from these flag sections to arbitrary finite-length objects proves that the generalized $i$-eigencomponent is $f_i$ and the generalized $-n-i$-eigencomponent is $e_i$, with the block shifts of step 1.1. [F4, F6, step 1.1]

2.3 **Commutation with duality.** Extend the semisimple restricted duality [F3] through the fixed-centre equivalence [F4]; transpose fixes $I_n$, so its scalar is retained. For a finite-dimensional weight module $W$, the evaluation map $DM\otimes DW\to D(M\otimes W)$, $(\varphi\otimes\eta)(m\otimes w)=\varphi(m)\eta(w)$, is a natural isomorphism: at each total weight only finitely many weights of $W$ occur, and all the participating weight spaces are finite dimensional. The diagonal tensor action and the transpose anti-involution make this map $\mathfrak{gl}_n$-linear. In the standard coordinate bases, the dot forms on $V$ and $V^*$ identify $DV\cong V$ and $D(V^*)\cong V^*$: the matrices are $x$ on $V$ and $-x^{\mathsf T}$ on $V^*$, and in each case the transpose action is the adjoint for the dot form. Thus $D(M\otimes V)\cong DM\otimes V$, and likewise for $V^*$. Exactness and preservation of the simple composition factors show that $D$ preserves every finite-length central-character block, so $D\operatorname{pr}_\beta\cong\operatorname{pr}_\beta D$. Combining the two natural isomorphisms gives $Df_i\cong f_iD$ and $De_i\cong e_iD$. [F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

[[def-integral-parabolic-category-o-block-for-higher-level-schur-weyl-duality]],
and with the general translation machinery of
[[def-translation-functor-between-o-blocks]] and
[[prop-translation-functors-are-exact-and-biadjoint-across-a-wall]].

[F1] Semisimple-ambient translation and projection ([[def-translation-functor-between-o-blocks]], [[prop-translation-functors-are-exact-and-biadjoint-across-a-wall]], [[thm-category-o-decomposes-by-generalized-central-character]]): exactness and biadjunction of the finite tensor/block-projection functors, and the decomposition of $\mathcal O$ by generalized central characters.
proof_uses: 1.1 **Definition of the functors.** Tensoring with $V$ or $V^{*}$ preserves $\mathcal O$ and parabolic local finiteness: tensor a finite parabolic span of a vector with the finite tensor factor. By the fixed-centre equivalence in [F4], the exact semisimple central-character projections in [F1] extend to $\mathfrak{gl}_n$: first project to an $I_n$ eigenvalue and then to the corresponding $\mathfrak{sl}_n$ central character. Tensoring with $V$ shifts the centre scalar by $1$, and tensoring with $V^*$ shifts it by $-1$. Thus these projections define the stated functors. Replacing $i$ by $i+1$ changes the Fock weight by $-\alpha_i$, so a source weight $\Lambda-\alpha$ becomes $\Lambda-(\alpha+\alpha_i)$; the reverse move gives $\alpha-\alpha_i$. A target with no admitted tableau is the zero category and its projection is zero. [F1, F4, construct, algebra]

2.1 **Exactness and biadjunction.** Tensoring with a finite-dimensional module is exact, and the fixed-centre block projections of step 1.1 are exact, hence so are $f_i,e_i$. For $W=V$ or $V^*$, evaluation and coevaluation give both adjunctions between $-\otimes W$ and $-\otimes W^*$; $W^{**}=W$ supplies the second direction. These maps are $\mathfrak{gl}_n$-linear, preserve the Cartan-semisimple and locally parabolic-finite categories, and respect the scalar-centre shifts. For a source block $\alpha$ and target block $\beta=\alpha+\alpha_i$, no maps connect distinct central-character components. Therefore projection restricts both adjunctions to $\operatorname{Hom}(f_iM,N)\cong\operatorname{Hom}(M,e_iN)$ and $\operatorname{Hom}(N,f_iM)\cong\operatorname{Hom}(e_iN,M)$, with the evaluation/coevaluation units and counits. This proves biadjunction without a regular-wall hypothesis, including zero target blocks. [F1, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

Let
$$U_0:=\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus\{\infty\},\qquad U_\infty:=\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus\{0\}.$$
Define charts
$$\phi_0:U_0\to\mathbb C,\ \phi_0(z)=z,$$
and
$$\phi_\infty:U_\infty\to\mathbb C,\qquad \phi_\infty(z)=\begin{cases}1/z,&z\in\mathbb C^\times,\\ 0,&z=\infty.\end{cases}$$
On the overlap $U_0\cap U_\infty=\mathbb C^\times$ the transition maps are
$$\phi_\infty\circ\phi_0^{-1}(w)=1/w,\qquad \phi_0\circ\phi_\infty^{-1}(w)=1/w,$$
which are holomorphic on $\mathbb C^\times$. These are the standard holomorphic
charts of the Riemann sphere.

If $V\subseteq\widehat{\mathbb C}$ is open and $f:V\to\mathbb C$, then $f$ is
**holomorphic at $\infty$** when $\infty\in V$ and the chart expression
$$F(w):=f(\phi_\infty^{-1}(w))=\begin{cases}f(1/w),&w\neq0,\\ f(\infty),&w=0\end{cases}$$
is holomorphic at $0$. A scalar-valued function defined on a punctured
neighbourhood of $\infty$ has a **pole at $\infty$** when the punctured chart
expression $w\mapsto f(1/w)$ has a pole at $0$ in the sense of
[[def-isolated-singularity-types]].

Let $\mathcal A(\xi_0,\Omega)$ be a complete analytic function
([[def-complete-analytic-function]]).

Its **germ space** is the underlying set

$$\mathcal R(\xi_0,\Omega):=\mathcal A(\xi_0,\Omega).$$

If $(f,U)$ is a function element whose germ $[f]_z$ lies in
$\mathcal R(\xi_0,\Omega)$ for every $z \in U$, define the associated subset

$$N(f,U):=\{[f]_z \in \mathcal R(\xi_0,\Omega): z \in U\}.$$

These sets are the intended basic neighbourhoods of the germ space.

The **projection**

$$p:\mathcal R(\xi_0,\Omega)\longrightarrow\Omega$$

is the base-point map

$$p([f]_z)=z.$$

When the neighbourhoods $N(f,U)$ are proved to form a compatible holomorphic
atlas, this germ space is called the **Riemann surface of the complete analytic
function**.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C$ be a plane domain and let $u:\Omega\to[-\infty,\infty)$
be subharmonic on $\Omega$ ([[def-plane-subharmonic-function]]); in particular
$u$ is not identically $-\infty$ on any component. Then $u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$
([[thm-plane-subharmonic-functions-are-locally-integrable]]), so for every
compactly supported smooth test function $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ the
Lebesgue integral $\int_\Omega u\,\Delta\varphi\,dA$ converges absolutely: the
support of $\Delta\varphi$ is compact and $\Delta\varphi$ is bounded, so
$\int_\Omega|u\,\Delta\varphi|\,dA\le\|\Delta\varphi\|_\infty\int_{\operatorname{supp}\Delta\varphi}|u|\,dA<\infty$.
The **distributional Riesz functional** of $u$ is

$$\mu_u(\varphi):=\frac1{2\pi}\int_\Omega u\,\Delta\varphi\,dA\qquad(\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)),$$

where $\Delta=\partial_x^2+\partial_y^2$ is the Laplacian, $dA$ is area Lebesgue
measure, and $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ is the test space of [[def-distribution]]
with the distributional derivative conventions of [[def-distributional-derivative]].
The value is complex in general and is real for real-valued test functions.
The functional $\mu_u$ depends only on the almost-everywhere
representative of $u$: if $u=v$ a.e. then $u\,\Delta\varphi=v\,\Delta\varphi$
a.e. for every test function, so the integrals agree. Linearity in $\varphi$ is
inherited from the linearity of differentiation and integration.

The normalization factor $(2\pi)^{-1}$ is chosen so that, under Countable
Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), a logarithmic point potential has unit
mass at its pole: $\Delta\log|z-a|=2\pi\delta_a$ in the
distributional sense, that is, $\mu_{\log|{\cdot}-a|}=\delta_a$
([[thm-minus-laplacian-of-the-fundamental-solution-is-dirac]]).

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $A$ be a unital
complex Banach algebra, let $a \in A$, and let $E \subseteq \sigma_A(a)$ be
**clopen in the spectrum**, that is, both $E$ and
$\sigma_A(a)\setminus E$ are relatively open in $\sigma_A(a)$
([[def-spectrum-and-resolvent-set-in-a-banach-algebra]]). Equivalently
$E \subseteq \sigma_A(a)$ is closed in $\mathbb C$ — hence compact — and
$\sigma_A(a)\setminus E$ is compact as well, and the two are disjoint.

Choose disjoint open sets $U_1 \supseteq E$ and $U_0 \supseteq
\sigma_A(a)\setminus E$; such sets exist because $E$ and
$\sigma_A(a)\setminus E$ are disjoint compact subsets of the plane. Let

$$\chi_E(z) := \begin{cases} 1, & z \in U_1,\\ 0, & z \in U_0,\end{cases}$$

a locally constant function on the open neighbourhood $U_1 \cup U_0$ of
$\sigma_A(a)$, hence holomorphic there. The **Riesz spectral projection of $a$
associated with $E$** is the calculus value

$$P_E \;:=\; \chi_E(a) \;=\; \frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_\Gamma \chi_E(z)\, R(z,a)\,dz \;\in\; A ,$$

where $\Gamma$ is any cycle with trace in $(U_1\cup U_0)\setminus\sigma_A(a)$
whose index is $1$ at every point of $E$, whose index is $0$ at every point of
$\sigma_A(a)\setminus E$, and whose index is $0$ outside $U_1\cup U_0$ — for
instance the difference $c_{\mathrm{all}} - c_{E}$, where $c_{\mathrm{all}}$ is
admissible for $(\chi_E, U_1\cup U_0)$ and $c_E$ is a cycle with index $1$ on
the compact set $\sigma_A(a)\setminus E$ and index $0$ outside $U_0$ (the zero
cycle when $\sigma_A(a)\setminus E=\varnothing$): the difference has index
$1-0=1$ on $E$, index $1-1=0$ on $\sigma_A(a)\setminus E$, and index $0$
outside $U_1\cup U_0$, because $c_{\mathrm{all}}$ has index $0$ there and
$c_E$ has index $0$ outside $U_0\subseteq U_1\cup U_0$. Such cycles exist by
[[lem-admissible-cycle-around-a-compact-plane-set]] applied to the two compact
sets $\sigma_A(a)$ and $\sigma_A(a)\setminus E$.

Here the equality with the displayed integral, and its independence of the
separating cycle, do not use contour independence outside its admissible-cycle
hypothesis. Indeed, put
$F(z)=\chi_E(z)R(z,a)$ on
$\Omega:=(U_1\setminus E)\cup U_0$. This is Banach-valued holomorphic: it is
$R(z,a)$ on $U_1\setminus E$ and identically zero on $U_0$, so in particular
it extends holomorphically across $\sigma_A(a)\setminus E$. If
$c_{\mathrm{all}}$ is admissible and $\Gamma$ has the separating indices just
specified, then $c_{\mathrm{all}}-\Gamma$ has index zero on $E$ and outside
$U_1\cup U_0$, hence is null-homologous in $\Omega$. Therefore
[[lem-banach-valued-cauchy-integral-vanishes]] gives
$$\int_{c_{\mathrm{all}}}F(z)\,dz=\int_\Gamma F(z)\,dz.$$
The left side is the defining calculus integral for $\chi_E(a)$. Thus every
such $\Gamma$ gives $P_E$, while germ independence of the calculus makes the
value independent of the chosen $U_0,U_1$.

Let $S^1$ be oriented and parametrised as $\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z$ with the
positive orientation, let $\partial_\theta$ be the corresponding positively
oriented unit tangent vector field of $S^1$, and let $f:S^1\to\mathbb R^2$ be a
smooth immersion, that is, a regular closed curve
([[def-immersion-submersion-and-constant-rank-map]],
[[def-smooth-manifold]]). Writing $T\mathbb R^2\cong\mathbb R^2\times\mathbb R^2$
for the canonical identification, the differential
([[def-differential-of-a-smooth-map]], [[def-tangent-bundle-as-a-disjoint-union]])
gives for each $\theta$ the velocity vector $df_\theta(\partial_\theta)$, which
is nonzero because $f$ is an immersion.

The **normalised velocity**, or unit tangent, of $f$ is the map
$$\tau_f:S^1\longrightarrow S^1,\qquad \tau_f(\theta)=\frac{df_\theta(\partial_\theta)}{\lvert df_\theta(\partial_\theta)\rvert},$$
which is continuous because the velocity never vanishes and every nonzero
vector is a positive multiple of a unique unit vector.

The **rotation number** (also **rotation index**) of $f$ is
$$\operatorname{rot}(f):=\deg(\tau_f)\in\mathbb Z,$$
the degree of the unit tangent map. Concretely, after choosing the base point
$\theta_0=[0]$, identifying the unit circle with $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ by the
standard parametrisation and rotating the *target* circle by a constant so that
$\tau_f(\theta_0)$ corresponds to $[0]$, the class of $\tau_f$ is a based loop
in the sense of [[def-degree-of-a-circle-loop]], and its degree is the integer
$\operatorname{rot}(f)$; the constant rotation of the target plane changes
neither the winding number nor the degree, and the degree descends to based
loop classes ([[cor-degree-descends-to-circle-loop-classes]]), so the value is
independent of the choice of $\theta_0$ and of the lift used to compute it
([[thm-circle-loops-are-path-homotopic-iff-they-have-equal-degree]]).

Equivalent formulations, all taking the same value:

- The velocity curve $t\mapsto f'(t)$ is a closed $C^1$, hence rectifiable,
  loop in $\mathbb C^\times=\mathbb R^2\setminus\{0\}$, and
  $\operatorname{rot}(f)$ is its **winding number about the origin**: the
  normalised velocity $t\mapsto f'(t)/\lvert f'(t)\rvert$ is exactly
  $\tau_f$, and after the constant nonzero complex multiplication
  $\gamma\mapsto\gamma/\gamma(t_0)$ of the target plane, which changes neither
  the winding number about $0$ nor the degree of the normalised loop,
  [[thm-winding-number-equals-circle-degree]] identifies $n(\gamma,0)$ with the
  degree of the normalised loop, while
  [[cor-winding-number-classifies-loops-in-the-punctured-plane]] identifies that
  winding number with the class in $\pi_1(\mathbb C^\times,1)\cong\mathbb Z$.
- $\operatorname{rot}(f)$ equals $\frac{1}{2\pi}$ times the **total signed
  turning angle** of the tangent, i.e. the rotation index of the regular closed
  plane curve $f$ in the sense of
  [[def-rotation-index-of-a-regular-closed-plane-curve]], where the tangent
  angle is lifted continuously and the corner jumps are zero for a smooth
  curve.

The normalisation is fixed by the round unit circle: the immersion
$\theta\mapsto(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$ traversed once in the positive direction
has unit tangent $(-\sin\theta,\cos\theta)$ winding once positively, hence rotation number $+1$, and its reverse has
rotation number $-1$. Reversing the orientation of the domain negates the
rotation number, while a regular (orientation-preserving) reparametrisation
leaves it unchanged. Indeed, if $h$ is a positively oriented circle
diffeomorphism with increasing lift $H$ satisfying
$H(\theta+2\pi)=H(\theta)+2\pi$, then the chain rule gives
$\tau_{f\circ h}=\tau_f\circ h$: composing a tangent-angle lift with $H$
preserves its total increment. For the reversal $a(\theta)=-\theta$,
$\tau_{f\circ a}(\theta)=-\tau_f(-\theta)$, so an angle lift is
$\alpha(-\theta)+\pi$ when $\alpha$ lifts $\tau_f$; its total increment is
the negative of that of $\alpha$.

No convexity, simplicity, self-intersection restriction or properness is
imposed; $\operatorname{rot}$ is an invariant of the oriented immersed circle,
not of its image.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C$ be a plane domain, let
$P\subseteq\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus\Omega$, and let $f:\Omega\to\mathbb C$
be holomorphic.

One says that **$f$ is Runge-approximable on $\Omega$ with poles in $P$** when
there is a sequence of rational functions $(r_n)$ such that every finite pole of
$r_n$ lies in $P\cap\mathbb C$, the only possible pole at infinity also lies in
$P$, and

$$r_n\to f\qquad\text{locally uniformly on }\Omega.$$

If $\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus\Omega$ is connected and $P=\{\infty\}$, this is
simply **polynomial approximation on $\Omega$**.

Let $X$ be a Banach space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$
([[def-banach-space]], [[rem-real-and-complex-normed-space-convention]]) and let
$A:D(A)\subseteq X\to X$ be a closed densely defined linear operator with
resolvent $R(\lambda,A)=(\lambda I-A)^{-1}$
([[def-resolvent-of-a-closed-operator]],
[[def-densely-defined-closed-and-closable-operator]],
[[def-unbounded-linear-operator-domain-and-graph]]).

For a real $X$, all complex resolvents below are those of the closed complexified operator $A_{\mathbb C}(x,y)=(Ax,Ay)$ on $D(A)\times D(A)$ in the canonical complexification ([[lem-canonical-banach-complexification-of-a-real-banach-space]]). Closedness and density follow coordinatewise, since its norm is equivalent to the product norm.

For $\delta\in(0,\pi/2]$ and $\omega\in\mathbb R$, $A$ (or the pair
$(A,\omega)$) is **sectorial of angle $\delta$ with vertex $\omega$ in the
$e^{tA}$ convention** if the open sector $\omega+\Sigma_{\pi/2+\delta}$
([[def-complex-sector-and-bounded-analytic-semigroup]]) is contained in the
resolvent set $\rho(A)$, and for every $\varepsilon\in(0,\delta)$ there is a
constant $M_\varepsilon\ge1$ with
$$\|R(\lambda,A)\|\le\frac{M_\varepsilon}{|\lambda-\omega|}\qquad\text{for all }\lambda\in\omega+\Sigma_{\pi/2+\delta-\varepsilon}.$$

### The sign dictionary

The definition is equivalent to the pair of statements that the spectrum of
$A$ is contained in the complementary closed left sector
$$\sigma(A)\subseteq\omega+\bigl(\{\lambda\ne0:|\arg(-\lambda)|\le\pi/2-\delta\}\cup\{0\}\bigr)$$
and that the stated $M_\varepsilon/|\lambda-\omega|$ bound holds on the
right-opening sector. Writing $B:=-A+\omega I$ one has
$$(\mu I-B)=(\mu-\omega)I+A=-\bigl((\omega-\mu)I-A\bigr),$$
hence $R(\mu,B)=-R(\omega-\mu,A)$; substituting $\lambda=\omega-\mu$, the
resolvent bound of $A$ on $\omega+\Sigma_{\pi/2+\delta-\varepsilon}$ becomes
the bound $\|R(\mu,B)\|\le M_\varepsilon/|\mu|$ on the reflected left-opening
sector $-\Sigma_{\pi/2+\delta-\varepsilon}$ for $\mu$, so that sector lies in
$\rho(B)$ and the spectrum of $B$ lies in the closed sector $\{\mu\ne0:|\arg\mu|\le\pi/2-\delta\}\cup\{0\}$.

This dictionary is why every theorem on this page states its convention: a
source that calls $A$ "sectorial" for the opposite operator $-A$, or that
writes $e^{-t(-A)}$, is using the Pazy-Lunardi sign and its sector and angle
must be reflected before transfer. The free use of laplace-transform-shaped
formulas below is always in the $e^{tA}$ convention fixed here: the resolvent
sector of $A$ opens around the positive real direction, the spectral sector
lies to the left, and positive time corresponds to an integral of
$e^{\lambda z}R(\lambda,A)$.

Let $(f,U)$ be a function element and let $\zeta \in \partial U$.

The boundary point $\zeta$ is **regular for $(f,U)$** when there is a function
element $(g,V)$ with $\zeta \in V$ such that

$$g=f\qquad\text{on }U\cap V.$$

Since $V$ is an open neighbourhood of the boundary point $\zeta$, the
intersection $U\cap V$ is nonempty. So a regular boundary point is one across
which $(f,U)$ extends holomorphically on a full neighbourhood, not merely one
where some remote overlap carries a direct analytic continuation in the sense of
[[def-function-element-and-direct-analytic-continuation]].

The point $\zeta$ is a **singular boundary point** of $(f,U)$ when it is not
regular.

If $B \subseteq \partial U$ and every point of $B$ is singular for $(f,U)$, then
$B$ is a **natural boundary** for $(f,U)$. In particular, saying that the whole
boundary $\partial U$ is natural means that $(f,U)$ admits no holomorphic
extension across any boundary point.

[[def-dot-action-facets-and-single-wall-translation-data]].

**(1) Dot-antidominant integral weights.** A weight $\mu$ is **dot-antidominant**
if $\langle\mu+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle\le0$ for every $\alpha\in\Phi^+$, and
**integral** if $\langle\mu,\alpha_i^\vee\rangle\in\mathbb Z$ for all $i$
([[def-integral-weyl-group-of-a-weight]],
[[def-integral-dominant-and-strictly-dominant-weights]]).

**(2) The dot stabilizer.** Fix such a weight $\mu$ and put
$$J=J(\mu):=\{i:\langle\mu+\rho,\alpha_i^\vee\rangle=0\},\qquad W_\mu:=W_J=\langle s_i:i\in J\rangle.$$
Then the dot stabilizer $\{v\in W:v\cdot\mu=\mu\}$ equals $W_J$. Indeed, for
$i\in J$ the reflection $s_i$ fixes $\mu+\rho$, so $W_J$ lies in the
stabilizer; conversely the stabilizer of an integral dot-antidominant weight
is generated by the reflections it contains and is a standard parabolic
([[lem-finite-weyl-closed-chambers-and-stabilizers]], applied to the dominant
vector $-\mu-\rho$), and by
[[def-cg-parabolic-quotient-and-two-sided-minima]] a standard parabolic
subgroup is $W_I$ for the set $I$ of simple reflections it contains, which is
exactly $J$. In particular $w'\cdot\mu=w\cdot\mu$ if and only if
$w^{-1}w'\in W_J$, that is, $w'\in wW_J$.

**(3) The singular integral block.** The **singular integral block**
$\mathcal O_\mu$ is the block of
[[thm-central-character-summands-split-into-linkage-blocks]] of the central
character $\chi_\mu$ of $\mu$; by
[[cor-central-characters-are-dot-weyl-orbits]] two central characters agree
exactly when the highest weights lie in one dot orbit, and by
[[thm-category-o-decomposes-by-generalized-central-character]] the block is a
summand of $\mathcal O$. Its simple objects $L(w\cdot\mu)$, standard objects
$\Delta(w\cdot\mu)=M(w\cdot\mu)$, costandard objects $\nabla(w\cdot\mu)$ and
projective covers $P(w\cdot\mu)$ are indexed by $w\in W$
([[def-standard-and-costandard-objects-in-category-o]],
[[def-verma-module]]); by (2) the label $w\cdot\mu$ depends only on the coset
$wW_J$, so the labels can be normalized by the minimal right coset
representatives

$$W^J=\{w\in W:\ell(ws)>\ell(w)\ \text{for all }s\in J\},$$

which are exactly the elements of minimal length in the cosets $wW_J$
([[thm-hh-parabolic-minimal-representatives-and-length-additivity]] (3));
inversion carries $W^J$ onto the minimal left coset representatives ${}^JW$.

**(4) Highest-weight structure and multiplicities.** The block is a
highest-weight category: it has enough projectives
([[thm-category-o-has-enough-projectives]]), projective covers have finite
Verma flags ([[thm-projectives-in-category-o-have-verma-flags]]), the standard
classes and simple classes are bases of the Grothendieck group
([[def-grothendieck-group-and-character-of-category-o]],
[[prop-the-grothendieck-group-of-o-has-simple-and-standard-bases]]), and it
satisfies BGG reciprocity
$$(P(w\cdot\mu):\Delta(y\cdot\mu))=[M(y\cdot\mu):L(w\cdot\mu)]$$
([[thm-bgg-reciprocity]], [[def-verma-flag-and-its-multiplicities]]). The
multiplicity matrix is unitriangular for the refinement of the dominance order
on the dot orbit: $(P(w\cdot\mu):\Delta(w\cdot\mu))=1$, and
$(P(w\cdot\mu):\Delta(y\cdot\mu))\neq0$ only if $y\cdot\mu\ge w\cdot\mu$
([[cor-projective-standard-labels-lie-above-the-head]]); the ordinary
standard/costandard Hom and $\mathrm{Ext}^1$ vanishing used on this page is
[[lem-standard-costandard-hom-and-ext-vanishing]].

**(5) Regular versus singular.** The block is **regular** when $J=\varnothing$
(the weight lies on no wall) and **singular** when $J\neq\varnothing$; the
singular translation statements of this page use this notation, and
$J=\varnothing$ recovers the regular case. The genuine regular-parabolic
multiplicity statements below have their own separate explicit dominant
regular base and are not consequences of the notation here.

rows.consumer_statement_or_definition:
Assume [[def-countable-choice|countable choice]]. The **Smirnov class**
$N^+(\mathbb D)$ contains $0$ and consists otherwise of the nonzero $f\in N(\mathbb D)$ such that, with $f^*$ the
boundary function of
[[thm-nevanlinna-boundary-values-and-log-integrability]] (so that
$\log|f^*|\in L^1(\mathbb T,m)$, extended by $-\infty$ where $f^*=0$),
$$\log|f(z)|\le P[\log|f^*|](z)\qquad\text{for every }z\in\mathbb D .$$
For the zero function, the boundary function is zero; we interpret both sides
of the displayed inequality as $-\infty$. Its boundary logarithm is not an
$L^1$ datum, and the finite-measure Poisson construction is used only for
nonzero functions. The Poisson integral for the nonzero case is the one of
[[def-poisson-integral-of-finite-boundary-measure]].

By the Poisson-Jensen inequality of
[[lem-poisson-jensen-inequality-hardy-functions]], every $f\in H^p(\mathbb D)$,
$0<p\le\infty$, lies in $N^+(\mathbb D)$ by the displayed inequality; hence
$$H^p(\mathbb D)\subseteq N^+(\mathbb D)\subseteq N(\mathbb D)\qquad(0<p\le\infty),$$
the second inclusion being part of the definition.

Equivalently, $N^+(\mathbb D)$ is the class of quotients $g/h$ with
$g,h\in H^\infty(\mathbb D)$ and $h$ outer (and then $h$ may be normalized by
$h(0)>0$); this equivalence is proved in
[[lem-smirnov-class-quotient-characterisation]]. The class $N^+$ is a complex vector space, as certified using the quotient characterization just proved by [[lem-smirnov-class-quotient-characterisation]], its `justified_by` supplier. Indeed, for nonzero $f_j=g_j/h_j$ with bounded holomorphic numerators and bounded outer denominators, $h_1h_2$ is bounded and outer: its boundary logarithm is the sum of the two integrable boundary logarithms, and its interior log-modulus is their Poisson integral by linearity, in the outer convention of [[def-inner-singular-inner-and-outer-functions]]. Thus $f_1+f_2=(g_1h_2+g_2h_1)/(h_1h_2)$ has bounded numerator and bounded outer denominator. Let $G$ be a topological group and let $(\pi,H)$ be a strongly continuous unitary representation ([[def-strongly-continuous-unitary-representation]]) on a Hilbert space $H$ ([[def-hilbert-space]]). Put
$$H^G:=\{\xi\in H:\pi(g)\xi=\xi\text{ for every }g\in G\}.$$
This is a closed invariant subspace: if $\xi_n\in H^G$ and $\xi_n\to\xi$, then for every $g$ the isometry $\pi(g)$ gives $\|\pi(g)\xi-\xi\|\le2\|\xi-\xi_n\|\to0$. Its orthogonal complement $H^G{}^\perp$ ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]) is also closed and $G$-invariant by [[lem-unitary-invariant-subspaces-have-invariant-orthogonal-complements]], so the restriction $\pi|_{H^G{}^\perp}$ is a strongly continuous unitary representation. The representation $\pi$ has **spectral gap** if
$$1_G\not\prec\pi|_{H^G{}^\perp},$$
where $1_G$ is the trivial representation and $\prec$ is weak containment ([[def-weak-containment-of-unitary-representations]]).

If $G$ is locally compact Hausdorff ([[def-locally-compact-space]], [[def-hausdorff-space]]) and AC is assumed ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), this is equivalent by [[lem-weak-containment-of-the-trivial-representation-and-almost-invariant-vectors]] to the existence of a compact $Q\subseteq G$ containing the identity and an $\varepsilon>0$ such that
$$\sup_{g\in Q}\|\pi(g)\xi-\xi\|\ge\varepsilon\|\xi\|\qquad\text{for every }\xi\in H^G{}^\perp.$$
No displacement equivalence is asserted for general topological groups.

rows.consumer_statement_or_definition:
Assume AC. Let $T$ be a bounded normal operator on a **nonzero separable**
complex Hilbert space $H$ ([[def-separable-space]]) with spectral projection
valued measure $E$ on $\sigma(T)$ and spectral measure class to be described
below.

**Step 1: a countable cyclic decomposition.** By the multiplication-operator
form of the spectral theorem applied to a dense sequence, fix once and for all
a finite or countable family $(x_j)_{j\in J}$ of nonzero vectors with
$$H=\bigoplus_{j\in J}H_{x_j},\qquad \mu_j:=E_{x_j}=\langle E(\cdot)x_j,x_j\rangle,$$
where $H_{x_j}$ is the cyclic subspace of $x_j$ and each $\mu_j$ is a nonzero
finite positive regular Borel measure on $\sigma(T)$
([[thm-multiplication-operator-form-of-the-bounded-normal-spectral-theorem]],
[[def-cyclic-vector-and-cyclic-normal-operator]],
[[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]]). The index set $J$ is a finite
or countable subset of $\mathbb N$, listed in increasing order, and summands
with $x_j=0$ are omitted.

**Step 2: a common dominating measure.** Put
$$\mu:=\sum_{j\in J}\frac{2^{-j}}{1+\mu_j(\sigma(T))}\,\mu_j .$$
Then $\mu$ is a finite positive regular Borel measure with $\mu_j\ll\mu$ for every $j$; let
$$h_j:=\frac{d\mu_j}{d\mu},\qquad F_j:=\{z\in\sigma(T):h_j(z)>0\}$$
be the Radon–Nikodym derivative and its positivity set
([[thm-radon-nikodym-density-exists-and-is-unique-up-to-almost-everywhere-equality]]).

**Step 3: the multiplicity function.** Define the **multiplicity function** of
the decomposition by
$$m(z):=\sum_{j\in J}\mathbf 1_{F_j}(z)\in\{0,1,2,\dots\}\cup\{\infty\}\qquad(z\in\sigma(T)).$$
It is a Borel function, and $z\mapsto m(z)$ is the *fiber dimension* function of
the model below. The set $S(z):=\{j\in J:z\in F_j\}$ of **active coordinates**
has cardinality $m(z)$, and for $r\ge1$ the $r$-th active coordinate is
$$k_r(z):=\min\{k\in J:\ \#(S(z)\cap\{j\in J:j\le k\})=r\},\qquad z\in A_r:=\{z:m(z)\ge r\},$$
a Borel function on the Borel set $A_r$; the sets $A_1\supseteq A_2\supseteq
\cdots$ are decreasing and $\bigcup_{r}A_r$ is $\mu$-conull.

**Step 4: the standard measurable-field model.** The **standard model** of the
decomposition is the space
$$L^2(\sigma(T),\mu,m):=\Bigl\{f=(f_r)_{r\ge1}:\ f_r \text{ Borel},\ f_r=0\ \mu\text{-a.e. on }\{m<r\},\ \sum_{r\ge1}\int|f_r|^2\,d\mu<\infty\Bigr\}$$
of measurable fields with componentwise operations and inner product
$\langle f,g\rangle=\sum_r\int f_r\overline{g_r}\,d\mu$
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]],
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), where fields are identified
when they agree $\mu$-almost everywhere in every component. Its **fiber** at $z$ is
$\overline{\operatorname{span}}\{e_r:1\le r\le m(z)\}\subseteq\ell^2(\mathbb N)$, so the
fiber dimension is exactly $m(z)$, and the model is the direct sum
$\bigoplus_{r\ge1}L^2(\mu|_{A_r})$ of the ordinary $L^2$-spaces of the
restrictions of $\mu$ to the decreasing sets $A_r$ ([[def-hilbert-space]]).

**Claim of the definition (identification with the operator model).** The
rank enumeration of active coordinates together with the Radon–Nikodym
derivatives identifies the standard model unitarily with the orthogonal sum of
the cyclic $L^2$-summands: the map
$$W:L^2(\sigma(T),\mu,m)\longrightarrow\bigoplus_{j\in J}L^2(\sigma(T),\mu_j), \qquad (Wf)_j(z):=\frac{f_{r(z,j)}(z)}{\sqrt{h_j(z)}} \ \text{ for }z\in F_j,\quad (Wf)_j:=0\ \text{ off }F_j,$$
where $r(z,j)$ is the rank of $j$ in $S(z)$, is a well-defined unitary operator
intertwining the multiplications by every bounded Borel function and, in
particular, intertwining $M_z$ with $M_z$.

**Well-definedness.** (1) $\mu$ is finite and nonzero and $\mu_j\ll\mu$ for
each $j$, since the $j$-th summand of the sum dominates
$\frac{2^{-j}}{1+\mu_j(\sigma(T))}\mu_j$. It is regular: for any Borel
$A$ and $\varepsilon>0$, choose a finite initial segment of $J$ whose
weighted measure tail has total mass below $\varepsilon/2$. For each measure
in that segment, choose a compact subset of $A$ approximating $A$ from
inside, or an open superset approximating it from outside, with weighted
error summing to less than $\varepsilon/2$. The finite union of the compact
subsets lies in $A$ and the finite intersection of the open supersets
contains $A$; each approximates $\mu(A)$ within $\varepsilon$ because the
discarded tail has total mass below $\varepsilon/2$. (2) $h_j$ exists, is nonnegative
$\mu$-almost everywhere and is unique up to $\mu$-null sets (Radon–Nikodym);
$F_j=\{h_j>0\}$ is Borel and $\mu_j(\sigma(T)\setminus F_j)=\int_{\{h_j=0\}}h_j\,d\mu=0$.
(3) $\bigcup_jF_j$ is $\mu$-conull: since $h_j=0$ off $F_j$ one has
$\mu_j(\sigma(T)\setminus\bigcup_jF_j)=\int_{\sigma(T)\setminus\bigcup_jF_j}h_j\,d\mu=0$
for every $j$, so the dominating sum vanishes there, and therefore $m\ge1$
$\mu$-almost everywhere. (4) $m$ is Borel as a countable sum of indicators, and
$k_r$ is Borel on $A_r$ because
$\{k_r=k\}=F_k\cap\{\sum_{\ell<k,\ell\in J}\mathbf 1_{F_\ell}=r-1\}$ is a Borel
set. (5) $L^2(\sigma(T),\mu,m)$ is a Hilbert space: it is the orthogonal direct
sum $\bigoplus_rL^2(\mu|_{A_r})$, whose components are complete by Riesz–
Fischer. If $(f^{(n)})$ is Cauchy in the direct sum, each component converges
in $L^2(\mu|_{A_r})$ to some $f_r$. The finite partial sums of $\|f_r\|_2^2$
are bounded by the squared norms of the Cauchy sequence, so $(f_r)$ has finite
direct-sum norm. Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose $n_0$ such that
$\|f^{(n)}-f^{(q)}\|\le\varepsilon$ for $n,q\ge n_0$; for fixed $n\ge n_0$,
pass $q\to\infty$ in each finite coordinate sum and then take the supremum
over those sums to get $\|f^{(n)}-f\|\le\varepsilon$.
Thus the direct sum is complete ([[thm-riesz-fischer-completeness-of-l-p]]).
(6) $W$ is well defined: $(Wf)_j$ is Borel because on each Borel set
$\{r(z,j)=r\}$ it equals $f_r/\sqrt{h_j}$ with $h_j>0$ there, it vanishes off
$F_j$, and it is $\mu_j$-square-integrable because
$$\sum_{j\in J}\int|(Wf)_j|^2d\mu_j =\sum_{j\in J}\int_{F_j}|f_{r(z,j)}|^2\,d\mu =\sum_{r\ge1}\int_{A_r}|f_r|^2\,d\mu=\|f\|^2<+\infty,$$
using the positive-measure identity $\mu_j=h_j\,d\mu$ and the
nonnegative change-of-density integral
([[thm-integration-against-a-density]]);
the same display shows $W$ is isometric, and $W$ is onto with inverse
$(g_j)_j\mapsto f$, $f_r(z):=g_{k_r(z)}(z)\sqrt{h_{k_r(z)}(z)}$ on $A_r$ and
$f_r:=0$ otherwise, which is Borel by the same rank-measurability and is
square-integrable by the same computation; multiplicativity is componentwise
and gives $W M_\varphi=M_\varphi W$ for every bounded Borel $\varphi$, hence
$WM_z=M_zW$. (7) At this stage the data $(\mu,h_j,F_j,m)$ come from the chosen
decomposition; independence of the measure class and almost-everywhere
multiplicity is established later, after the intertwiner lemma. For this
decomposition the multiplicity function is the **fiber dimension**
$z\mapsto\dim H_z$ of the model, equal to $m(z)$; at a non-atomic point of
$\sigma(T)$ with respect to $E$ it is *not* the dimension of the eigenspace
$\ker(T-zI)$, which is the fiber of the atoms carried by $E(\{z\})$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Keep a nonempty pyramid $\lambda=(0\le p_1\le\cdots\le p_n)$ with $l=p_n>0$ columns of heights $q_1\ge\cdots\ge q_l$, the origin $c$, and $U_d=V_c^{\otimes d}$ of [[def-deformed-tensor-space-for-the-type-a-finite-w-algebra]]. The **stable range** is $q_l\ge d$: there are at least $d$ rows of maximum length $l$. Put $a_j=c_j+q_j-n$, $A_d=\operatorname{im}(W(\lambda)\to\operatorname{End}U_d)$ and $B_d=\operatorname{im}(H_d(\mathbf a)\to\operatorname{End}U_d^{\mathrm{op}})$.

For every complex origin the finite image algebras are mutual centralizers, and the raw Hecke action is faithful in the stable range. For an **admissible** origin, meaning $c_j-c_k\in\mathbb Z$ implies $c_j=c_k$, the following construction defines the central support outside that range. Append $t$ full ground rows of length $l$ until $q_l+t\ge d$, keeping $l$ and $c$ fixed. Then $n$ and every $q_j$ increase by $t$, so every $a_j$ stays fixed. In the enlarged tensor space $U_d^{\mathrm{big}}$, let $e$ be the projection onto tensors using only retained rows, equivalently having zero occupancy in every deleted row. A large tableau is **contractible** if every deleted-row entry is the ground entry $c_j+1-r$ in row $r$ and column $j$. The supporting central idempotent $f$ acts as one on precisely the contractible standard-labelled simples and as zero on the others. Through the faithful enlarged Hecke action it is a central idempotent of $H_d(\mathbf a)$, and
$$B_d\cong fH_d(\mathbf a)f,\qquad\ker\psi_d=(1-f)H_d(\mathbf a).$$

This $f$ is a sum of entire supporting central blocks. Individual residue idempotents $e(\mathbf i)$ need not be central; they do not individually define this two-sided corner. The unrestricted tensor model does not by itself supply the admissible central-support conclusion.

For the empty pyramid $l=N=0$, the convention is separate: in degree zero the tensor and image algebras are $\mathbb C$ with the identity corner $f=1$; in positive degree the tensor, image algebras and their module categories are zero and $f=0$. No $q_l$ or nonempty stable-range condition is used in that case.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) inherited from the category-$\mathcal O$ suppliers. Fix a finite genuine integral parabolic central summand $\mathcal C$ over $\mathbb C$, with its finite highest-weight structure from [[thm-parabolic-category-o-is-a-highest-weight-category]]. Connectedness is not required. Write $(\Lambda,\preceq)$ for its label poset, $L_\lambda$ for its simples, $\Delta_\lambda$ for its generalized standards, and $\nabla_\lambda=D\Delta_\lambda$ for its costandards. The duality $D$ is exact, contravariant and simple-preserving.

The projective cover $P_\lambda$ and injective envelope $I_\lambda=DP_\lambda$ have exact sequences
$$0\longrightarrow K_\lambda\longrightarrow P_\lambda\longrightarrow\Delta_\lambda\longrightarrow0,\qquad0\longrightarrow\nabla_\lambda\longrightarrow I_\lambda\longrightarrow C_\lambda\longrightarrow0,$$
where $K_\lambda$ has a finite standard flag with labels strictly greater than $\lambda$, and $C_\lambda=DK_\lambda$ has a finite costandard flag with such labels. Generally $I_\lambda$ is larger than $\nabla_\lambda$. Standards have simple heads, costandards simple socles, and their composition labels are $\preceq\lambda$. In this split setting,
$$\operatorname{Hom}(\Delta_\lambda,\nabla_\mu)=\delta_{\lambda\mu}\mathbb C,\qquad\operatorname{Ext}^j(\Delta_\lambda,\nabla_\mu)=0\quad(j>0),$$
and BGG reciprocity is $(P_\lambda:\Delta_\mu)=[\nabla_\mu:L_\lambda]=[\Delta_\mu:L_\lambda]$. Higher Ext vanishing is justified below from the standard-kernel sequences and the local Hom/$\operatorname{Ext}^1$ statement.

A **finite standard flag** of $N$ is a finite chain $0=N_0\subset N_1\subset\cdots\subset N_r=N$ with sections $\Delta_{\lambda_i}$; a **finite costandard flag** has sections $\nabla_{\lambda_i}$. The zero object has the empty flag. Write $\mathcal F(\Delta)$ and $\mathcal F(\nabla)$ for the corresponding full subcategories. They are exact categories with the short exact sequences inherited from $\mathcal C$, closed under finite sums, extensions and direct summands. Their flag multiplicities are independent of the chosen flag and satisfy
$$(N:\Delta_\lambda)=\dim\operatorname{Hom}(N,\nabla_\lambda),\qquad(M:\nabla_\lambda)=\dim\operatorname{Hom}(\Delta_\lambda,M).$$
For arbitrary objects of the fixed finite summand, the equivalent homological criteria are
$$\mathcal F(\Delta)=\{N:\operatorname{Ext}^1(N,\nabla_\lambda)=0\text{ for all }\lambda\}=\{N:\operatorname{Ext}^j(N,\nabla_\lambda)=0\text{ for all }\lambda,j>0\},$$
$$\mathcal F(\nabla)=\{M:\operatorname{Ext}^1(\Delta_\lambda,M)=0\text{ for all }\lambda\}=\{M:\operatorname{Ext}^j(\Delta_\lambda,M)=0\text{ for all }\lambda,j>0\}.$$
The duality exchanges the two flag categories. A **tilting object** belongs to their intersection.

An indecomposable tilting object is **normalized at** $\lambda$, and written $T_\lambda$, if it has an inclusion $\Delta_\lambda\hookrightarrow T_\lambda$ whose cokernel is standard-filtered by labels strictly smaller than $\lambda$. Its bottom standard occurs once and $\lambda$ is its unique maximal composition-support label. Such an object, when it exists, is unique up to isomorphism. Existence and classification are supplied later; they are not used to prove the criteria. For a lower ideal $\Gamma$ containing $\lambda$, this same object is normalized tilting in the corresponding Serre subcategory; it is unchanged by the truncation.

$$A(\nu)f_n=c_n(\nu)f_n\qquad(n\equiv\varepsilon\pmod2).$$

rows.consumer_statement_or_definition:
All contours on this page are positively oriented unless a local direction is
stated explicitly.

- The **upper semicircle contour of radius $R$** is the union of the real
  segment $[-R,R]$ and the arc
  $\gamma_R^+(t)=Re^{it}$ for $0\le t\le\pi$.
- The **lower semicircle contour of radius $R$** traverses the real segment
  from $R$ to $-R$ and then the lower arc
  $\gamma_R^-(t)=Re^{-it}$ with $t$ decreasing from $\pi$ to $0$.
- The **rectangle contour**
  $\partial[-R,R]\times[-T,T]$ is the positively oriented boundary of the
  Euclidean rectangle with vertices $\pm R\pm iT$.
- The **keyhole contour** about the positive real axis with radii
  $0<\varepsilon<R$ is the positively oriented boundary of the slit annulus
  $\{z:\varepsilon<|z|<R,\ z\notin[0,\infty)\}$: it consists of the upper lip
  $x+i0$ from $\varepsilon$ to $R$, the outer circle run counterclockwise, the
  lower lip $x-i0$ from $R$ to $\varepsilon$, and the inner circle run
  clockwise.
- An **upper indentation arc** around a real point $a$ of radius $\varepsilon$
  is the clockwise semicircle $a+\varepsilon e^{it}$ for $\pi\ge t\ge0$; a
  **lower indentation arc** is the counterclockwise semicircle
  $a+\varepsilon e^{it}$ for $\pi\le t\le2\pi$.
- The **sector contour** with opening angles $\alpha<\beta$ and radii
  $0<\varepsilon<R$ is the positively oriented boundary of
  $\{\varepsilon<|z|<R,\ \alpha<\arg z<\beta\}$.

When a keyhole or sector contour is used with a complex power, this page states
the branch explicitly. In the default keyhole convention the slit is the
positive real axis and
$z^{\alpha-1}=\exp((\alpha-1)\operatorname{Log} z)$ is taken with $\operatorname{Arg} z\in(0,2\pi)$; the
principal branch from
[[def-complex-logarithms-principal-logarithm-and-complex-powers]] and
[[cor-principal-logarithm-is-holomorphic-on-the-slit-plane]] is used only when
the slit is the negative real axis.

Let $A$ be a complex C\*-algebra ([[def-c-star-algebra]]) and recall that
positivity in $A$ is the algebraic condition $a=b^*b$, without spectral
hypotheses ([[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-elements-of-a-c-star-algebra]]).
A linear functional $\omega:A\to\mathbb C$ is **positive** if
$$\omega(a^*a)\ge0\qquad\text{for every }a\in A,$$
and a **state** if in addition $\|\omega\|=1$, the norm being the operator
norm of the bounded linear functional on $A$.

cited_passages:
- **The positive functionals form a convex cone.** If $\omega,\varphi$ are
  positive, $s,t\ge0$ and $a\in A$, then
  $(s\omega+t\varphi)(a^*a)=s\,\omega(a^*a)+t\,\varphi(a^*a)\ge0$. In
  particular the positive functionals of norm at most one form a convex set,
  since $\|s\omega+t\varphi\|\le s+t$ whenever $s,t\ge0$. Being bounded with
  norm one is part of the definition of a state, not a consequence claimed
  here.
- **Cauchy–Schwarz.** Every positive functional satisfies
  $$|\omega(b^*a)|^2\le\omega(a^*a)\,\omega(b^*b)\qquad(a,b\in A).$$
  Indeed, for all $z\in\mathbb C$ linearity gives
  $$\omega\bigl((a+zb)^*(a+zb)\bigr)=\omega(a^*a)+z\,\omega(a^*b)+\bar z\,\omega(b^*a)+|z|^2\omega(b^*b)\ge0.$$
  The left side is a nonnegative real number for every $z$. Taking $z=1$ and
  $z=i$ and using that both resulting values are real shows
  $\omega(a^*b)+\omega(b^*a)\in\mathbb R$ and
  $i\bigl(\omega(a^*b)-\omega(b^*a)\bigr)\in\mathbb R$; hence
  $\omega(b^*a)=\overline{\omega(a^*b)}$. Writing $p=\omega(a^*a)\ge0$,
  $q=\omega(b^*b)\ge0$ and $u=\omega(a^*b)$, the displayed inequality reads

Let $f$ be holomorphic on an open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C$, and let $a\in\Omega$. The Taylor series of $f$ at $a$ is $\sum_{n\ge0}f^{(n)}(a)(z-a)^n/n!$.

Every derivative $f^{(n)}(a)$ exists by [[thm-cauchy-integral-formula-higher-derivatives]], and $n!$ is the positive factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so each coefficient

$$c_n:=\frac{f^{(n)}(a)}{n!}$$

is a well-defined complex number. The resulting complex power series is understood according to [[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. This definition names the formal series; its convergence and equality with $f$ are conclusions of the Taylor expansion theorem.

rows.consumer_statement_or_definition:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $G$ be a locally compact, $\sigma$-compact group with a fixed left Haar measure, and let $\lambda_G$ be its left regular representation on $L^2(G)$ ([[def-left-and-right-regular-unitary-representations]], [[thm-regular-representations-are-unitary-and-strongly-continuous]]). A strongly continuous unitary representation $\pi$ of $G$ is **tempered** if it is weakly contained in $\lambda_G$ ([[def-strongly-continuous-unitary-representation]], [[def-weak-containment-of-unitary-representations]]); explicitly, each continuous positive-type coefficient $g\mapsto\langle\pi(g)\xi,\xi\rangle$ is approximable uniformly on compact subsets of $G$ by finite sums of positive-type coefficients of $\lambda_G$.

The **reduced (tempered) dual** is
$$\widehat G_{\mathrm{red}}:=\{[\sigma]\in\widehat G:\sigma\prec\lambda_G\},$$
the Fell support of the regular representation ([[def-fell-topology-on-the-unitary-dual]], [[def-unitary-dual-of-a-locally-compact-group]]). Thus an irreducible unitary representation is tempered exactly when its equivalence class is a point of $\widehat G_{\mathrm{red}}$. A reducible representation may be tempered by the same weak-containment condition, but it is not itself a point of the irreducible unitary dual.

**Choice.** AC is inherited through the Haar-based regular representation and the set and Fell constructions of the unitary dual; the weak-containment criterion itself uses no additional choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

rows.consumer_statement_or_definition:
Assume the Axiom of Choice, inherited from the published block theory
([[def-axiom-of-choice]],
[[thm-central-character-summands-split-into-linkage-blocks]]).

In the regular integral block $\mathcal O_\lambda$ of
[[def-regular-integral-category-o-block-and-its-antidominant-weight]] fix the
antidominant weight $w_0\cdot\lambda$ and let
$$P:=P(w_0\cdot\lambda)$$ be a projective cover of $L(w_0\cdot\lambda)$
([[thm-category-o-has-enough-projectives]]); it is unique up to isomorphism and
indecomposable ([[prop-projective-covers-in-o-are-indecomposable-and-unique]],
[[def-projective-object]]), and it is an injective object of
$\mathcal O_\lambda$. The **Soergel functor** is
$$V:=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O}(P,-)\colon\mathcal O_\lambda\longrightarrow \operatorname{End}_{\mathcal O}(P)^{\mathrm{op}}\text{-}\mathbf{mod},\qquad M\longmapsto \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O}(P,M),$$
with the left action of $\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal O}(P)^{\mathrm{op}}$ on
$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O}(P,M)$ induced by composition on the right of
the source: $a\cdot f=f\circ a$
([[def-projective-functors-on-a-regular-integral-category-o-block]]). Its
values on the standard objects and on the indecomposable projectives are
written $V\Delta(w\cdot\lambda):=V(\Delta(w\cdot\lambda))$ and
$VP(w\cdot\lambda):=V(P(w\cdot\lambda))$. The functor $V$ is exact, because
$P$ is projective, and hence left exact; the identity
$VP\cong\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal O}(P)$ with its regular module structure
is the Yoneda identification. Replacing the chosen projective cover $P$ by an
isomorphic one changes $V$ by a natural equivalence of functors compatible
with the endomorphism-ring identification, so the construction depends only
on the isomorphism class of $P$.

**Well-definedness: $P$ is injective.** We prove that $P$ is an injective
object of $\mathcal O_\lambda$ using only the listed suppliers, following the
argument of [Soe90, Sections 1.2 and 2.1] in its algebraic form. Put
$\eta:=-\rho$; then $W\cdot\eta=\{\eta\}$, because $w\cdot\eta=w(\eta+\rho)-\rho=-\rho$
for every $w$ ([[cor-central-characters-are-dot-weyl-orbits]]). By
[[thm-simple-objects-of-category-o-are-highest-weight-modules]] the simple
objects are the $L(\mu)$ with $L(\mu)$ determined by $\mu$, and the composition
factors of $M(\eta)$ have highest weights in $W\cdot\eta\cap(\eta-Q^+)=\{\eta\}$;
hence $M(\eta)=L(\eta)$ is simple. By BGG reciprocity
([[thm-bgg-reciprocity]]) applied to the single-label block, and the existence
of Verma flags for projectives ([[thm-projectives-in-category-o-have-verma-flags]]),
the projective cover $P(\eta)$ has a Verma flag with the single factor
$\Delta(\eta)=M(\eta)=L(\eta)$, so $P(\eta)\cong L(\eta)$; the block
$\mathcal O_\eta$ has a single simple object, which is projective, hence is
semisimple by enough projectives ([[thm-category-o-has-enough-projectives]]),
and therefore every object of $\mathcal O_\eta$, in particular $L(\eta)$, is
injective as well as projective in $\mathcal O_\eta$
([[def-injective-object]]). A projective object of a block is projective in
$\mathcal O$ ([[lem-block-projection-preserves-projectives]]), and an
injective object of a block is injective in $\mathcal O$ because the block
decomposition is a direct sum of abelian subcategories and the exact
projections restrict split exactness blockwise. Second, we identify a
projective-injective object
in the block $\mathcal O_\lambda$: let $E=L(\lambda+\rho)$ be the
finite-dimensional simple module of highest weight $\lambda+\rho$
([[thm-finite-dimensional-simple-modules-are-classified-by-dominant-highest-weights]])
and set
$$Q:=\operatorname{pr}_{\chi_\lambda}\bigl(E\otimes L(\eta)\bigr)\in\mathcal O_\lambda,$$
the exact central projection of [[def-translation-functor-between-o-blocks]].
Since $L(\eta)$ is projective and injective in $\mathcal O$, the tensor product
$E\otimes L(\eta)$ is projective and injective
([[lem-tensoring-a-projective-with-a-finite-dimensional-module-is-projective]]),
and its direct summand $Q$ is projective and injective in $\mathcal O$; the
general exact tensor-block biadjunction of
[[prop-translation-functors-are-exact-and-biadjoint-across-a-wall]] gives the
same conclusion with all adjoints and, by
[[lem-tensoring-a-projective-with-a-finite-dimensional-module-is-projective]],
injectivity (equivalently, $Q$ is a direct summand of a projective-injective
object, and injectivity passes to summands). Third, we compute a
one-dimensional Hom space: since $M(a)$ with $a=w_0\cdot\lambda$ is simple by
the same top-weight argument as for $\eta$ (every other highest weight in
$W\cdot a$ lies strictly above $a$ in the root order), the tensor product
$E^{*}\otimes M(a)$ has a finite Verma flag whose factors are the
$\Delta(a+\nu)$ with $\nu$ running through the weights of the dual module
$E^{*}$, by
[[lem-tensoring-with-a-finite-dimensional-module-preserves-verma-flags]]; here
$E^{*}=L(-w_0(\lambda+\rho))$ ([[prop-highest-weight-of-the-dual-representation]]).
Projecting to the central character $\chi_\eta$ retains exactly the factors
with $a+\nu\in W\cdot\eta=\{\eta\}$, that is $\nu=-w_0(\lambda+\rho)$, the
highest weight of $E^{*}$ of multiplicity one, so
$$\operatorname{pr}_{\chi_\eta}\bigl(E^{*}\otimes M(a)\bigr)=L(\eta).$$
The tensor-hom adjunction and the tensor-block adjunction now give
$$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O}(Q,L(a))\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O}(L(\eta),E^{*}\otimes M(a))\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O}(L(\eta),L(\eta))\cong\mathbb C,$$
because every homomorphism from the block-$\eta$ simple lands in the
$\chi_\eta$-summand and $L(\eta)$ is simple. Choose the nonzero, hence
surjective, element $q:Q\to L(a)$ and lift it through the projective cover
$P(a)\to L(a)$ to a map $Q\to P(a)$; its image is a submodule of $P(a)$
surjecting onto the head $L(a)$, hence is all of $P(a)$ by essentiality of a
projective cover, so the lift is surjective and splits by projectivity of
$P(a)$. Therefore $P(a)$ is a direct summand of the injective object $Q$
([[def-injective-object]]), and direct summands of injective objects are
injective, so $P=P(w_0\cdot\lambda)$ is injective. This argument uses
[[thm-bgg-verma-homomorphism-criterion]] only through the standard embedding
criterion implicit in the top-weight computations, and it does not assume the
Endomorphismensatz.

**The once-each flag.** The tensor flag of $E\otimes M(-\rho)$ has labels
$-\rho+\gamma$ for weights $\gamma$ of $E=L(\lambda+\rho)$. Projection to
$\chi_\lambda$ keeps precisely $\gamma\in W(\lambda+\rho)$, each of
multiplicity one by [[lem-weight-norm-bound-for-finite-dimensional-simple-modules]].
Thus $Q$ has each $\Delta(x\cdot\lambda)$ once. Every such Verma contains
$M(w_0\cdot\lambda)=L(a)$ by
[[lem-dominant-integral-dot-translates-embed-in-the-verma-module]]. BGG
reciprocity gives $(P(a):\Delta(x\cdot\lambda))\ge1$; the splitting
$Q=P(a)\oplus Q'$ and
[[lem-direct-summands-of-verma-filtered-objects-are-verma-filtered]] give the
opposite bound one. Hence all these multiplicities equal one, $Q'$ has
an empty flag and is zero, and $Q=P(a)$. Since $P(a)$ is projective,
$V$ is exact and $\dim VX=[X:L(a)]$ for finite-length $X$: on simples its
values are $\mathbb C$ at the head label and zero otherwise. Consequently
$\dim V\Delta(x\cdot\lambda)=1$ for every $x$. Every simple submodule of a
Verma is itself a simple Verma: its universal Verma map into that Verma is
injective. Thus the unique simple standard $L(a)$ is its only possible
socle label, and [[thm-verma-homomorphism-spaces-have-dimension-at-most-one]]
makes this socle a single copy of $L(a)$.

rows.consumer_statement_or_definition:
Assume the Axiom of Choice, inherited from the published block theory
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $S=S(\mathfrak h)$ be the symmetric algebra of
the Cartan subalgebra of [[def-bgg-category-o]], graded by $\deg\mathfrak h=2$
as fixed on this page ([[def-graded-ring-module-bimodule-and-internal-shift]],
[[def-multivariate-polynomial-ring-by-iteration]]). Let
$\mathfrak b=\mathfrak h\oplus\mathfrak n^+$ act on $S\otimes\mathbb C_\lambda$
by
$$x\cdot(s\otimes1)=xs\otimes1+\lambda(x)s\otimes1\quad(x\in\mathfrak h),\qquad x\cdot(s\otimes1)=0\quad(x\in\mathfrak n^+),$$
where for $x\in\mathfrak h$, $xs$ means multiplication by the
linear polynomial $x\in S(\mathfrak h)$; $\mathfrak n^+$ acts trivially. Put
$$M_S(\lambda):=U(\mathfrak g)\otimes_{U(\mathfrak b)}(S\otimes\mathbb C_\lambda),$$
a module over $\mathfrak g\otimes S$: the left $\mathfrak g$-action is induced,
and $S$ acts on the right by multiplication on the last factor, which commutes
with $\mathfrak g$. Specializing at a closed point $\epsilon$ of
$\operatorname{Spec} S$ gives
$$M_S(\lambda)\otimes_S\mathbb C_\epsilon\cong M(\lambda+\epsilon),$$
the Verma module of [[def-verma-module]]; this is the universal family of
Verma modules with deformation parameter $\epsilon$.

**The family.** For a localization $T$ of $S$ put
$M_T(\lambda):=M_S(\lambda)\otimes_S T$, and let $\mathcal D_T(\lambda)$ be the
full subcategory of $\mathfrak g\otimes T$-modules that are direct summands of
a finite direct sum of modules $E\otimes M_T(\lambda)$ for finite-dimensional
$\mathfrak g$-modules $E$. Write $\mathcal D_R(\lambda)$ for
$R=S_{(0)}$, the localization of $S$ at the origin of
$\operatorname{Spec} S$. The **deformed family** is the assignment
$T\mapsto\mathcal D_T(\lambda)$ together with the specialization functors
$-\otimes_T\kappa(p)$ at closed points $p$ of $\operatorname{Spec} T$, where
$\kappa(p)=T/p$ is the residue field. The image of the tautological map
$\mathfrak h\to T\to\kappa(p)$ is the parameter $\epsilon_p$, and
$M_T(\lambda)\otimes_T\kappa(p)$ is the Verma module over $\kappa(p)$ with
highest weight $\lambda+\epsilon_p$ for $\mathfrak g\otimes_{\mathbb C}\kappa(p)$.
For a complex-valued point $\epsilon:T\to\mathbb C$, this is precisely
$-\otimes_T\mathbb C_\epsilon$ and the ordinary complex Verma module
$M(\lambda+\epsilon)$. An arbitrary localization can have closed points
whose residue fields are larger than $\mathbb C$; for example,
$T=\mathbb C(t)$ has only the residue field $\mathbb C(t)$ and has no
complex-valued point. By the tensor identity for finite-dimensional modules
and the Verma flags of tensor products
([[lem-tensoring-with-a-finite-dimensional-module-preserves-verma-flags]]) the
specializations have Verma constituents over their residue fields of highest
weights $\lambda+\nu+\epsilon_p$, where $\nu$ runs through the weights of the
finite-dimensional tensor factors. At complex-valued points they can meet several
central-character blocks, whose labels are the dot-Weyl orbits through these
highest weights ([[cor-central-characters-are-dot-weyl-orbits]]); a generic
parameter is generally nonintegral, and the distinct constituent labels have distinct central characters at the
generic parameter: an equality $\lambda+\gamma+\tau+\rho=w(\lambda+\gamma'+\tau+\rho)$
as affine functions of $\tau$ forces $w=1$ by comparing linear parts,
and then $\gamma=\gamma'$ ([[cor-central-characters-are-dot-weyl-orbits]]).

**Selected components.** For a regular dominant integral source $\lambda$ as in
[[def-regular-integral-category-o-block-and-its-antidominant-weight]] and a
dot-dominant integral target $\nu$, so that $\nu+\rho$ lies in the closed
positive chamber, denote by $\mathcal D_R^{[\nu]}(\lambda)$ the component of
$\mathcal D_R(\lambda)$ whose closed fiber at the origin lies in the selected
target block $\mathcal O_\nu$ of
[[def-translation-functor-between-o-blocks]]. Finite Verma flags of the
deformed tensor products and pairwise-unit resultants of their
central-character polynomials define this component by actual central
idempotents over $R$, obtained from [[thm-chinese-remainder-theorem-for-comaximal-ideals]].
Indeed choose a linear combination $z$ of central elements separating the
finitely many distinct special characters. On each deformed Verma factor,
$z$ acts by a polynomial $c_i(\tau)$ by
[[lem-harish-chandra-projection-computes-highest-weight-scalars]], and a flag
is annihilated by $\prod_i(z-c_i(\tau))$. Group these factors by their
constant values at the origin; differences from different groups are units
in $R$, so their product polynomials are comaximal in $R[X]$. CRT gives
mutually orthogonal polynomial projectors, whose images are the selected
components and whose sum is the identity. Other central-character components remain part of the full tensor
family; thus whole-family statements and selected-block statements are
distinguished.

**Weight structure.** Write $\tau:\mathfrak h\to T$ for the tautological linear map.
Modules in $\mathcal D_T(\lambda)$ carry a **deformed weight decomposition**
$X=\bigoplus_\xi X^\xi$, where
$$X^\xi=\{m:(h-\tau(h))m=\xi(h)m\text{ for every }h\in\mathfrak h\}.$$
These are eigenmodules for $h-\tau(h)$, not ordinary complex weight spaces
for $h$. They are finite projective, hence locally free of finite rank over $T$, as follows from the PBW model of Verma modules and the
flatness of the localization
([[thm-pbw-ordered-monomial-basis-for-the-enveloping-algebra]]). The
conventions are those of [Soe90, Section 2.1]; no choice beyond the inherited
Axiom of Choice of the block theory is used.
