Every real part of a function holomorphic in a chart is harmonic ([[thm-c2-holomorphic-components-are-harmonic]]), finite constants are harmonic, and a subharmonic function is upper semicontinuous and is not identically $-\infty$ on any component of its domain ([[def-plane-subharmonic-function]], [[def-harmonic-and-subharmonic-riemann-surface-functions]]).

To use the harmonic-majorant characterization, fix a closed disc $\overline{D(a,r)}\subseteq\Omega$ and a continuous $k$ on it, harmonic on $D(a,r)$, with $k\ge f$ on the boundary. If $k<f$ somewhere, set $s:=f-k$. Then $s$ is extended-valued upper semicontinuous, is positive somewhere, and satisfies $s\le0$ on the boundary; it may equal $-\infty$. It is bounded above on the compact disc: the open sets $\{s<n\}$ for positive integers $n$ cover it, so a finite subcover and nesting give a common upper bound. Thus $M:=\sup s$ is finite and positive. For each real $b<M$, the set $E_b:=\{s\ge b\}$ is closed by [F10] and nonempty by the definition of $M$; these sets have the finite-intersection property, so compactness gives a point $z_1\in\bigcap_{b<M}E_b$, where $s(z_1)=M$. Since $s\le0$ on the boundary, $z_1$ is interior. Let $Z:=\{z\in D(a,r):s(z)=M\}$; it is nonempty and closed in the open disc by upper semicontinuity. [F2, F3]

Define $w:=u$ on $\Omega\setminus B$ and $w:=\max\{u,v\}$ on $B$. Then $w$ is upper semicontinuous on $\Omega$: at points of $B$, $w$ is a finite maximum of upper semicontinuous functions; at points of $\Omega\setminus\overline B$ it equals $u$; and at $\eta\in\partial B\cap\Omega$ the limsup of $w$ is the larger of the limsups of $u$ and of $v$ along $B$, at most $\max\{u(\eta),u(\eta)\}=u(\eta)=w(\eta)$ by the seam hypothesis. proof_uses: 13.1 **Poisson modification on the surface.** Let $B\subseteq D$ be a coordinate disc with $\overline B\subseteq D$, written $B=\theta^{-1}(D(w_0,r))$ for a chart $\theta$ and an open disc $D(w_0,r)$ whose closure lies in $\theta(\operatorname{dom}\theta\cap D)$. For $v\in\mathcal P$ let $P_\theta v$ denote the plane Poisson modification of $v_\theta$ on the disc $D(w_0,r)$, which is well defined by [F4], and define the surface modification $$\tilde v:=\begin{cases}P_\theta v\circ\theta & \text{on }B,\\ v & \text{on }D\setminus B.\end{cases}$$ Then $\tilde v$ is harmonic on $B$ and $\tilde v\ge v$ on $B$, because the plane modification has these properties and harmonicity and the inequality are read in the chart $\theta$; and $\limsup_{z\to\eta,\,z\in B}\tilde v(z)\le v(\eta)$ for every $\eta\in\partial B$: if $\varphi_n\downarrow v_\theta$ is the decreasing sequence of continuous boundary approximants used to define the modification and $h_n$ are their harmonic Poisson extensions, then $P_\theta v=\inf_nh_n\le h_n$ on the disc, so $\limsup_{z\to\eta,\,z\in B}\tilde v(z)\le\limsup h_n(\theta(z))=\varphi_n(\theta(\eta))$ for every $n$, and letting $n\to\infty$ gives the bound $v(\eta)$. [F4, step 12.1]

15.1 **Monotonicity and directedness.** If $v,w\in\mathcal P$ satisfy $v\le w$ on $D$, then $\tilde v\le\tilde w$ on $B$: choose decreasing continuous approximants $\alpha_n\downarrow v_\theta$ and $\beta_n\downarrow w_\theta$ on the circle $\partial D(w_0,r)$ and set $\gamma_n:=\min\{\alpha_n,\beta_n\}$; then the $\gamma_n$ are continuous and decrease to $\min\{v_\theta,w_\theta\}=v_\theta$, while $\gamma_n\le\beta_n$, so positivity of the Poisson kernel [F4] gives $P[\gamma_n]\le P[\beta_n]$ on $D(w_0,r)$ and hence $P_\theta v=\inf_nP[\gamma_n]\le\inf_nP[\beta_n]=P_\theta w$, that is, $\tilde v\le\tilde w$. Also, if $v,w\in\mathcal P$ then $t:=\max\{v,w\}\in\mathcal P$: it is subharmonic on $D$ since both are, and at each $\eta\in\partial D$ its limsup is at most $\max\{\limsup v,\limsup w\}\le\varphi(\eta)$. By monotonicity $\tilde t\ge\tilde v,\tilde w$ on $B$. [F3, F4, step 14.1]

16.1 **Harnack control.** Define $h_*(q):=\sup\{\tilde v(q):v\in\mathcal P\}$ on $B$. Every $\tilde v$ is harmonic on $B$ and satisfies $\tilde v\le U\le H$ on $B$, so $h_*\le H$ on $B$; and $h_*\ge m$ since $m\in\mathcal P$ and $\tilde m\ge m$. Fix $a\in B$ and $\varepsilon>0$. Since $h_*(a)$ is a real number and is the supremum of the values $\tilde v(a)$, there is $v\in\mathcal P$ with $\tilde v(a)>h_*(a)-\varepsilon$. For any $w\in\mathcal P$ put $t:=\max\{v,w\}$; then $\tilde t\ge\tilde v,\tilde w$ and $$0\le(\tilde t-\tilde v)(a)\le h_*(a)-\tilde v(a)<\varepsilon,$$ while $\tilde t-\tilde v$ is harmonic and nonnegative on $B$ by step 15.1. [F4, step 12.1, step 14.1, step 15.1, choose]

17.1 $h_*$ is harmonic on $B$. Choose a chart subdisc $\theta^{-1}(D(a,\rho))\subseteq B$ centred at the point $a$ of step 16.1, and fix $r<\rho$. For $\varepsilon>0$ choose $v$ as in step 16.1 and let $w\in\mathcal P$ be arbitrary. The nonnegative harmonic function $u:=\tilde t-\tilde v$ on $B$ satisfies $u(a)<\varepsilon$, so Harnack's inequality [F4] applied on the disc $D(a,\rho)$ gives $$0\le\tilde t(z)-\tilde v(z)=u(z)\le\frac{\rho+r}{\rho-r}\,u(a)<C\varepsilon \qquad(z\in\overline{D(a,r)}),$$ with $C:=(\rho+r)/(\rho-r)$ independent of $w$. Hence $\tilde w\le\tilde v+C\varepsilon$ on $\overline{D(a,r)}$ for every $w\in\mathcal P$, and taking the supremum over $w$ gives $h_*-\tilde v\le C\varepsilon$ on $\overline{D(a,r)}$, while $h_*\ge\tilde v$. So for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is a function harmonic on $B$ that approximates $h_*$ uniformly on $\overline{D(a,r)}$ within $C\varepsilon$; in particular $h_*(b)=\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}k_\varepsilon(b)$ where $k_\varepsilon$ is such an approximant, and the circle average of $h_*$ over $\partial D(b,s)$ differs from $h_*(b)$ by at most $2C\varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon>0$, hence equals it. Thus $h_*$ satisfies the local mean-value property on $B$ and is continuous, so it is harmonic on $B$ by the converse of the mean-value property [F4]. [F4, step 16.1]

17.2 $h_*=H$ on $B$. Fix $a\in B$ and $\varepsilon>0$, and choose $D(a,\rho)\subseteq\theta(B)$ centred at $\theta(a)$, denoting this coordinate again by $a$. Choose $0<r<\rho$ so small that $$\left(\frac{\rho+r}{\rho-r}-1\right)(M-H(a)+2\varepsilon)<\varepsilon.$$ By the definition of the regularization in step 12.1, there is $z\in D(a,r)$ with $U(z)>H(a)-\varepsilon$, and then some $v\in\mathcal P$ has $v(z)>U(z)-\varepsilon>H(a)-2\varepsilon$. Thus $\tilde v(z)\ge v(z)>H(a)-2\varepsilon$. The nonnegative function $k:=M-\tilde v$ is harmonic on $B$ by step 14.1. Harnack's inequality [F4], applied at the actual distance $|z-a|<r$, gives $$k(a)\le\frac{\rho+|z-a|}{\rho-|z-a|}k(z)\le\frac{\rho+r}{\rho-r}(M-H(a)+2\varepsilon)<M-H(a)+3\varepsilon.$$ Hence $h_*(a)\ge\tilde v(a)>H(a)-3\varepsilon$. Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ gives $h_*(a)\ge H(a)$; the reverse inequality is step 16.1. [F4, step 12.1, step 14.1, step 16.1]

Restrictions of subharmonic functions to open subsets are subharmonic, and on a plane domain: nonnegative linear combinations and finite maxima of subharmonic functions are subharmonic ([[lem-positive-linear-combinations-and-finite-maxima-preserve-subharmonicity]]); a subharmonic function attaining a finite interior maximum on a domain is constant there ([[thm-maximum-principle-for-plane-subharmonic-functions]]); the upper-semicontinuous regularization of the supremum of a locally bounded-above family of subharmonic functions is subharmonic ([[thm-upper-envelope-theorem-for-plane-subharmonic-functions]]); subharmonic pieces glue across a seam when the inside limsup is at most the outside value ([[lem-gluing-lemma-for-plane-subharmonic-functions]]); subharmonicity is equivalent to the harmonic comparison on all compactly contained discs ([[thm-harmonic-majorant-characterization-of-plane-subharmonicity]]); and biholomorphic change of coordinates preserves subharmonicity in both directions ([[lem-biholomorphic-invariance-of-plane-subharmonicity]]).
proof_uses: 1.2 **Locality of plane subharmonicity.** Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C$ be a plane domain and let $f:\Omega\to[-\infty,\infty)$ be upper semicontinuous, not identically $-\infty$ on any component of $\Omega$, and subharmonic near each of its points. To use the harmonic-majorant characterization, fix a closed disc $\overline{D(a,r)}\subseteq\Omega$ and a continuous $k$ on it, harmonic on $D(a,r)$, with $k\ge f$ on the boundary. If $k<f$ somewhere, set $s:=f-k$. Then $s$ is extended-valued upper semicontinuous, is positive somewhere, and satisfies $s\le0$ on the boundary; it may equal $-\infty$. It is bounded above on the compact disc: the open sets $\{s<n\}$ for positive integers $n$ cover it, so a finite subcover and nesting give a common upper bound. Thus $M:=\sup s$ is finite and positive. For each real $b<M$, the set $E_b:=\{s\ge b\}$ is closed by [F10] and nonempty by the definition of $M$; these sets have the finite-intersection property, so compactness gives a point $z_1\in\bigcap_{b<M}E_b$, where $s(z_1)=M$. Since $s\le0$ on the boundary, $z_1$ is interior. Let $Z:=\{z\in D(a,r):s(z)=M\}$; it is nonempty and closed in the open disc by upper semicontinuity. [F2, F3]

2.2 $Z$ is open in $D(a,r)$: given $z\in Z$, choose $\rho>0$ with $\overline{D(z,\rho)}\subseteq D(a,r)$ and with $D(z,\rho)$ contained in a neighbourhood of $z$ on which $f$ is subharmonic. On the disc $D(z,\rho)$ the function $f$ is subharmonic and $-k$ is subharmonic (it is harmonic), so $s=f+(-k)$ is subharmonic on $D(z,\rho)$; it attains the maximum $M$ at the interior point $z$ and therefore is constant equal to $M$ on $D(z,\rho)$ by the strong maximum principle, that is, $D(z,\rho)\subseteq Z$. Since $D(a,r)$ is connected and $Z\neq\varnothing$ is both open and closed in it, $Z=D(a,r)$ and $s\equiv M$ on the disc. [F3, step 1.2]

3.2 Step 2.2 leads to a contradiction, completing step 1.2: for $b\in\partial D(a,r)$ the upper semicontinuity of $s$ at $b$ (as a function defined on a neighbourhood of $\overline{D(a,r)}$) gives $s(b)\ge\limsup_{D(a,r)\ni z\to b}s(z)=M>0$, contradicting $s\le0$ on the boundary circle. Hence no such counterexample exists, the harmonic comparison of step 1.2 always holds, and the harmonic-majorant characterization makes $f$ subharmonic on $\Omega$. [F3, step 2.2]

4.3 **Gluing subharmonic functions on a surface.** Let $\Omega\subseteq X$ be open, let $u$ be subharmonic on $\Omega$, let $B\subseteq\Omega$ be any open subset, let $v$ be subharmonic on $B$, and assume $\limsup_{z\to\eta,\,z\in B}v(z)\le u(\eta)$ for every $\eta\in\partial B\cap\Omega$. Define $w:=u$ on $\Omega\setminus B$ and $w:=\max\{u,v\}$ on $B$. Then $w$ is upper semicontinuous on $\Omega$: at points of $B$, $w$ is a finite maximum of upper semicontinuous functions; at points of $\Omega\setminus\overline B$ it equals $u$; and at $\eta\in\partial B\cap\Omega$ the limsup of $w$ is the larger of the limsups of $u$ and of $v$ along $B$, at most $\max\{u(\eta),u(\eta)\}=u(\eta)=w(\eta)$ by the seam hypothesis. Also $w\ge u$, and $u$ is not identically $-\infty$ on any component of $\Omega$, so neither is $w$. [F2, F3, step 3.2, construct]

5.2 For every point $p\in\Omega$ there is a chart $\theta$ with $p$ in its domain such that the chart expression $w_\theta$ is plane subharmonic on a neighbourhood of $\theta(p)$. If $p\notin\overline B$, take a chart whose domain is contained in $\Omega\setminus\overline B$; then $w_\theta=u_\theta$ is plane subharmonic by [F2]. If $p\in B$, take a chart with domain contained in $B$; then $w_\theta=\max\{u_\theta,v_\theta\}$ is a finite maximum of plane subharmonic functions, hence plane subharmonic by [F3]. If $p\in\partial B\cap\Omega$, take a coordinate-disc neighbourhood $T$ of $p$ contained in $\Omega$, with chart $\theta:T\to D(0,r)$. Apply the plane gluing lemma [F3] with ambient domain $\theta(T)$ and open inside set $\theta(T\cap B)$. The chart expression of $u$ is subharmonic on $\theta(T)$, that of $v$ is subharmonic on each component of $\theta(T\cap B)$, and every seam point inside $\theta(T)$ corresponds to a point of $\partial B\cap T$, where step 4.3 supplies the limsup bound. Thus $w_\theta$ is subharmonic near $\theta(p)$. [F2, F3, step 4.3, cases]

6.3 $w$ is subharmonic on $\Omega$. Let $\theta$ be any chart with $\operatorname{dom}\theta\cap\Omega\neq\varnothing$. By step 5.2 and the biholomorphic invariance of subharmonicity [F3], every point of $\theta(\operatorname{dom}\theta\cap\Omega)$ has a plane neighbourhood on which $w_\theta$ is subharmonic: for a point $\theta(p)$, use the chart $\theta_p$ of step 5.2 and write $w_\theta=w_{\theta_p}\circ(\theta_p\circ\theta^{-1})$ on the overlap, a composition of the plane subharmonic function $w_{\theta_p}$ with the biholomorphism $\theta_p\circ\theta^{-1}$ between plane domains. Moreover $w_\theta$ is upper semicontinuous and is not identically $-\infty$ on any component, because these properties hold for $w$ by step 4.3 and are read in charts. By the locality of plane subharmonicity, step 3.2, applied separately to each component, $w_\theta$ is plane subharmonic on every component of $\theta(\operatorname{dom}\theta\cap\Omega)$. As $\theta$ was an arbitrary chart, $w$ is subharmonic on $\Omega$. [F2, F3, step 3.2, step 5.2]

9.1 **Maximum principle.** Let $v$ be subharmonic on $D$ and let $B\in\mathbb R$ satisfy $\limsup_{q\to\eta,\,q\in D}v(q)\le B$ for every $\eta\in\partial D$. Then $v\le B$ on $D$. For any real $b>B$, the set $E_b:=\{q\in D:v(q)\ge b\}$ is closed in $\overline D$: it is closed inside $D$ by upper semicontinuity, and its closure cannot meet $\partial D$ by the boundary limsup bound. Thus $E_b$ is compact. If $s:=\sup_Dv=+\infty$, the nonempty nested compact sets $E_n$ for integers $n>B$ have the finite-intersection property, so some point satisfies $v(q)\ge n$ for every such $n$, impossible because subharmonic functions have no $+\infty$ values. Hence $s<+\infty$. If $s>B$, the nested nonempty compact sets $E_b$ for $B<b<s$ again have the finite-intersection property; a point in their intersection has $v(q)\ge b$ for every $b<s$, so $v(q)=s$. Since $s>B$, the point is interior, and the strong maximum principle forces $v\equiv s$ on connected $D$. Taking any boundary point then gives $s=\limsup_{q\to\eta}v(q)\le B$, a contradiction. Therefore $s\le B$. [F2, F3, F9, step 8.1]

10.1 In the situation of step 9.1 the maximum set $\{q\in D:v(q)=s\}$ is open: for $q$ in it, take a chart $\theta$ around $q$ with $\theta(q)=0$ and $\theta(\operatorname{dom}\theta\cap D)$ a plane domain; the chart expression $v_\theta$ is plane subharmonic and attains the finite maximum $s$ at the interior point $0$, so by the strong maximum principle $v_\theta$ is constant on $\theta(\operatorname{dom}\theta\cap D)$ and $v$ is constant on a neighbourhood of $q$. The set is also closed in $D$, because it is $D\cap\{v\ge s\}$ and superlevel sets of the upper semicontinuous function $v$ are closed. Since $D$ is connected the set is all of $D$, so $v\equiv s>B$ on $D$. But $\partial D\neq\varnothing$: otherwise $D$ would be open and closed in the connected space $X$, forcing $D=X$ and contradicting compactness of $\overline D$. At any $\eta\in\partial D$ the boundary hypothesis then gives the contradiction $s=\limsup_{q\to\eta}v(q)\le B$, so $s\le B$ and the maximum principle holds for all $v$. [F2, F3, F9, step 9.1, cases]

12.1 **The envelope.** Let $H$ be the upper-semicontinuous regularization of $U$, $H(x):=\limsup_{y\to x,\,y\in D}U(y)$, equivalently the least upper semicontinuous majorant of $U$ [F5]. Then $U\le H$ and, since $m\le U\le M$, also $m\le H\le M$. Moreover $H$ is subharmonic on $D$: for every chart $\theta$ the family of plane subharmonic functions $\{v_\theta:v\in\mathcal P\}$ on the plane domain $\theta(\operatorname{dom}\theta\cap D)$ is nonempty and bounded above by $M$, its pointwise supremum is $U_\theta$ and its upper-semicontinuous regularization is $H_\theta$ (regularization is a local, hence chart-invariant, operation); so the upper envelope theorem [F3] makes $H_\theta$ plane subharmonic. As $\theta$ was arbitrary, $H$ is subharmonic on $D$. [F3, F5, step 11.1]

15.1 **Monotonicity and directedness.** If $v,w\in\mathcal P$ satisfy $v\le w$ on $D$, then $\tilde v\le\tilde w$ on $B$: choose decreasing continuous approximants $\alpha_n\downarrow v_\theta$ and $\beta_n\downarrow w_\theta$ on the circle $\partial D(w_0,r)$ and set $\gamma_n:=\min\{\alpha_n,\beta_n\}$; then the $\gamma_n$ are continuous and decrease to $\min\{v_\theta,w_\theta\}=v_\theta$, while $\gamma_n\le\beta_n$, so positivity of the Poisson kernel [F4] gives $P[\gamma_n]\le P[\beta_n]$ on $D(w_0,r)$ and hence $P_\theta v=\inf_nP[\gamma_n]\le\inf_nP[\beta_n]=P_\theta w$, that is, $\tilde v\le\tilde w$. Also, if $v,w\in\mathcal P$ then $t:=\max\{v,w\}\in\mathcal P$: it is subharmonic on $D$ since both are, and at each $\eta\in\partial D$ its limsup is at most $\max\{\limsup v,\limsup w\}\le\varphi(\eta)$. By monotonicity $\tilde t\ge\tilde v,\tilde w$ on $B$. [F3, F4, step 14.1]

If $k<f$ somewhere, set $s:=f-k$. Then $s$ is extended-valued upper semicontinuous, is positive somewhere, and satisfies $s\le0$ on the boundary; it may equal $-\infty$. proof_uses: 1.2 **Locality of plane subharmonicity.** Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C$ be a plane domain and let $f:\Omega\to[-\infty,\infty)$ be upper semicontinuous, not identically $-\infty$ on any component of $\Omega$, and subharmonic near each of its points. To use the harmonic-majorant characterization, fix a closed disc $\overline{D(a,r)}\subseteq\Omega$ and a continuous $k$ on it, harmonic on $D(a,r)$, with $k\ge f$ on the boundary. If $k<f$ somewhere, set $s:=f-k$. Then $s$ is extended-valued upper semicontinuous, is positive somewhere, and satisfies $s\le0$ on the boundary; it may equal $-\infty$. It is bounded above on the compact disc: the open sets $\{s<n\}$ for positive integers $n$ cover it, so a finite subcover and nesting give a common upper bound. Thus $M:=\sup s$ is finite and positive. For each real $b<M$, the set $E_b:=\{s\ge b\}$ is closed by [F10] and nonempty by the definition of $M$; these sets have the finite-intersection property, so compactness gives a point $z_1\in\bigcap_{b<M}E_b$, where $s(z_1)=M$. Since $s\le0$ on the boundary, $z_1$ is interior. Let $Z:=\{z\in D(a,r):s(z)=M\}$; it is nonempty and closed in the open disc by upper semicontinuity. [F2, F3]

2.2 $Z$ is open in $D(a,r)$: given $z\in Z$, choose $\rho>0$ with $\overline{D(z,\rho)}\subseteq D(a,r)$ and with $D(z,\rho)$ contained in a neighbourhood of $z$ on which $f$ is subharmonic. On the disc $D(z,\rho)$ the function $f$ is subharmonic and $-k$ is subharmonic (it is harmonic), so $s=f+(-k)$ is subharmonic on $D(z,\rho)$; it attains the maximum $M$ at the interior point $z$ and therefore is constant equal to $M$ on $D(z,\rho)$ by the strong maximum principle, that is, $D(z,\rho)\subseteq Z$. Since $D(a,r)$ is connected and $Z\neq\varnothing$ is both open and closed in it, $Z=D(a,r)$ and $s\equiv M$ on the disc. [F3, step 1.2]

3.2 Step 2.2 leads to a contradiction, completing step 1.2: for $b\in\partial D(a,r)$ the upper semicontinuity of $s$ at $b$ (as a function defined on a neighbourhood of $\overline{D(a,r)}$) gives $s(b)\ge\limsup_{D(a,r)\ni z\to b}s(z)=M>0$, contradicting $s\le0$ on the boundary circle. Hence no such counterexample exists, the harmonic comparison of step 1.2 always holds, and the harmonic-majorant characterization makes $f$ subharmonic on $\Omega$. [F3, step 2.2]

Define $w:=u$ on $\Omega\setminus B$ and $w:=\max\{u,v\}$ on $B$. Also $w\ge u$, and $u$ is not identically $-\infty$ on any component of $\Omega$, so neither is $w$. [F2, F3, step 3.2, construct]

5.2 For every point $p\in\Omega$ there is a chart $\theta$ with $p$ in its domain such that the chart expression $w_\theta$ is plane subharmonic on a neighbourhood of $\theta(p)$. If $p\notin\overline B$, take a chart whose domain is contained in $\Omega\setminus\overline B$; then $w_\theta=u_\theta$ is plane subharmonic by [F2]. If $p\in B$, take a chart with domain contained in $B$; then $w_\theta=\max\{u_\theta,v_\theta\}$ is a finite maximum of plane subharmonic functions, hence plane subharmonic by [F3]. If $p\in\partial B\cap\Omega$, take a coordinate-disc neighbourhood $T$ of $p$ contained in $\Omega$, with chart $\theta:T\to D(0,r)$. Apply the plane gluing lemma [F3] with ambient domain $\theta(T)$ and open inside set $\theta(T\cap B)$. The chart expression of $u$ is subharmonic on $\theta(T)$, that of $v$ is subharmonic on each component of $\theta(T\cap B)$, and every seam point inside $\theta(T)$ corresponds to a point of $\partial B\cap T$, where step 4.3 supplies the limsup bound. Thus $w_\theta$ is subharmonic near $\theta(p)$. [F2, F3, step 4.3, cases]

6.3 $w$ is subharmonic on $\Omega$. Let $\theta$ be any chart with $\operatorname{dom}\theta\cap\Omega\neq\varnothing$. By step 5.2 and the biholomorphic invariance of subharmonicity [F3], every point of $\theta(\operatorname{dom}\theta\cap\Omega)$ has a plane neighbourhood on which $w_\theta$ is subharmonic: for a point $\theta(p)$, use the chart $\theta_p$ of step 5.2 and write $w_\theta=w_{\theta_p}\circ(\theta_p\circ\theta^{-1})$ on the overlap, a composition of the plane subharmonic function $w_{\theta_p}$ with the biholomorphism $\theta_p\circ\theta^{-1}$ between plane domains. Moreover $w_\theta$ is upper semicontinuous and is not identically $-\infty$ on any component, because these properties hold for $w$ by step 4.3 and are read in charts. By the locality of plane subharmonicity, step 3.2, applied separately to each component, $w_\theta$ is plane subharmonic on every component of $\theta(\operatorname{dom}\theta\cap\Omega)$. As $\theta$ was an arbitrary chart, $w$ is subharmonic on $\Omega$. [F2, F3, step 3.2, step 5.2]

9.1 **Maximum principle.** Let $v$ be subharmonic on $D$ and let $B\in\mathbb R$ satisfy $\limsup_{q\to\eta,\,q\in D}v(q)\le B$ for every $\eta\in\partial D$. Then $v\le B$ on $D$. For any real $b>B$, the set $E_b:=\{q\in D:v(q)\ge b\}$ is closed in $\overline D$: it is closed inside $D$ by upper semicontinuity, and its closure cannot meet $\partial D$ by the boundary limsup bound. Thus $E_b$ is compact. If $s:=\sup_Dv=+\infty$, the nonempty nested compact sets $E_n$ for integers $n>B$ have the finite-intersection property, so some point satisfies $v(q)\ge n$ for every such $n$, impossible because subharmonic functions have no $+\infty$ values. Hence $s<+\infty$. If $s>B$, the nested nonempty compact sets $E_b$ for $B<b<s$ again have the finite-intersection property; a point in their intersection has $v(q)\ge b$ for every $b<s$, so $v(q)=s$. Since $s>B$, the point is interior, and the strong maximum principle forces $v\equiv s$ on connected $D$. Taking any boundary point then gives $s=\limsup_{q\to\eta}v(q)\le B$, a contradiction. 16.1 **Harnack control.** Define $h_*(q):=\sup\{\tilde v(q):v\in\mathcal P\}$ on $B$. For $v\in\mathcal P$ let $P_\theta v$ denote the plane Poisson modification of $v_\theta$ on the disc $D(w_0,r)$, which is well defined by [F4], and define the surface modification $$\tilde v:=\begin{cases}P_\theta v\circ\theta & \text{on }B,\\ v & \text{on }D\setminus B.\end{cases}$$ Then $\tilde v$ is harmonic on $B$ and $\tilde v\ge v$ on $B$, because the plane modification has these properties and harmonicity and the inequality are read in the chart $\theta$; and $\limsup_{z\to\eta,\,z\in B}\tilde v(z)\le v(\eta)$ for every $\eta\in\partial B$: if $\varphi_n\downarrow v_\theta$ is the decreasing sequence of continuous boundary approximants used to define the modification and $h_n$ are their harmonic Poisson extensions, then $P_\theta v=\inf_nh_n\le h_n$ on the disc, so $\limsup_{z\to\eta,\,z\in B}\tilde v(z)\le\limsup h_n(\theta(z))=\varphi_n(\theta(\eta))$ for every $n$, and letting $n\to\infty$ gives the bound $v(\eta)$. [F4, step 12.1]

15.1 **Monotonicity and directedness.** If $v,w\in\mathcal P$ satisfy $v\le w$ on $D$, then $\tilde v\le\tilde w$ on $B$: choose decreasing continuous approximants $\alpha_n\downarrow v_\theta$ and $\beta_n\downarrow w_\theta$ on the circle $\partial D(w_0,r)$ and set $\gamma_n:=\min\{\alpha_n,\beta_n\}$; then the $\gamma_n$ are continuous and decrease to $\min\{v_\theta,w_\theta\}=v_\theta$, while $\gamma_n\le\beta_n$, so positivity of the Poisson kernel [F4] gives $P[\gamma_n]\le P[\beta_n]$ on $D(w_0,r)$ and hence $P_\theta v=\inf_nP[\gamma_n]\le\inf_nP[\beta_n]=P_\theta w$, that is, $\tilde v\le\tilde w$. Also, if $v,w\in\mathcal P$ then $t:=\max\{v,w\}\in\mathcal P$: it is subharmonic on $D$ since both are, and at each $\eta\in\partial D$ its limsup is at most $\max\{\limsup v,\limsup w\}\le\varphi(\eta)$. By monotonicity $\tilde t\ge\tilde v,\tilde w$ on $B$. [F3, F4, step 14.1]

16.1 **Harnack control.** Define $h_*(q):=\sup\{\tilde v(q):v\in\mathcal P\}$ on $B$. Every $\tilde v$ is harmonic on $B$ and satisfies $\tilde v\le U\le H$ on $B$, so $h_*\le H$ on $B$; and $h_*\ge m$ since $m\in\mathcal P$ and $\tilde m\ge m$. Fix $a\in B$ and $\varepsilon>0$. Since $h_*(a)$ is a real number and is the supremum of the values $\tilde v(a)$, there is $v\in\mathcal P$ with $\tilde v(a)>h_*(a)-\varepsilon$. For any $w\in\mathcal P$ put $t:=\max\{v,w\}$; then $\tilde t\ge\tilde v,\tilde w$ and $$0\le(\tilde t-\tilde v)(a)\le h_*(a)-\tilde v(a)<\varepsilon,$$ while $\tilde t-\tilde v$ is harmonic and nonnegative on $B$ by step 15.1. [F4, step 12.1, step 14.1, step 15.1, choose]

17.1 $h_*$ is harmonic on $B$. Choose a chart subdisc $\theta^{-1}(D(a,\rho))\subseteq B$ centred at the point $a$ of step 16.1, and fix $r<\rho$. For $\varepsilon>0$ choose $v$ as in step 16.1 and let $w\in\mathcal P$ be arbitrary. The nonnegative harmonic function $u:=\tilde t-\tilde v$ on $B$ satisfies $u(a)<\varepsilon$, so Harnack's inequality [F4] applied on the disc $D(a,\rho)$ gives $$0\le\tilde t(z)-\tilde v(z)=u(z)\le\frac{\rho+r}{\rho-r}\,u(a)<C\varepsilon \qquad(z\in\overline{D(a,r)}),$$ with $C:=(\rho+r)/(\rho-r)$ independent of $w$. Hence $\tilde w\le\tilde v+C\varepsilon$ on $\overline{D(a,r)}$ for every $w\in\mathcal P$, and taking the supremum over $w$ gives $h_*-\tilde v\le C\varepsilon$ on $\overline{D(a,r)}$, while $h_*\ge\tilde v$. So for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is a function harmonic on $B$ that approximates $h_*$ uniformly on $\overline{D(a,r)}$ within $C\varepsilon$; in particular $h_*(b)=\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}k_\varepsilon(b)$ where $k_\varepsilon$ is such an approximant, and the circle average of $h_*$ over $\partial D(b,s)$ differs from $h_*(b)$ by at most $2C\varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon>0$, hence equals it. Thus $h_*$ satisfies the local mean-value property on $B$ and is continuous, so it is harmonic on $B$ by the converse of the mean-value property [F4]. [F4, step 16.1]

17.2 $h_*=H$ on $B$. Fix $a\in B$ and $\varepsilon>0$, and choose $D(a,\rho)\subseteq\theta(B)$ centred at $\theta(a)$, denoting this coordinate again by $a$. Choose $0<r<\rho$ so small that $$\left(\frac{\rho+r}{\rho-r}-1\right)(M-H(a)+2\varepsilon)<\varepsilon.$$ By the definition of the regularization in step 12.1, there is $z\in D(a,r)$ with $U(z)>H(a)-\varepsilon$, and then some $v\in\mathcal P$ has $v(z)>U(z)-\varepsilon>H(a)-2\varepsilon$. Thus $\tilde v(z)\ge v(z)>H(a)-2\varepsilon$. The nonnegative function $k:=M-\tilde v$ is harmonic on $B$ by step 14.1. Harnack's inequality [F4], applied at the actual distance $|z-a|<r$, gives $$k(a)\le\frac{\rho+|z-a|}{\rho-|z-a|}k(z)\le\frac{\rho+r}{\rho-r}(M-H(a)+2\varepsilon)<M-H(a)+3\varepsilon.$$ Hence $h_*(a)\ge\tilde v(a)>H(a)-3\varepsilon$. Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ gives $h_*(a)\ge H(a)$; the reverse inequality is step 16.1. [F4, step 12.1, step 14.1, step 16.1]

cited_passages: [F3] Plane subharmonic toolkit. Restrictions of subharmonic functions to open subsets are subharmonic, and on a plane domain: nonnegative linear combinations and finite maxima of subharmonic functions are subharmonic ([[lem-positive-linear-combinations-and-finite-maxima-preserve-subharmonicity]]); a subharmonic function attaining a finite interior maximum on a domain is constant there ([[thm-maximum-principle-for-plane-subharmonic-functions]]); the upper-semicontinuous regularization of the supremum of a locally bounded-above family of subharmonic functions is subharmonic ([[thm-upper-envelope-theorem-for-plane-subharmonic-functions]]); subharmonic pieces glue across a seam when the inside limsup is at most the outside value ([[lem-gluing-lemma-for-plane-subharmonic-functions]]); subharmonicity is equivalent to the harmonic comparison on all compactly contained discs ([[thm-harmonic-majorant-characterization-of-plane-subharmonicity]]); and biholomorphic change of coordinates preserves subharmonicity in both directions ([[lem-biholomorphic-invariance-of-plane-subharmonicity]]).
proof_uses: 1.2 **Locality of plane subharmonicity.** Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C$ be a plane domain and let $f:\Omega\to[-\infty,\infty)$ be upper semicontinuous, not identically $-\infty$ on any component of $\Omega$, and subharmonic near each of its points. To use the harmonic-majorant characterization, fix a closed disc $\overline{D(a,r)}\subseteq\Omega$ and a continuous $k$ on it, harmonic on $D(a,r)$, with $k\ge f$ on the boundary. If $k<f$ somewhere, set $s:=f-k$. Then $s$ is extended-valued upper semicontinuous, is positive somewhere, and satisfies $s\le0$ on the boundary; it may equal $-\infty$. It is bounded above on the compact disc: the open sets $\{s<n\}$ for positive integers $n$ cover it, so a finite subcover and nesting give a common upper bound. Thus $M:=\sup s$ is finite and positive. For each real $b<M$, the set $E_b:=\{s\ge b\}$ is closed by [F10] and nonempty by the definition of $M$; these sets have the finite-intersection property, so compactness gives a point $z_1\in\bigcap_{b<M}E_b$, where $s(z_1)=M$. Since $s\le0$ on the boundary, $z_1$ is interior. Let $Z:=\{z\in D(a,r):s(z)=M\}$; it is nonempty and closed in the open disc by upper semicontinuity. [F2, F3]

2.2 $Z$ is open in $D(a,r)$: given $z\in Z$, choose $\rho>0$ with $\overline{D(z,\rho)}\subseteq D(a,r)$ and with $D(z,\rho)$ contained in a neighbourhood of $z$ on which $f$ is subharmonic. On the disc $D(z,\rho)$ the function $f$ is subharmonic and $-k$ is subharmonic (it is harmonic), so $s=f+(-k)$ is subharmonic on $D(z,\rho)$; it attains the maximum $M$ at the interior point $z$ and therefore is constant equal to $M$ on $D(z,\rho)$ by the strong maximum principle, that is, $D(z,\rho)\subseteq Z$. Since $D(a,r)$ is connected and $Z\neq\varnothing$ is both open and closed in it, $Z=D(a,r)$ and $s\equiv M$ on the disc. [F3, step 1.2]

3.2 Step 2.2 leads to a contradiction, completing step 1.2: for $b\in\partial D(a,r)$ the upper semicontinuity of $s$ at $b$ (as a function defined on a neighbourhood of $\overline{D(a,r)}$) gives $s(b)\ge\limsup_{D(a,r)\ni z\to b}s(z)=M>0$, contradicting $s\le0$ on the boundary circle. Hence no such counterexample exists, the harmonic comparison of step 1.2 always holds, and the harmonic-majorant characterization makes $f$ subharmonic on $\Omega$. [F3, step 2.2]

4.3 **Gluing subharmonic functions on a surface.** Let $\Omega\subseteq X$ be open, let $u$ be subharmonic on $\Omega$, let $B\subseteq\Omega$ be any open subset, let $v$ be subharmonic on $B$, and assume $\limsup_{z\to\eta,\,z\in B}v(z)\le u(\eta)$ for every $\eta\in\partial B\cap\Omega$. Define $w:=u$ on $\Omega\setminus B$ and $w:=\max\{u,v\}$ on $B$. Then $w$ is upper semicontinuous on $\Omega$: at points of $B$, $w$ is a finite maximum of upper semicontinuous functions; at points of $\Omega\setminus\overline B$ it equals $u$; and at $\eta\in\partial B\cap\Omega$ the limsup of $w$ is the larger of the limsups of $u$ and of $v$ along $B$, at most $\max\{u(\eta),u(\eta)\}=u(\eta)=w(\eta)$ by the seam hypothesis. Also $w\ge u$, and $u$ is not identically $-\infty$ on any component of $\Omega$, so neither is $w$. [F2, F3, step 3.2, construct]

5.2 For every point $p\in\Omega$ there is a chart $\theta$ with $p$ in its domain such that the chart expression $w_\theta$ is plane subharmonic on a neighbourhood of $\theta(p)$. If $p\notin\overline B$, take a chart whose domain is contained in $\Omega\setminus\overline B$; then $w_\theta=u_\theta$ is plane subharmonic by [F2]. If $p\in B$, take a chart with domain contained in $B$; then $w_\theta=\max\{u_\theta,v_\theta\}$ is a finite maximum of plane subharmonic functions, hence plane subharmonic by [F3]. If $p\in\partial B\cap\Omega$, take a coordinate-disc neighbourhood $T$ of $p$ contained in $\Omega$, with chart $\theta:T\to D(0,r)$. Apply the plane gluing lemma [F3] with ambient domain $\theta(T)$ and open inside set $\theta(T\cap B)$. The chart expression of $u$ is subharmonic on $\theta(T)$, that of $v$ is subharmonic on each component of $\theta(T\cap B)$, and every seam point inside $\theta(T)$ corresponds to a point of $\partial B\cap T$, where step 4.3 supplies the limsup bound. Thus $w_\theta$ is subharmonic near $\theta(p)$. [F2, F3, step 4.3, cases]

6.3 $w$ is subharmonic on $\Omega$. Let $\theta$ be any chart with $\operatorname{dom}\theta\cap\Omega\neq\varnothing$. By step 5.2 and the biholomorphic invariance of subharmonicity [F3], every point of $\theta(\operatorname{dom}\theta\cap\Omega)$ has a plane neighbourhood on which $w_\theta$ is subharmonic: for a point $\theta(p)$, use the chart $\theta_p$ of step 5.2 and write $w_\theta=w_{\theta_p}\circ(\theta_p\circ\theta^{-1})$ on the overlap, a composition of the plane subharmonic function $w_{\theta_p}$ with the biholomorphism $\theta_p\circ\theta^{-1}$ between plane domains. Moreover $w_\theta$ is upper semicontinuous and is not identically $-\infty$ on any component, because these properties hold for $w$ by step 4.3 and are read in charts. By the locality of plane subharmonicity, step 3.2, applied separately to each component, $w_\theta$ is plane subharmonic on every component of $\theta(\operatorname{dom}\theta\cap\Omega)$. As $\theta$ was an arbitrary chart, $w$ is subharmonic on $\Omega$. [F2, F3, step 3.2, step 5.2]

9.1 **Maximum principle.** Let $v$ be subharmonic on $D$ and let $B\in\mathbb R$ satisfy $\limsup_{q\to\eta,\,q\in D}v(q)\le B$ for every $\eta\in\partial D$. Then $v\le B$ on $D$. For any real $b>B$, the set $E_b:=\{q\in D:v(q)\ge b\}$ is closed in $\overline D$: it is closed inside $D$ by upper semicontinuity, and its closure cannot meet $\partial D$ by the boundary limsup bound. Thus $E_b$ is compact. If $s:=\sup_Dv=+\infty$, the nonempty nested compact sets $E_n$ for integers $n>B$ have the finite-intersection property, so some point satisfies $v(q)\ge n$ for every such $n$, impossible because subharmonic functions have no $+\infty$ values. Hence $s<+\infty$. If $s>B$, the nested nonempty compact sets $E_b$ for $B<b<s$ again have the finite-intersection property; a point in their intersection has $v(q)\ge b$ for every $b<s$, so $v(q)=s$. Since $s>B$, the point is interior, and the strong maximum principle forces $v\equiv s$ on connected $D$. Taking any boundary point then gives $s=\limsup_{q\to\eta}v(q)\le B$, a contradiction. Therefore $s\le B$. [F2, F3, F9, step 8.1]

10.1 In the situation of step 9.1 the maximum set $\{q\in D:v(q)=s\}$ is open: for $q$ in it, take a chart $\theta$ around $q$ with $\theta(q)=0$ and $\theta(\operatorname{dom}\theta\cap D)$ a plane domain; the chart expression $v_\theta$ is plane subharmonic and attains the finite maximum $s$ at the interior point $0$, so by the strong maximum principle $v_\theta$ is constant on $\theta(\operatorname{dom}\theta\cap D)$ and $v$ is constant on a neighbourhood of $q$. The set is also closed in $D$, because it is $D\cap\{v\ge s\}$ and superlevel sets of the upper semicontinuous function $v$ are closed. Since $D$ is connected the set is all of $D$, so $v\equiv s>B$ on $D$. But $\partial D\neq\varnothing$: otherwise $D$ would be open and closed in the connected space $X$, forcing $D=X$ and contradicting compactness of $\overline D$. At any $\eta\in\partial D$ the boundary hypothesis then gives the contradiction $s=\limsup_{q\to\eta}v(q)\le B$, so $s\le B$ and the maximum principle holds for all $v$. [F2, F3, F9, step 9.1, cases]

12.1 **The envelope.** Let $H$ be the upper-semicontinuous regularization of $U$, $H(x):=\limsup_{y\to x,\,y\in D}U(y)$, equivalently the least upper semicontinuous majorant of $U$ [F5]. Then $U\le H$ and, since $m\le U\le M$, also $m\le H\le M$. Moreover $H$ is subharmonic on $D$: for every chart $\theta$ the family of plane subharmonic functions $\{v_\theta:v\in\mathcal P\}$ on the plane domain $\theta(\operatorname{dom}\theta\cap D)$ is nonempty and bounded above by $M$, its pointwise supremum is $U_\theta$ and its upper-semicontinuous regularization is $H_\theta$ (regularization is a local, hence chart-invariant, operation); so the upper envelope theorem [F3] makes $H_\theta$ plane subharmonic. As $\theta$ was arbitrary, $H$ is subharmonic on $D$. [F3, F5, step 11.1]

15.1 **Monotonicity and directedness.** If $v,w\in\mathcal P$ satisfy $v\le w$ on $D$, then $\tilde v\le\tilde w$ on $B$: choose decreasing continuous approximants $\alpha_n\downarrow v_\theta$ and $\beta_n\downarrow w_\theta$ on the circle $\partial D(w_0,r)$ and set $\gamma_n:=\min\{\alpha_n,\beta_n\}$; then the $\gamma_n$ are continuous and decrease to $\min\{v_\theta,w_\theta\}=v_\theta$, while $\gamma_n\le\beta_n$, so positivity of the Poisson kernel [F4] gives $P[\gamma_n]\le P[\beta_n]$ on $D(w_0,r)$ and hence $P_\theta v=\inf_nP[\gamma_n]\le\inf_nP[\beta_n]=P_\theta w$, that is, $\tilde v\le\tilde w$. Also, if $v,w\in\mathcal P$ then $t:=\max\{v,w\}\in\mathcal P$: it is subharmonic on $D$ since both are, and at each $\eta\in\partial D$ its limsup is at most $\max\{\limsup v,\limsup w\}\le\varphi(\eta)$. By monotonicity $\tilde t\ge\tilde v,\tilde w$ on $B$. [F3, F4, step 14.1]

proof_uses: 1.2 **The Casimir scalars on flag sections.** Write $C=\sum_{a,b}E_{ab}E_{ba}$. The matrix-unit brackets show that $C$ is central and that its highest-weight scalar is $c(\lambda)=\sum_j\lambda_j(\lambda_j+n+1-2j)$: commute each positive root factor past its negative partner and apply it to the highest vector. Moreover $\Delta(C)=C\otimes1+1\otimes C+2x$ and $c(V)=c(V^{*})=n$. On a valid generalized-standard section of highest weight $\lambda+\varepsilon_j$, $x$ therefore has scalar $(c(\lambda+\varepsilon_j)-c(\lambda)-n)/2=\lambda_j+1-j=a_j$; the section $\lambda-\varepsilon_j$ has scalar $-a_j-n+1$. Thus $i\to i+1$ selects scalar $i$, and $i+1\to i$ selects scalar $-n-i$. The generalized-standard tensor flags will be constructed below; these formulas concern their sections and do not assert scalar action on arbitrary weight vectors. [F2, F3, algebra]

2.2 **Multiplicity-free generalized-standard flags.** Filter $V|_{\mathfrak p}$ by its successive Levi blocks and $V^{*}|_{\mathfrak p}$ by the reverse blocks; each section is a natural or dual natural Levi module with radical acting by zero. For a finite Levi simple $E(\lambda)$, the Weyl numerator identity $A(\lambda+\rho_{\mathfrak l})\sum_j e^{\varepsilon_j}=\sum_j A(\lambda+\rho_{\mathfrak l}+\varepsilon_j)$ gives $E(\lambda)\otimes V_b=\bigoplus_jE(\lambda+\varepsilon_j)$ over the dominant valid moves in block $b$: an invalid move makes two shifted coordinates equal and its alternating numerator zero. The same identity with $-\varepsilon_j$ treats the dual. Levi complete reducibility, part of the parabolic structure [F3], turns these character identities into multiplicity-one decompositions. The tensor identity for induction maps $u\otimes(e\otimes v)$ to $\sum(u_{(1)}\otimes e)\otimes u_{(2)}v$, with inverse given by the antipode; the coproduct/antipode identities verify balancing and inverse composition. PBW makes induction exact, so the resulting filtration of $\Delta(A)\otimes V$ or $\Delta(A)\otimes V^{*}$ has precisely the generalized-standard sections for these valid moves. Their central characters are the changed entry multisets, and step 1.2 gives the Casimir scalar on each section. Exact block or generalized-eigenspace projection therefore retains precisely the specified moves, each once. [F2, F3, F5, step 1.2, algebra]

4.1 **The integral Fock $K_0$ action.** The standard classes form a basis in each block by [F3], and the monomials of [F4] have exactly those labels, so $[\Delta(A)]\mapsto M_A$ is an isomorphism of abelian groups. On a tensor of minuscule wedges, $f_i^r$ counts ordered choices of $r$ distinct movable columns; every subset occurs $r!$ times, and the same holds for $e_i^r$. Thus the divided class operators are integral as well. Each residue operator is nilpotent on any fixed weight calculation by the finite-cut Fock action; positivity in the simple basis and finite length then imply the corresponding iterated functor vanishes. Let $X$ be a Banach space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$
([[def-banach-space]], [[rem-real-and-complex-normed-space-convention]]) and let
$A:D(A)\subseteq X\to X$ be a closed linear operator with resolvent
$R(\lambda,A)=(\lambda I-A)^{-1}\in\mathcal B(X)$ for $\lambda\in\rho(A)$
([[def-resolvent-of-a-closed-operator]]). Then:

1. $\rho(A)$ is open: if $\lambda_0\in\rho(A)$ and
   $|\lambda-\lambda_0|\,\|R(\lambda_0,A)\|<1$, then $\lambda\in\rho(A)$ and
   $$R(\lambda,A)=\sum_{n\ge0}(\lambda_0-\lambda)^nR(\lambda_0,A)^{n+1},$$
   the series converging in the operator norm;
2. the resolvent identity
   $$R(\lambda,A)-R(\mu,A)=(\mu-\lambda)R(\lambda,A)R(\mu,A)=(\mu-\lambda)R(\mu,A)R(\lambda,A)$$
   holds for all $\lambda,\mu\in\rho(A)$;
3. $\lambda\mapsto R(\lambda,A)$ is differentiable on $\rho(A)$ in the operator
   norm with derivative $R'(\lambda,A)=-R(\lambda,A)^2$; when $\mathbb K=\mathbb C$
   this is norm-holomorphy ([[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]]);
4. for every $z\in\mathbb C$ the map
   $\lambda\mapsto e^{\lambda z}R(\lambda,A)$ is differentiable on $\rho(A)$ in
   the operator norm with derivative
   $ze^{\lambda z}R(\lambda,A)-e^{\lambda z}R(\lambda,A)^2$, and norm-holomorphic
   when $\mathbb K=\mathbb C$; for $\mathbb K=\mathbb R$ the complex scalar
   $e^{\lambda z}$ acts through the canonical complexification of $X$
   ([[lem-canonical-banach-complexification-of-a-real-banach-space]]).

No choice principle is used.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $G$ be a
complex reductive affine algebraic group and let $X$ be an affine algebraic
set with an algebraic $G$-action ([[def-rational-action-on-affine-variety]]);
write $A=\mathbb C[X]$ and let $R_X:A\to A^G$ be the Reynolds operator of
[[thm-complete-reducibility-and-reynolds-operator-for-complex-reductive-group]].
Then:

[F1] *Properties of the Reynolds operator.* The projection $R_A:A\to A^G$ is $G$-equivariant, restricts to the identity of $A^G$, is natural under morphisms of rational $G$-modules and is $A^G$-linear: $R_A(ab)=a\,R_A(b)$ for $a\in A^G$, $b\in A$ ([[thm-complete-reducibility-and-reynolds-operator-for-complex-reductive-group]]).
proof_uses: 1.1 Part (a): [F1] gives $R_X(ab)=aR_X(b)$ for $a\in A^G$, $b\in A$, so $R_X$ is $A^G$-linear; it is idempotent because it restricts to the identity on $A^G$ and its values lie in $A^G$, so $R_X(R_Xb)=R_Xb$; and its image is exactly $A^G$, since every invariant is fixed and every value is invariant. [F1, F2]

2.1 Part (b): let $I\subseteq A^G$ be an ideal. The extension $IA$ is $G$-stable, so by [F1] and step 1.1, $R_X(IA)=IR_X(A)=IA^G=I$. If $IA=JA$ for ideals of $A^G$, then $I=R_X(IA)=R_X(JA)=J$, so $I\mapsto IA$ is injective. An ascending chain $I_1\subseteq I_2\subseteq\dots$ of ideals of $A^G$ gives the ascending chain $I_nA$ of ideals of $A$, which stabilizes when $A$ is Noetherian by the ascending chain condition; applying $R_X$ to a stable equality and using $R_X(I_nA)=I_n$ gives $I_n=R_X(I_nA)=R_X(I_{n+1}A)=I_{n+1}$, so $A^G$ is Noetherian. [F1, F3, F5, step 1.1]

2.2 Part (c): let $\varphi:A\to B$ be a surjective $G$-equivariant homomorphism of rational $G$-algebras. Clearly $\varphi(A^G)\subseteq B^G$. Conversely, if $b\in B^G$, choose $a\in A$ with $\varphi(a)=b$; naturality of the Reynolds operator [F1] gives $b=R_B(b)=R_B(\varphi(a))=\varphi(R_A(a))\in\varphi(A^G)$. Hence $\varphi(A^G)=B^G$. [F1, step 1.1]

3.1 Part (d): if $A=\bigoplus_nA_n$ is a $G$-stable grading, the degree projections are $G$-equivariant, so by naturality $R_X$ preserves each degree and $A^G=\bigoplus_nA_n^G$. For a homogeneous ideal $I\subseteq A^G$ its extension $IA$ is homogeneous; for an ascending chain of homogeneous ideals $I_n$, all extensions $I_nA$ are homogeneous. Thus $R_X$ preserves homogeneity, and the computations of steps 1.1, 2.1 and 2.2 apply verbatim: $R_X(IA)=I$, the map $I\mapsto IA$ is injective on homogeneous ideals, and $A^G$ is Noetherian when $A$ is; the surjectivity statement of part (c) holds for surjective graded equivariant maps by the same argument. [F1, F4, step 2.1, step 2.2] ∎

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\Omega'$ be complex domains, let $\Gamma$ be a path family in $\Omega$, and let $\rho,\sigma:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ be Borel with $\rho\le\sigma$. Let $\ell_\rho$, $A$, $\lambda$, and $\mu$ be as in [[def-extremal-length-and-curve-family-modulus]]. Then:

(i) **Parameterization independence.** If $\gamma:[a,b]\to\Omega$ is rectifiable and $h:[a',b']\to[a,b]$ is continuous, nondecreasing, and onto, then $\ell_\rho(\gamma\circ h)=\ell_\rho(\gamma)$. With the arc-length parametrization $\widetilde\gamma:[0,L]\to\Omega$ of [[thm-every-rectifiable-path-has-an-arc-length-parametrization]], one has
$$\ell_\rho(\gamma)=\int_0^L\rho(\widetilde\gamma(s))\,ds.$$

(ii) **Subpath additivity.** Write $\nu_\gamma=dS_\gamma$ for the Lebesgue-Stieltjes measure of the extended arc-length function in [[def-extremal-length-and-curve-family-modulus]]. For $a\le u\le v\le b$,
$$\ell_\rho(\gamma|_{[u,v]})=\int_{[u,v]}\rho(\gamma(t))\,d\nu_\gamma(t).$$
Consequently, if $[u_j,v_j]\subseteq[a,b]$ are pairwise disjoint parameter intervals, then $\sum_j\ell_\rho(\gamma|_{[u_j,v_j]})\le\ell_\rho(\gamma)$.

(iii) **Agreement with the absolute line integral.** If $\rho$ is finite-valued and continuous on $\Omega$, then for every rectifiable path $\gamma$ in $\Omega$ the value $\ell_\rho(\gamma)$ equals the published absolute line integral $\int_\gamma\rho\,|dz|$ ([[def-absolute-line-integral-over-a-rectifiable-path]], [[thm-existence-of-complex-line-integrals-on-rectifiable-paths]]). In particular, $\ell_1(\gamma)$ is the arc length of $\gamma$.

(iv) **Monotonicity and area additivity.** For every path, $\ell_\rho(\gamma)\le\ell_\sigma(\gamma)$, hence $\ell_\rho(\Gamma)\le\ell_\sigma(\Gamma)$. If pairwise disjoint Borel sets $E_1,\ldots,E_k\subseteq\Omega$ satisfy $\rho=0$ off their union, then
$$A(\rho)=\sum_{j=1}^k\int_{E_j}\rho^2\,dA.$$

$$Tf\in L^{q_\theta}(\nu),\qquad \|Tf\|_{q_\theta}\le M_0^{1-\theta}M_1^\theta\|f\|_{p_\theta}.$$
The same conclusion holds on arbitrary source and target measure spaces when $q_0,q_1<\infty$. At theta equal to zero or one use the given endpoint estimates, with no convention for $0^0$.

spectral projection valued measure $E$, and set
$U(t):=e^{itT}=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{it\lambda}\,dE(\lambda)$ for $t\in\mathbb R$.
Then $U$ is a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group,
$U(t)D(T)=D(T)$ and $TU(t)=U(t)T$ on $D(T)$, and the derivative
$\lim_{t\to0}\frac1t(U(t)x-x)$ exists exactly for $x\in D(T)$, where it equals
$iTx$. Thus the generator of $U$ is $G=iT$, with $D(G)=D(T)$.

Then there exist a measurable field $(\pi_x)_{x\in X}$ of strongly continuous unitary representations of $G$ on the fibres, defined for every $x$ by an arbitrary choice on a null set, such that for every $g\in G$ $$U\pi(g)U^{-1}=\int_X^\oplus\pi_x(g)\,d\mu(x),$$ and the field $x\mapsto\pi_x(G)''$ of von Neumann algebras generated by the fibres is a measurable field in the sense of [[def-measurable-field-of-von-neumann-algebras]]; moreover $\pi_x$ is nondegenerate for $\mu$-almost every $x$.

([[def-countable-choice-principle-for-foliation-pair]]). A relative generic
characteristic disk with closed transverse boundary and with distinct singular
images in distinct ambient leaves
([[lem-characteristic-disk-singular-images-can-be-separated-into-distinct-leaves-rel-collar]])
has an inclusion-minimal simple regular or homoclinic characteristic cycle
whose ambient holonomy germ is nonidentity

cited_passages: [F8] A simple closed piecewise-$C^1$ curve with finitely many corners and distinct one-sided tangents at each corner bounds exactly one bounded component ([[lem-finitely-cornered-regular-plane-curve-separates-without-choice]]).
proof_uses: 7.1 **The limiting cycle and area minimality.** If $G$ is a regular circle or a simple homoclinic loop, then $G$ is a simple cycle with nonidentity word $H$ and domain of area $\operatorname{area}(K)=\lim_n\operatorname{area}(K_n)=A$, so it attains the infimum. If $G$ has two edges, at least one of the two simple lobes has nonidentity word by the factorization in step 2.1; let $L$ be that lobe. Its boundary lies in $G=\partial K$, and its entire bounded Jordan domain is contained in every $K_n$, because $L\subseteq K\subseteq\operatorname{int}K_n$ by strict nesting, while the connected unbounded exterior of $K_n$ lies in the unbounded component of the complement of $L$. The boundary $C_n$ lies in that same component by its exterior collars, so the bounded lobe cannot leave $K_n$; passing to the limit its area is at most $\lim_n\operatorname{area}(K_n)=A$, while by definition of the infimum it is at least $A$, so it equals $A$ and $L$ attains the infimum. [step 6.1, F7, F8]

cited_passages: [F1] Every regular point of the disk lies on a characteristic trajectory; the one-sided limit sets of an orbit with precompact closure are nonempty, compact, connected and invariant, and are either a singleton equilibrium, a single periodic orbit, or consist of finitely many equilibria and saddle-to-saddle connecting trajectories ([[lem-local-generalized-poincare-bendixson-for-a-precompact-planar-orbit]]).
proof_uses: 1.1 Call a characteristic cycle **simple** when it is either a regular periodic orbit or a homoclinic orbit through one saddle whose source closure is a simple closed curve, and let its **domain** be the bounded component of the complement of that curve. Its **ambient holonomy** is the holonomy germ of the based leafwise loop obtained by following the cycle once around, in the sense of [[def-holonomy-representation-and-holonomy-group-of-a-leaf]]. Extend X C¹ to a neighborhood of the disk by [[lem-c1-planar-fields-on-a-closed-disk-extend-to-a-neighborhood]], and choose the sign of the characteristic field so it points inward on the transverse boundary; its normal component is nonzero and has one sign there. Begin with an orbit entering the boundary outside the finitely many stable separatrices of the saddles: its positive orbit stays in the compact disk, so [F1] applies to its limit set. [given, F1]

2.1 **A nonidentity simple cycle exists.** The entering orbit cannot converge to a saddle, since it was chosen off the finitely many stable separatrices; nor can a center belong to its limit set, since small invariant center circles cannot be crossed. By [F1], the limit is a periodic orbit or a connected finite saddle graph. Every connecting edge maps into one ambient leaf, and the singular leaves are distinct, so a connected saddle graph has just one vertex, with one or two homoclinic edges by [F2]. Trim each edge by short transverse ports and use one Morse box at the saddle. In that box $uv$ is constant along an orbit; on either fixed nonzero sign, its quadrant arcs pair the incoming ports with the outgoing ports deterministically. Together with the at most two edge strips, this gives a return itinerary of one or two edges. A sufficiently late entering orbit follows one such itinerary repeatedly; it avoids the axes and cannot change its side without crossing a separatrix. The compact edge strips and single target box define one ambient transverse return map H on an interval about the limiting port. At the source port its pulled-back transverse function is a local diffeomorphism, so the source return map is conjugate to H on that approached side. If H were the identity on a neighborhood of the limiting parameter, sufficiently late returns would be periodic, contradicting the nonclosed entering orbit. Thus the limiting word has nonidentity germ. In the two-edge case its word is the product of the two homoclinic lobe words with fixed transport conjugations; if both were identity, so would be their product. Therefore a simple periodic or homoclinic cycle has nonidentity ambient holonomy. [F1, F2, F4, F5, F9, step 1.1]

5.1 **The nested boundary limit is a finite graph or circle.** The whole sequence $C_n$ converges in Hausdorff distance to $G=\partial K$. A limit of points of late $C_n$ lies in every $K_j$ and cannot lie in $\operatorname{int}K$, because a ball contained in $K$ is disjoint from every boundary $C_n$. Conversely, for $z\in\partial K$ and any small ball about $z$, choose $w$ in that ball outside $K$. It is outside some $K_j$ and hence all later $K_n$, whereas $z\in K_n$; the segment from $z$ to $w$ meets every later $C_n$ in the ball. Finite covers and compactness give both uniform Hausdorff bounds. A Hausdorff limit of these connected compact circles is connected: two separated compact pieces of $G$ would give disjoint small neighborhoods which every late connected $C_n$ must meet while staying in their union. Flow dependence F5 makes $G$ invariant. At a regular point, each nearby $C_n$ crosses a fixed short section at most once by F4; its limit therefore has exactly one transverse coordinate there and is one local flow arc. A periodic component is consequently open as well as closed in $G$, so connectedness makes it all of $G$. Otherwise a regular orbit in $G$ cannot accumulate at a regular point: repeated visits to its flow box would give distinct intersections with that short section, contradicting the same local one-arc property. Its compact connected alpha- and omega-limits are therefore single equilibria by F1. Centers are excluded by step 4.1 and their invariant local disks. Hence every regular edge ends at saddles, and the finitely many half-branches of F2 give only finitely many edges. Thus $G$ is a regular circle or a finite connected saddle graph. This uses no unsupported hyperspace selection or period-annulus hypothesis. [F1, F2, F4, F5, F6, step 4.1]

Assume AC. Work in genuine type-$A$ parabolic category $\mathcal O$ for
$\mathfrak{gl}_N(\mathbb C)$ with its fixed Borel. Its column Levi has ordered
blocks of heights $q_1\ge\cdots\ge q_l$. All entries in column $j$ lie in
$c_j+\mathbb Z$, where the original admissibility condition is
$c_j-c_k\in\mathbb Z\Rightarrow c_j=c_k$. Use the source highest-weight
convention $\eta_i=a_i+i-1$ and half-sum
$\rho_i=(N+1-2i)/2$, with the column reading prescribed by the source Borel.
For each occurring entry coset $\kappa$ retain its columns in their original
order. Fix an order on the finite set of cosets; no order on $\mathbb C$ is used.

Subject to the local HC tensor-projective comparison stated in [F1], stable
sorting of the coordinates by $\kappa$ gives an exact, complex-linear
equivalence of the genuine parabolic categories, carrying each ordinary
Verma label by the dot permutation and carrying the corresponding generalized
standard, simple head and projective cover. On each linkage block, the sorted
category is equivalent to the product of the corresponding parabolic blocks
for $\mathfrak{gl}_{N_\kappa}$, where
$N_\kappa=\sum_{j\in\kappa}q_j$. Product means the abelian category generated
by finite presentations of outer tensor products, equivalently modules over
the tensor product of the finite block endomorphism algebras.

For the original pyramid with $n$ rows put $n_\kappa=\max_{j\in\kappa}q_j$.
The component integral entry dictionary is exactly
$$a_i^{\mathrm{int}}=a_i-c_\kappa+n-n_\kappa,\qquad m_j=q_j-n_\kappa,\qquad \inf I_\kappa=1-n_\kappa.$$
Thus $m_j+1-\inf I_\kappa=q_j$, with the original nonincreasing retained
heights and charges. For the admitted-ground subcategories, where each original entry has a
nonnegative integral difference from its own ground entry, this dictionary
lands in the bounded-below admitted integral component models of [F4]. For
other genuine parabolic blocks it records the integral weight/coset
dictionary and the trace shift, without asserting membership in that fixed
admitted cut. If the component follows $B_\kappa$ sorted coordinates, its
Levi highest weight and the integral highest weight differ by the scalar
trace-character shift
$$\delta_\kappa=B_\kappa+c_\kappa-n+n_\kappa.$$
This shift is a Lie algebra character and requires no integrality of
$c_\kappa$. Singular repeated-entry linkage blocks are included. The original
complex origins, component entry multisets and their scalar centres remain
recorded; different complex cosets are not merged into one integral block.

Sorting commutes coherently with finite tensoring and its invariant Casimir
and permutation maps. The separated product decomposition is blockwise and
does not assert that unrestricted tensoring is componentwise. The proof gives
its actual filtration and block-projection comparison. Choices of sorting
word with the same stable permutation yield the natural comparison fixed on
the chosen reference highest vector and its tensor-projective presentations.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $G:\mathbb C^n\to\mathbb C$ be separately holomorphic:
for every $j$ and every fixed $w\in\mathbb C^n$, the one-variable map
$$z\mapsto G(w_1,\dots,w_{j-1},z,w_{j+1},\dots,w_n)$$
is entire on $\mathbb C$. If there are nondegenerate intervals
$I_1,\dots,I_n\subseteq\mathbb R$ with $G=0$ on
$I_1\times\cdots\times I_n$, then $G\equiv0$ on $\mathbb C^n$.

proof_uses: 1.1 Base case $n=1$. Here $G$ is an entire function of one variable and vanishes on the nondegenerate interval $I_1$. Choose $p$ in the interior of $I_1$; by [F3], $p$ is an accumulation point in $\mathbb C$ of the set where $G$ and the zero function agree, and both are entire [F2]. The identity theorem [F1] on the domain $\mathbb C$ gives $G\equiv0$. [base, F1, F2, F3, given]

4.1 The slice in the first variable. For the fixed $z'$ of step 1.2, the one-variable map $w\mapsto G(w,z')$ is entire by [F2] and vanishes on the nondegenerate interval $\operatorname{int}I_1$ by step 3.1. Its zero set therefore has the accumulation point $p$ of [F3] inside the domain $\mathbb C$, and [F1] gives $G(w,z')=0$ for every $w\in\mathbb C$. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.2, step 3.1]

$$w'\mathbin\cdot\mu=w\mathbin\cdot\lambda+\gamma,$$

$(E\otimes\Delta(w\mathbin\cdot\lambda):\Delta(\eta))=\dim E_{\eta-w\cdot\lambda}$

$\eta=w\mathbin\cdot\mu$, where it equals one.

vector ([[def-almost-invariant-vectors-for-a-unitary-representation]]) has a

(T) ([[def-relative-property-t-for-a-pair]]).

$$L_Xf=\frac{d}{dt}\bigg|_{t=0}\Pi_\nu(\exp(tX))f\qquad(X\in\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb R)),$$

$$[L_W, L_{E_\pm}]=\pm2L_{E_\pm},\qquad[L_{E_+}, L_{E_-}]=L_W,$$

$$L_Wf_n=nf_n,\qquad L_{E_\pm}f_n=\frac{1+\nu\pm n}{2}f_{n\pm2}.$$

rows.consumer_statement_or_definition:
Let $f$ be holomorphic on $\mathbb D$ with $f\not\equiv0$. Then
$f\in N^+(\mathbb D)$ if and only if there are $g,h\in H^\infty(\mathbb D)$
with $h$ outer (equivalently $\log|h^*|\in L^1$ and
$\log|h(z)|=P[\log|h^*|](z)$ for all $z$) such that $f=g/h$. Moreover $h$ may
be chosen with $h(0)>0$ and $|h|\le1$, and the representation is not unique:
$(g,h)$ may be replaced by $(g\varphi,h\varphi)$ for any bounded outer
$\varphi\in H^\infty$.

cited_passages: [L3] If $H\ge0$ has $\log H\in L^1$, the outer function $[H]$ is holomorphic and zero-free, with $\log|[H]|=P[\log H]$ and $[H](0)=\exp(\int\log H)>0$. In particular, for $\varphi\ge0$ in $L^1$, $h=[e^{-\varphi}]$ satisfies $\log|h|=-P[\varphi]\le0$, hence $|h|\le1$. Products of bounded outer functions remain bounded and outer, by adding their integrable boundary logarithms and their Poisson log-modulus identities. ([[lem-outer-function-properties]], [[def-inner-singular-inner-and-outer-functions]])
proof_uses: 2.1 A Smirnov function is such a quotient. Assume $f\in N^+(\mathbb D)$, so by [L1] $\log|f^*|\in L^1$ and $\log|f|\le P[\log|f^*|]$. Put $\varphi:=\log^+|f^*|+1\ge1$, an $L^1$ function, and $h:=[e^{-\varphi}]$. By [L3], $h$ is outer with $0<h(0)=e^{-\int\varphi}\le e^{-1}<1$ and $|h|=e^{-P[\varphi]}\le1$, so $h\in H^\infty$ and $h$ is outer. Let $g:=fh$, holomorphic on $\mathbb D$. Then $$\log|g|=\log|f|-P[\varphi]\le P[\log|f^*|]-P[\varphi]=P\bigl[\log|f^*|-\log^+|f^*|-1\bigr]=P\bigl[-\log^-\!|f^*|-1\bigr]\le-1,$$ because $-\log^-|f^*|-1\le-1$ pointwise, and the Poisson integral of a function $\le-1$ is $\le-1$. Hence $|g|\le e^{-1}<1$ and $g\in H^\infty(\mathbb D)$, while $f=g/h$ with $h$ outer, $h(0)>0$, $|h|\le1$. [step 1.1, L1, L3, algebra]

3.1 Non-uniqueness and normalization. If $f=g/h$ with $g,h\in H^\infty$ and $h$ outer, and $\varphi\in H^\infty$ is outer, both products $g\varphi,h\varphi$ are bounded holomorphic by [L5]. The denominator is outer by [L3] and is zero-free. Therefore $(g\varphi)/(h\varphi)=f$ is another representation with an outer denominator. Taking, for example, the constant outer multiplier $2$ gives a distinct pair, so the representation is not unique. Step 2.1 already constructs a denominator with $h(0)>0$ and $|h|\le1$. A merely zero-free bounded multiplier preserves the quotient but need not preserve an outer denominator. [step 1.1, step 2.1, L3, L5, algebra]

rows.consumer_statement_or_definition: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K\subset\mathbb C$ be a compact subset of a straight line or a round circle, let $U\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open with $K\subset U$, and let $h:U\to\mathbb C$ be a homeomorphic embedding ([[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]]) that is $K_0$-quasiconformal on $U\setminus K$, where $K_0\ge1$. Then $h$ is $K_0$-quasiconformal on $U$, with the same maximal dilatation bound. For the sphere clause, a homeomorphism is $K_0$-quasiconformal when its local expressions in holomorphic charts are analytically $K_0$-quasiconformal ([[def-riemann-sphere-holomorphic-charts]], [[def-acl-sobolev-quasiconformal-homeomorphism]]). In particular, the same conclusion holds for a homeomorphism of the Riemann sphere that is quasiconformal off a round circle or a generalized straight line $L\cup\{\infty\}$.

[F1] Each component of $U\setminus K$ is a complex domain ([[def-complex-domain]]). Under AC, geometric and analytic $K_0$-quasiconformality agree on every such component; the analytic form has weak derivatives in $L^2_{\rm loc}$ and satisfies $|h_{\bar z}|\le k_0|h_z|$ with $k_0=(K_0-1)/(K_0+1)$ ([[def-acl-sobolev-quasiconformal-homeomorphism]], [[def-geometric-quasiconformal-homeomorphism]], [[thm-geometric-and-analytic-quasiconformality-equivalent]]).
proof_uses: 1.1 If $K=\varnothing$, the assertion is the hypothesis. Otherwise, [F10] makes the image under $h$ of each component of $U\setminus K$ open, so both it and the source component are complex domains. By [F1], the map on each component is analytically $K_0$-quasiconformal. Its weak coordinate derivatives are locally square integrable there and satisfy the same Beltrami bound. [F1, F10, given]

3.1 Also discard the null line families on a countable rational-box cover of $O$ where the ACL representative or its agreement almost everywhere with $h$ fails; [F4]–[F5] justify this common exceptional family. Fix one of the remaining good coordinate lines. Its intersection with $K$ is finite except for at most one exceptional line when $K$ lies in a straight line parallel to the chosen direction; that one line is a null member of the parallel family. For a circle there are at most two intersection points on every coordinate line. On each open interval left after removing these finitely many points, [F1] and [F5] give an absolutely continuous representative with derivative $g_i$ a.e. The representative agrees a.e. with the continuous restriction of $h$, so the two agree everywhere on each such interval. Since $g_i\in L^1$ on the whole line interval, [F6] and continuity of $h$ at the finitely many missing points show that the restriction of $h$ on the full interval is the indefinite integral of $g_i$ plus a constant. It is therefore absolutely continuous across every point of $K$. [F1, F5, F6, step 2.1, given]

4.1 Applying step 2.1 in both coordinate directions on a countable rational-box cover of $U$ shows that $h$ itself is ACL on $U$. On every relatively compact rational box, the derivatives $g_i$ belong to $L^2$ by step 1.2; the ACL characterization [F5] therefore identifies them as the weak derivatives of $h$, so $h\in W^{1,2}_{\rm loc}(U)$. Since $K$ has planar measure zero, the inequality $|h_{\bar z}|\le k_0|h_z|$ continues to hold almost everywhere on $U$. Hence $h$ is analytically $K_0$-quasiconformal on $U$, and [F1] gives geometric $K_0$-quasiconformality with the same bound. [F1, F3, F5, step 1.2, step 3.1, given]

Then $h$ is $K_0$-quasiconformal on $U$, with the same maximal dilatation bound. For the sphere clause, a homeomorphism is $K_0$-quasiconformal when its local expressions in holomorphic charts are analytically $K_0$-quasiconformal ([[def-riemann-sphere-holomorphic-charts]], [[def-acl-sobolev-quasiconformal-homeomorphism]]). In particular, the same conclusion holds for a homeomorphism of the Riemann sphere that is quasiconformal off a round circle or a generalized straight line $L\cup\{\infty\}$.

proof_uses: 1.2 On an overlap, fix a point and restrict to a standard source chart $z$ around it. Write $a_i=(\Phi_i)_z$, $b_i=(\Phi_i)_{\bar z}$ and likewise $a_j,b_j$. The pullback law [F1] makes both local equations use the same chart representative $\mu_z$, so $b_i=\mu_z a_i$ and $b_j=\mu_z a_j$. The transition $\tau=\Phi_i\circ\Phi_j^{-1}$ is $C^1$; the real chain rule and inverse derivative formula [F7] give $\tau_{\bar w}=(b_i a_j-a_i b_j)/(|a_j|^2-|b_j|^2)=0$, whose denominator is $J_{\Phi_j}>0$ by [F2]. 1.3 Let $X$ be the sphere with this atlas. Its topological properties are unchanged: it is a Riemann surface by [F3], compact and simply connected by [F4]. The last two targets are not compact: the disks $D(0,n)$ for $n\ge1$ cover $\mathbb C$ with no finite subcover, and the disks $D(0,1-1/n)$ for $n\ge2$ cover $\mathbb D$ with no finite subcover. Hence its target must be $\widehat{\mathbb C}$; write $H:X\to\widehat{\mathbb C}$ for this biholomorphism. [F3, F4, F5, F10, F13, algebra]

proof_uses: 1.1 Preservation of the upper aisle. Choose the finite compatible smooth target stratification of [F1] adapted to $A$, with the compatible refinements of [F3] available on affine charts, and work with the connected components $T$ of the full inverse images $a^{-1}(S)$. Smooth base change makes each nonempty such component smooth of dimension $\dim_{\mathbb C}S+d$, and smooth local charts make this the product pullback stratification. It has the frontier and Whitney conditions locally because the target stratification does and a smooth chart adds a ball factor; finitely many algebraic components give a finite global stratification. This choice matters: a further arbitrary source refinement need not have the full relative dimension. Write $e=\dim_{\mathbb C}S$ and $a_T:T\to S$. Composition of inverse images gives $i_T^*a^*A=a_T^*i_S^*A$, and exactness gives $H^q(i_T^*a^*A[d])=a_T^*H^{q+d}(i_S^*A)$. For $A$ in the upper aisle this vanishes whenever $q+d>-e$, or $q>-(e+d)$, precisely the source support inequality. Independence of compatible refinement [F1] proves upper-aisle preservation on $D_c^b$. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, construct, algebra]

2.1 Preservation of the lower aisle. The ordinary six-operation construction [F2] gives $D_Xa^*\cong a^!D_Y$ and the complex-orientation normalization $a^!\cong a^*[2d]$, where the relative dimension is $d$. Consequently $D_X(a^*A[d])\cong a^*D_YA[d]$. The ordinary middle-perverse core of [F1] identifies the lower aisle as the duality image of the upper aisle, and both the duality exchange of [F1] and the pullback comparison of [F2] are used here, so the first step proves preservation of the lower aisle as well. The orientation unit is nonzero over every field, exact finite-dimensional duality is field-general, and $[2d]$ is a cohomological shift rather than a scalar inversion; thus the support-and-duality argument applies to arbitrary $k$. [given, F1, F2, step 1.1]

3.1 Truncation, cohomology and reflection. Applying the t-exact functor $a^*[d]$ of steps 1.1 and 2.1 to a truncation triangle produces the unique target truncation triangle, proving that it commutes with perverse truncation and perverse cohomology. If $a$ is surjective, inverse image is stalkwise conservative and reflects ordinary cohomological vanishings; applying the same dimension calculation as in step 1.1 to the support and dual support inequalities reflects both perverse inequalities. The dimension count is the same over every field, and no characteristic hypothesis enters, so the stated conservativity and reflection hold for arbitrary $k$. [given, F1, F2, F3, step 1.1] ∎

rows.consumer_statement_or_definition:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), inherited through the smooth-projective
flag-variety and Euler-to-Chern suppliers. Let $Q$ be any finite loopless quiver, allowing
multiple arrows and arrows in both directions, let $V=\bigoplus_vV_v$ be finite-dimensional over
$\mathbb C$, and put $G=\prod_v\mathrm{GL}(V_v)$ and
$E_V=\bigoplus_{h:v\to w}\operatorname{Hom}(V_v,V_w)$. For a word $\nu$ of vertex labels with
multiplicities $\dim V_v$, let $B_\nu$ be its graded complete flag variety and
$X_\nu=\{(x,F)\in E_V\times B_\nu:x_h(F^a_v)\subseteq F^a_w\text{ for all }a,h\}$. Then
$X_\nu\to B_\nu$ is a complex algebraic vector bundle, $X_\nu$ is smooth, and
$\pi_\nu:X_\nu\to E_V$ is projective. Every middle-forgetting projection
$X_\nu\times_{E_V}X_\eta\times_{E_V}X_\theta\to X_\nu\times_{E_V}X_\theta$ is proper. All
orientations and refined middle-diagonal operations required by the preceding Ext/convolution
theorems exist equivariantly, without a smoothness or transversality assertion for fiber products.
With $d_\nu=\dim_{\mathbb C}X_\nu$ and $L_\nu=R\pi_{\nu!}k[d_\nu]$, those theorems apply in every
corner. Smooth vector-bundle projections and flag-bundle projections have their complex-oriented
pullbacks, and zero-section self-intersection is cap product with the top Chern class of the
bundle.

rows.consumer_statement_or_definition:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), inherited from the
Jacobian-criterion, ample-powers, Chern-form and comparison suppliers below.
Let $X$ be a smooth projective complex scheme of pure dimension $n\ge0$.

Then the closed points of $X$ carry a structure of **complex manifold**
$X^{\mathrm{an}}$, its **analytification**: if $X\ne\varnothing$ and $n\ge1$
this is a compact Hausdorff second-countable smooth complex manifold of complex
dimension $n$
([[def-complex-manifolds-and-holomorphic-vector-bundles]]); if $n=0$ it is the
finite discrete set $X(\mathbb C)$ with its unique complex structure in the
convention of
[[def-compact-kahler-manifold-and-hodge-polarization-conventions]]; and if
$X=\varnothing$ then $X^{\mathrm{an}}=\varnothing$. Every standard smooth
algebraic chart of $X$ supplies holomorphic coordinate charts of $X^{\mathrm{an}}$
after shrinking to local analytic graph neighbourhoods around its complex points;
the whole algebraic chart need not be a single holomorphic coordinate chart.
More generally, every morphism between smooth separated finite-type complex schemes of pure dimensions induces a holomorphic map between their analytifications. These analytifications are constructed by the same local charts and need not be compact; separatedness and finite type ensure that they are Hausdorff and second-countable.

Moreover, for every ample invertible sheaf $A$ on $X$ there is a smooth
positive closed real $(1,1)$-form $\eta_A$ on $X^{\mathrm{an}}$ whose de Rham
class is the real image of the topological first Chern class
$c_1(A):=c_1(A^{\mathrm{an}})\in H^2(X^{\mathrm{an}};\mathbb Z)$:
$$J_{X^{\mathrm{an}}}[\eta_A]=\rho_{X^{\mathrm{an}}}\bigl(c_1(A)\bigr),$$
where $J$ is the de Rham comparison and $\rho$ the change of coefficients
$\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R$
([[lem-rational-cohomology-scalar-comparison-for-compact-smooth-manifolds]]).
In dimension $n=0$ and for $X=\varnothing$ every $2$-form and every degree-two
cohomology class is zero and $\eta_A=0$, so the identity holds trivially.

rows.consumer_statement_or_definition: Assume AC. Let $p:X'\to X$ be a proper morphism between smooth projective complex varieties of equal pure dimension, restricting to the identity on a common open variety $U$. Then $H^n(X,\mathbb Q)$ and $H^n(X',\mathbb Q)$ have the same image in $H^n(U,\mathbb Q)$ for every $n$. Consequently the compactification-image formula of logarithmic weights extends from an SNC compactification to every smooth projective compactification.

cited_passages: [F1] Analytification and orientation ([[lem-smooth-projective-analytification-has-rational-kahler-polarization]], [[def-compact-kahler-manifold-and-hodge-polarization-conventions]], [[def-analytic-topology-and-finite-smooth-algebraic-stratifications]]). A smooth projective complex variety of pure dimension $d$ has an analytification that is a compact Hausdorff second-countable complex manifold of complex dimension $d$, a finite discrete set when $d=0$; every standard smooth algebraic chart supplies holomorphic coordinate charts after local analytic shrinking and every morphism of smooth complex varieties induces a holomorphic, hence continuous, map. A complex manifold carries the canonical orientation for which $(v_1,Jv_1,\dots,v_d,Jv_d)$ is positive on a complex basis, and it is boundaryless; an ample class is represented by a positive closed real $(1,1)$-form, so $X$ and $X'$ are compact Kaehler, hence compact oriented boundaryless $2d$-manifolds, and every open subvariety is an oriented complex submanifold. The analytic topology of a complex algebraic variety is the one of the cited definition, and regular maps are continuous for it.
proof_uses: 1.1 Structure of the spaces. For the first sentence, discard the open-and-closed components of $X$ and $X'$ that do not meet $U$. Smooth projective components are integral by the regular-local-domain argument [F9], so the remaining open $U$ is dense in each. On each retained component of $X'$, its dense part in $U$ maps to one component of $X$; continuity makes the entire component map into that closed target component. Thus $p$ restricts to the retained unions. Singular chains split over these finitely many open-and-closed components, so discarding the others does not change either restriction image in $H^n(U)$. We may therefore assume the embeddings dense. By [F1], $X$ and $X'$ are compact oriented boundaryless $2d$-manifolds, $U$ is an oriented boundaryless $2d$-manifold, and $j,j'$ are orientation-preserving open embeddings; $p$ is continuous with $p\circ j'=j$. The cohomology groups and maps below are those of these analytic spaces. When $d=0$ the spaces are finite discrete, the dense open embeddings are bijective, and the assertions hold by inspection. [F1, F9, given, algebra]

5.1 Equality of the images. Let $b\in H^n(X;\mathbb Q)$. Then $(j')^*(p^*b)=(p\circ j')^*b=j^*b$, by functoriality of pullback [F1, F3], so the image of $H^n(X;\mathbb Q)$ in $H^n(U;\mathbb Q)$ is contained in the image of $H^n(X';\mathbb Q)$. Conversely, if $a\in H^n(X';\mathbb Q)$, step 4.1 exhibits $(j')^*a=j^*(T_na)$ with $T_na\in H^n(X;\mathbb Q)$, so the reverse inclusion holds and the two images agree for every $n$ with $0\le n\le 2d$. For $n<0$ or $n>2d$ both cohomology groups vanish by duality [F2] and the vanishing conventions of [F3], so both images are $\{0\}$; if $U=\varnothing$ then $X=X'=\varnothing$ because $U$ has dense image, and all groups vanish. This proves the first sentence of the statement. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.2, step 4.1, given]

7.1 Choice accounting and boundary cases. AC is assumed in the statement and is consumed exactly through the suppliers of [F1]--[F9]: the analytification with its Chern-form, Jacobian-criterion, ample-power and comparison inputs, Poincare duality with its orientation classes and exhaustions, the full-dual universal coefficient statement, the compact-support colimit and excision, the resolution, principalization and Serre-generation inputs of [F8], and the regular-local-domain supplier of [F9]; all cap, cup, pairing and sequence computations are choice-free. Assume AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). For a smooth projective morphism
$f:X\to S$ of smooth quasiprojective complex varieties, $R^mf_*\mathbb Q$ is a
finite-rank local system ([[def-local-system-of-r-modules-and-its-pullback]]),
with full monodromy-stable integral lattice obtained from
$R^mf_*\mathbb Z$ modulo torsion, and with a continuous pure Hodge
decomposition of weight $m$ ([[def-geometric-polarizable-hodge-variation]]). A
relatively ample line bundle supplies flat Lefschetz operators and a flat
rational polarization of this variation. Products, sums, Tate twists, exterior
powers and Hodge direct summands have the corresponding geometric realizations
and full integral lattices. Pullbacks of algebraic maps between smooth
projective fibers preserve rational Hodge structures.

At any point only finitely many $W_i$ can intervene; their representative germs agree on a smaller neighbourhood, so this assignment has the required germ. Consequently every $\mathcal C^q$ is flasque. The stalk complex of $\mathbb Z_M\to\mathcal C^\bullet$ is exact: stalk preservation, exact filtered colimits and contraction of cofinal contractible neighbourhoods in [F11] give $\mathbb Z$ in degree zero and zero in higher degrees. The acyclic-resolution theorem therefore applies. proof_uses: 1.1 Analytic submersion and properness. The relative projective embedding is a closed immersion $X\hookrightarrow S\times\mathbb P^N$. The smooth quasiprojective source and base are Hausdorff second-countable complex manifolds; they are metrizable as locally closed subspaces of projective space. Each fibre is a compact smooth projective complex manifold, possibly empty or with components of different dimensions, and [F1] supplies a Kähler form on each component. An empty fibre contributes zero; its zero-dimensional components are finite sets with constant type $(0,0)$ and require no elliptic argument. The relative projective embedding restricts the Fubini–Study form to a smooth family of fibrewise Kähler metrics. On the fixed compact $F$ let $\Delta_t:H^2\to L^2$ be the corresponding Laplacians, using one reference metric for the Sobolev norms. Their coefficients vary continuously, so $\Delta_t-\Delta_0$ tends to zero in operator norm $H^2\to L^2$. They give the subspaces $H_t^{p,q}$ under the harmonic/de Rham identification. The pure decomposition, conjugation symmetry and metric independence in [F6] consequently give the required continuous pure Hodge decomposition of weight $m$.
