Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Define a square-integrable irreducible unitary representation to mean one for which every matrix coefficient lies in $L^2(G)$; this is the discrete-series convention of Frahm's SL$(2,\mathbb R)$ Plancherel notes. Let $D_1^-$ and $D_1^+$ be the two limits of discrete series of [[def-limits-of-discrete-series-for-sl2-r]]. Neither is square-integrable. In the compact picture of $I_{1,0}$, the normalized weight-one vector $f_1(k_\theta)=e^{i\theta}$ in $D_1^+$ has coefficient
$$\langle\Pi_0(a_\tau)f_1,f_1\rangle=\operatorname{sech}(\tau/2),\qquad a_\tau=\operatorname{diag}(e^{\tau/2},e^{-\tau/2}),$$
and
$$\int_G|\langle\Pi_0(g)f_1,f_1\rangle|^2\,dg=2\pi\int_0^\infty\operatorname{sech}^2(\tau/2)\sinh\tau\,d\tau=+\infty.$$
Complex conjugation gives the same nonintegrable coefficient modulus on $D_1^-$. This statement establishes failure of the all-coefficients criterion; it makes no claim about Plancherel support or occurrence in the regular representation.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) and $I$ bounded below. The
standard-class map $[M(A)]\mapsto M_A$ identifies the direct-sum $K_0$ of the
genuine tableau parabolic blocks with the full integral Fock module, with
matching multiset degrees and the residue Chevalley action of
$\mathfrak{gl}_{I^+}$. For every projective $P$ and finite-length $N$,
$$\dim\operatorname{Hom}(P,N)=\langle[P],[N]\rangle\quad\text{at }s=1 .$$
In particular $\langle P_A,L_B\rangle=\delta_{AB}$; no false standard/simple
orthogonality $\langle M_A,L_B\rangle=\delta$ is asserted. The projective,
simple and tilting basis identifications are proved separately.

proof_uses: 1.1 **The standard-class map is an isomorphism.** In each finite block the standard classes form a basis of the Grothendieck group and characters are injective, while the residue functors act on the standard basis by the explicit single-entry moves; the Fock monomials satisfy the identical relations and have the same degrees. Hence $[M(A)]\mapsto M_A$ is a degree-preserving isomorphism in each block, and it extends to the direct sum over the blocks because the direct sum decomposition is by central character on both sides. [F1, F3, algebra]

2.1 **The transition matrix and duality at $1$.** Write $D_{A,B}=d_{A,B}(1)=[M(B):L(A)]$ with simple rows and standard columns. Then $[M(B)]=\sum_A D_{A,B}[L(A)]$, so it is the simple-to-standard expansion that uses $D^{-1}$. BGG reciprocity instead gives $[P(A):M(B)]=D_{A,B}$, hence $[P(A)]=\sum_BD_{A,B}[M(B)]$; this matrix is the transposed standard/simple multiplicity array when rows are projective labels, not its inverse. Under the standard-class map these are exactly the defining $P_A$ and $L_A$ expansions. On the actual finite type-$A$ cuts, each nonconstant term of the quasi-$R$ root-factor expansion has a factor $s-s^{-1}$ and coefficients regular at $s=1$ (the quantum-factorial denominators have nonzero ordinary-factorial values there). Thus the tensor bar matrix specializes to the identity; passage to the primitive wedge factors preserves this specialization. The source monomial Gram matrices, which are its inverse, are consequently the identity at $1$. Multiplying the $D$ projective array by the $D^{-1}$ simple array yields $\langle P_A,L_B\rangle=\delta_{AB}$. No inverse BGG multiplicity matrix is asserted. [F1, F2, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

rows.consumer_statement_or_definition:
The Riemann sphere $\widehat{\mathbb C}$, the complex plane $\mathbb C$, and
the unit disc $\mathbb D$ are pairwise non-biholomorphic.

proof_uses: 1.1 If there were a biholomorphism from $\widehat{\mathbb C}$ onto $\mathbb C$ or onto $\mathbb D$, then [F2] would make the target compact because $\widehat{\mathbb C}$ is compact, but neither $\mathbb C$ nor $\mathbb D$ is compact. Hence the sphere is biholomorphic to neither the plane nor the disc. [F1, F2, given]

rows.consumer_statement_or_definition:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. For admissible origins $c$ the genuine Whittaker functor $V$ of
[[def-the-whittaker-functor-from-the-relevant-parabolic-o-summand]] is exact
on $\mathcal O_c^d$, and
$$\gamma\colon\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(T,-)\to\operatorname{Hom}_{W}(V_c^{\otimes d},V(-))$$
is a natural isomorphism, where $T=P_c\otimes V^{\otimes d}$. Both $V$ and the
Hecke quotient $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(T,-)$ are fully faithful on
all projective objects of the relevant summand, and the quotient is also fully
faithful on tiltings. $T$ is a self-dual prinjective detecting object
containing all standard-labelled projective-injective covers, each individually self-dual, but it need not be a
generator of the entire category-$\mathcal O$ summand. $V(T)=V_c^{\otimes d}$
is a projective generator of $W_d$-mod, and $V$ preserves projectivity on
$\operatorname{add}(T)$; it need not send every projective of $\mathcal O$ to
a projective $W$-module. The composite of $V$ with the Morita equivalence is
the Serre quotient killing exactly the off-standard simples.

cited_passages: [F2] Finite parabolic whole-block summands have projective covers, injective hulls, BGG reciprocity, standard/costandard Hom and Ext vanishing, and simple-preserving restricted duality ([[thm-parabolic-category-o-is-a-highest-weight-category]], [[def-integral-parabolic-category-o-block-for-higher-level-schur-weyl-duality]], [[def-standard-costandard-filtered-and-tilting-objects-in-a-highest-weight-category]]). In source Bruhat order, $[N(C):L(A)]$ vanishes unless $A\le C$, and $\operatorname{Ext}^1(N(C),N(A))=0$ unless $C<A$. PBW and ordinary polynomial Schur modules are [[thm-pbw-ordered-monomial-basis-for-the-enveloping-algebra]] and [[thm-schur-weyl-decomposition-with-length-cutoff]].

PBW gives exact $R$ and $R(N(C') oxtimes N(C''))=N(C)$. The top Levi slice of a simple is its Levi simple: a proper submodule of that slice would generate a proper global submodule by PBW. There are no additional lower $\mathfrak r$-invariants, since moving opposite-radical PBW monomials across the nondegenerate contravariant form pairs a lower invariant to zero against every vector. Hence $H(L(C))=L(C') oxtimes L(C'')$. For a costandard, invariant functionals vanish on all positive-degree opposite-radical monomials, giving $H(
abla(C))=
abla(C') oxtimes
abla(C'')$. Taking the exact top eigenvalue slice of the first-block trace, when $B,C$ have the same degree split, now gives $[N(C):L(B)]=[N(C'):L(B')][N(C''):L(B'')]$: smaller top eigenvalues contribute nothing and the top Levi simple determines its concatenated label uniquely. 2.1 **Actual standard embeddings.** Given $C$, shift columns $j\ge2$ upward by integers $k_j\ge0$, chosen successively so each shifted entry in column $j$ exceeds every earlier-column entry in its coset. The resulting $B$ is standard and Bruhat-minimal, hence $N(B)=L(B)$ by [F2]. Write column $j$ of $C$ as $a_{j,1}<\cdots<a_{j,q_j}$ and set $\mathcal E_j=(e_{a_{j,q_j}}\cdots e_{a_{j,q_j}+k_j-1})\cdots(e_{a_{j,1}}\cdots e_{a_{j,1}+k_j-1})$, composing rightmost first. Apply $\mathcal E_2$, then $\mathcal E_3$, through $\mathcal E_l$: the smallest entry is lowered first. In each elementary standard flag, alternative valid lowers occur in earlier columns, hence have strictly smaller prefix Bruhat label. Our desired section is largest and can be moved to the bottom: each adjacent swap splits by the Ext ordering in [F2]. Thus each move gives an actual monomorphism of standards, and exact subsequent residue functors preserve it. Composition gives $N(C)\hookrightarrow\mathcal E_l\cdots\mathcal E_2L(B)$. If $L(A)\hookrightarrow N(C)$, biadjunction gives a surjection from an iterated $f_i$ image of $L(A)$ onto the standard simple $L(B)$; step 1.1 forbids this for off-standard $A$. Every standard therefore has standard-labelled socle. [F2, F3, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

2.2 **An actual cover isomorphism.** Append the ground last column to $B'$. Every $C\ge B$ retains that ground column: a same-coset Bruhat move toward a larger label increases earlier-column sums, so the last-column sum cannot exceed its ground sum, whereas polynomiality makes each last-column entry at least its ground value. Equality forces all of them to be ground; admissibility excludes cross-coset swaps. Thus all $C\ge B$ have degree split $(d',0)$. Adjointness and step 1.2 show that $X=R(P(B')\boxtimes\mathbb C_{c_l+q_l-n})$ has simple head $L(B)$. Lift the cover map to obtain $P(B)\twoheadrightarrow X$, whose image is all of $X$ because it surjects onto its head. By BGG and step 1.2 their standard-flag multiplicities agree in the fixed split and vanish elsewhere. The kernel of this existing epimorphism therefore has every composition multiplicity zero and is zero. Consequently $X\cong P(B)$; an equality of characters has only been used to kill the kernel of an already constructed map. [F2, step 1.2, construct, algebra]

Tensoring by $V$ preserves both projectives and injectives because the distinct tensor functor $-\otimes V^*$ is exact and adjoint on both sides. The tensor product contravariant form gives $T\cong DT$. Every simple submodule of a standard-filtered object embeds in one of its successive standard sections, by taking the first section meeting it; hence step 2.1 proves standard socle for every projective and for $T$. Duality gives standard head for $T$. Every standard label of positive degree is $\widetilde f_iB$ for a lower-degree standard label by [F3]; induction using the actual crystal head of $f_iL(B)$ gives $T\twoheadrightarrow L(A)$. Lift this epimorphism through $P(A)\twoheadrightarrow L(A)$; essentiality makes the lift surjective and projectivity splits it. Thus the indecomposable summands of $T$ are exactly the standard-labelled covers, all with positive multiplicity and all injective. Moreover $I(A)=DP(A)\in\operatorname{add}(DT)=\operatorname{add}(T)$ for every standard $A$. This hull membership does not presume individual summand self-duality. Removing the last column and using tensor identity gives $Z(A,c)=R(Z(A',c')\boxtimes\mathbb C_{c_l+q_l-n})\otimes\bigotimes_{i=N-q_l+1}^{N}\operatorname{Sym}^{a_i}(V)$. By induction and step 2.2 the first factor is a sum of actual projective covers. The remaining finite tensor product preserves projectives by its exact distinct-dual adjoint. Polynomial labels form whole blocks: their shared entry multiset cannot admit a below-ground entry, since column strictness would put an entry below the common coset minimum in the bottom row. Thus these ambient projectives lie in the required finite polynomial summand. Every $Z(A,c)$ is genuinely projective. [F2, step 2.2, construct, algebra]

4.1 **Every cover occurs and the quotient has a standard flag.** For a label $B$, take $A=B-A_c$. Project each prefix onto its last-column Levi quotient. The tensor product of the resulting row symmetric powers surjects onto $V(B)$: row symmetrization followed by column antisymmetrization of the row-filled tensor produces a nonzero polynomial highest vector, and Levi complete reducibility gives the simple Schur quotient. Exact induction gives $Z(A,c)\twoheadrightarrow N(B)\twoheadrightarrow L(B)$, and projectivity plus essentiality of the cover makes $P(B)$ a split summand of $Z(A,c)$. Averaging symmetrizers embed $Z_A$ as a $\mathfrak p$-submodule of $V^{\otimes d}$; PBW preserves this injection and identifies the ambient induction with $T$. Its finite $\mathfrak p$-quotient has polynomial Levi simple sections: the radical acts nilpotently by the column filtration, and its invariant subspace in each simple section is Levi-stable and therefore the whole section. A tilting's standard flag gives standard socle by step 2.1, and its costandard flag gives standard head by duality. Thus the quotient is fully faithful on all tiltings. Applying exact $\pi$ makes $\pi N(A)$ a nonzero quotient of this indecomposable projective, so it has the same unique simple head. Through Morita, the actual finite-Levi standard $V(A)=V_{\!\mathrm{Wh}}N(A)$ likewise has unique simple head $L_W(A)$. This does not assert that a specified finite-Levi highest vector generates it. On the actual tensor space and every finite-Levi standard of degree $d$ its eigenvalues are $\kappa_r+h$, $0\le h\le d$, since the remaining weight is polynomial row occupancy. Thus the SAME finite-image element $e=\prod_{r\text{ deleted}}\prod_{h=1}^{d}(1-(D_r^{(1)}-\kappa_r)/h)$ is the zero-deleted-occupancy projector on both tensor space and all these standards. The actual dot formula preserves row multisets, so $e$ commutes with dots and crossings and belongs to the left image by the independent raw first centralizer of [F1]. Each right matrix restricts identically under the retained-box embedding: left neighbours and row/column indices agree and its scalar $a_j$ is unchanged. Therefore $eU^+=U$ as right Hecke modules. In the original path expansion, Levi projection kills off-column factors and each surviving strictly-forward path has at most one factor in each column. A deleted intermediate row changes removed-coordinate occupancy in a column with no later factor there to undo it; compression therefore kills that monomial. Remaining paths are exactly the small paths. The head shift in column $j$ changes by $-(j-1)t$, cancelling the retained source-reading shift $+(j-1)t$; its normalized highest weight remains the entry plus row index minus one. The corner action and its Gauss coefficients consequently give $eV(A^+)=V(A)$ for contractible labels and zero for noncontractible labels, as actual module identifications. [F1, F2, F4, step 8.1, construct, algebra]

rows.consumer_statement_or_definition:
For every real $x\ge2$,

$$\prod_{p\le x}\left(1-\frac1p\right) =\frac{e^{-\gamma}}{\log x}\left(1+O(1/\log x)\right),$$

where $\gamma$ is the Euler-Mascheroni constant of
[[def-euler-mascheroni-constant]].

cited_passages: [L4] The logarithm laws and the reciprocal-Gamma product identify the same $\gamma$ as the Euler-Mascheroni constant ([[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]], [[thm-gamma-weierstrass-product]], [[def-euler-mascheroni-constant]]).
proof_uses: 1.2 Every factor $1-1/p$ is positive. Applying [L3] with $u=1/p$ and summing the resulting absolutely convergent series gives $$-\log\prod_{p\le x}\left(1-\frac1p\right)=\sum_{p\le x}\sum_{k\ge1}\frac1{kp^k}.$$ [L3, L4, given, algebra]

3.1 Combining steps 1.1, 1.2, and 2.1 yields $$\log\prod_{p\le x}\left(1-\frac1p\right)=-\log\log x-\gamma+O(1/\log x).$$ Exponentiating the bounded $O(1/\log x)$ term gives $$\prod_{p\le x}\left(1-\frac1p\right)=\frac{e^{-\gamma}}{\log x}\left(1+O(1/\log x)\right).$$ [L4, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

For any ordered triples $(a,b,c)$ and $(a',b',c')$ of distinct points of
$\widehat{\mathbb C}$, there is a unique Möbius transformation $M$ with
$$M(a)=a',\qquad M(b)=b',\qquad M(c)=c'.$$
In particular every ordered triple of distinct sphere points can be normalized to
$(0,1,\infty)$.

cited_passages: [L1] The inverse of a Möbius transformation is again Möbius ([[thm-mobius-transformations-biholomorphic-sphere]], [[thm-mobius-group-and-projective-linear-identification]]).
proof_uses: 1.2 The composition $(N')^{-1}\circ N$ is Möbius by [L1] and carries $(a,b,c)$ to $(a',b',c')$, so the required map exists. [L1, given]

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be a compact Riemann surface
([[def-riemann-surface-and-holomorphic-atlas]]). Then:

1. the holomorphic atlas of $X$ canonically orients $X$; the orientation is
   determined by the complex structure, and the charts of the atlas are
   mutually orientation-preserving for it
   ([[def-r-orientation-of-a-topological-manifold]]);
2. $X$ is homeomorphic to the sphere with $g$ handles for a unique $g\ge0$:
   writing $\#_gT^2$ for the connected sum of $g$ copies of the torus, with
   $\#_0T^2=S^2$, there is exactly one $g\ge0$ with
   $X\cong\#_gT^2$.

The finite chart triangulation of
[[lem-finite-analytic-chart-triangulation-compact-riemann-surface]] supplies
the finite triangulation on which the polygonal reduction operates, and the
reduction itself together with the uniqueness of $g$ is the content of
[[thm-classification-of-compact-connected-surfaces]]. The Axiom of Choice is
used exactly through that in-run classification theorem; the chart orientation
and the local triangulation are choice-free.

cited_passages: [F2] For holomorphic $f$ on an open set of $\mathbb C$ the real Jacobian determinant satisfies $\det Jf(z)=|f'(z)|^2\ge0$, with equality exactly where $f'(z)=0$ ([[cor-jacobian-determinant-of-a-holomorphic-map]]); an injective holomorphic map on a plane domain has nowhere-vanishing derivative ([[cor-injective-holomorphic-derivative-nonzero]]).
proof_uses: 1.2 (The holomorphic atlas orients $X$.) For charts $\varphi,\psi$ with transition $\tau=\psi\circ\varphi^{-1}$ on a plane domain, $\tau$ is biholomorphic onto its image, hence injective and holomorphic, so $\tau'\ne0$ everywhere by [F2] and then $\det J\tau=|\tau'|^2>0$ everywhere by [F2]. Transporting the standard orientation of $\mathbb C$ through each chart therefore gives local orientations that agree on every overlap; equivalently, the maximal atlas is an oriented atlas. The resulting local orientation data are canonical for the holomorphic structure: any chart compatible with the atlas has biholomorphic transitions to the charts of the atlas, hence the same Jacobian positivity, so it defines the same orientation. [F1, F2, F3]

2.1 (The atlas orientation is the integral orientability read by [F4].) The orientation of step 1.2 gives, at every $x\in X$ and in every chart around $x$, the generator of the local homology $H_2(X,X\setminus\{x\};\mathbb Z)$ determined by the standard orientation of the plane through that chart; the transition computation of step 1.2 shows the generator is independent of the chart, and it varies continuously because it is locally induced by one chart. Hence $X$ carries an integral orientation in the sense of [F3], so $X$ is orientable, and this orientation is canonical for the holomorphic structure. [F2, F3, step 1.2]

rows.consumer_statement_or_definition:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $(\lambda,\mu)$ be as
in [[lem-facet-tensor-weight-exclusion]]: $\lambda$ integral dot-antidominant
and dot-regular, $\mu$ integral dot-antidominant with $F_\mu$ in the closure
of the chamber $F_\lambda$, $J=J(\mu)$, $W_\mu=W_J$. Let $\nu$ be the unique
dominant weight of $W(\mu-\lambda)$ and let
$$T:=T_\lambda^\mu=\operatorname{pr}_{\chi_\mu}\circ(L(\nu)\otimes-)\circ\operatorname{incl}_{\chi_\lambda}\colon\mathcal O_\lambda\longrightarrow\mathcal O_\mu,\qquad T':=T_\mu^\lambda,$$
be the translation functors of [[def-translation-functor-between-o-blocks]],
which are exact and biadjoint
([[prop-translation-functors-are-exact-and-biadjoint-across-a-wall]]). Then:

**(1)** $T\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)\cong\Delta(w\cdot\mu)$ and
$T\nabla(w\cdot\lambda)\cong\nabla(w\cdot\mu)$ for every $w\in W$.

**(2)** $TL(w\cdot\lambda)\cong L(w\cdot\mu)$ if $w\in W^J$, and
$TL(w\cdot\lambda)=0$ otherwise; equivalently $TL(w\cdot\lambda)\neq0$ if and
only if $w$ lies in the set $W^J$ of minimal representatives of the cosets $wW_J$.

**(3) (Big projective on the wall.)** Let
$\Xi_\mu:=T_{-\rho}^{\mu}L(-\rho)$ be the translate of the simple object of
the most singular block. Then $\Xi_\mu$ is projective and injective in
$\mathcal O_\mu$, it is the projective cover $P(1\cdot\mu)$ of $L(\mu)$, and
$(\Xi_\mu:\Delta(w\cdot\mu))=1$ for every distinct orbit label (equivalently
for its representatives $w\in W^J$); consequently
$(P(\mu):\Delta(y\cdot\mu))=1$ for every distinct label $y\in W^J$ and
$[\Delta(w\cdot\mu):L(\mu)]=1$ for all $w\in W$.

cited_passages: [F1] $T=\operatorname{pr}_{\chi_\mu}\circ(E\otimes-)\circ\operatorname{incl}_{\chi_\lambda}$ and $T'=\operatorname{pr}_{\chi_\lambda}\circ(E^*\otimes-)\circ\operatorname{incl}_{\chi_\mu}$; inclusions and projections are exact, and $\mathcal O$ is the direct sum of its central-character blocks ([[def-translation-functor-between-o-blocks]], [[thm-category-o-decomposes-by-generalized-central-character]], [[cor-central-characters-are-dot-weyl-orbits]]).
proof_uses: 1.1 **Standards (first clause of (1)).** By [F3], the tensor $E\otimes\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)$ has a finite Verma flag by [F4] in which the unique factor with central character $\chi_\mu$ is $\Delta(w\cdot\mu)$, once. The exact projection $\operatorname{pr}_{\chi_\mu}$ applied to this flag kills every factor whose central character differs from $\chi_\mu$ and carries the remaining $\Delta(w\cdot\mu)$ isomorphically, so $T\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)\cong\Delta(w\cdot\mu)$ for every $w$. [F1, F3, F4, algebra]

1.2 **The big projective (3).** By [F9], $M(-\rho)=L(-\rho)$. Its dot orbit is a singleton, so BGG reciprocity [F7] gives a one-factor Verma flag for $P(-\rho)$, proving $P(-\rho)=L(-\rho)$. Simple-preserving duality makes it injective too. Put $E_0=L(w_0\mu_\bullet)$ and $S=T_{-\rho}^{\mu}$, whose adjoint is $S'=T_{\mu}^{-\rho}$; the ordinary dual $E_0^*$ has highest weight $-\mu_\bullet$. By [F2], $\Xi_\mu=SL(-\rho)$ is projective and injective. Tensoring $M(-\rho)$ with $E_0$ and projecting retains exactly the factors $\Delta(-\rho+\gamma)$ with $\gamma\in W\mu_\bullet$, each once by [F4], [F8]. These are precisely the distinct standards $\Delta(y\cdot\mu)$. Likewise, since $L(\mu)=M(\mu)$ by [F9], tensoring it with $E_0^*$ and projecting to $\chi_{-\rho}$ retains only $\Delta(-\rho)$, once, from the extremal weight $-\mu_\bullet$. Thus $S'L(\mu)=L(-\rho)$, and adjunction gives $\dim\operatorname{Hom}(\Xi_\mu,L(\mu))=1$. The resulting epimorphism splits off the projective cover $P(\mu)$: lift it through the cover, use essentiality to make the lift surjective, and split by projectivity. For every $y$, there is an injection $M(\mu)\hookrightarrow M(y\cdot\mu)$. Indeed induct on a reduced expression $y=s_i v$: [F10] gives $v^{-1}\alpha_i>0$, so $\langle v(\mu_\bullet),\alpha_i^\vee\rangle\le0$. If it is zero the weights coincide; otherwise the positive integral pairing at $s_i v\cdot\mu$ supplies the one-step strong linkage and the injection $M(v\cdot\mu)\hookrightarrow M(s_i v\cdot\mu)$ by [F7]. Compose these injections. BGG then gives $(P(\mu):\Delta(y\cdot\mu))\ge1$ for every distinct label. The direct-summand complement of $P(\mu)$ in $\Xi_\mu$ is projective and has a Verma flag by [F7]. Additivity and the already computed one-per-label flag of $\Xi_\mu$ force every flag multiplicity of the complement to vanish, so the complement is zero. Hence $\Xi_\mu=P(\mu)$ and all the displayed standard and composition multiplicities are one. [F1, F2, F4, F5, F6, F7, F8, F9, F10, algebra]

2.2 **Costandards (second clause of (1)).** The evaluation pairing gives $D(E\otimes M)\cong D(E)\otimes D(M)$ naturally, and $D(E)\cong E$ for the finite-dimensional simple $E$ by [F6]. Hence $E\otimes
abla(w\cdot\lambda)=E\otimes D\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)\cong D(E\otimes\Delta(w\cdot\lambda))$. Since $D$ preserves central-character blocks and is exact, it commutes with the inclusion and projection defining the translation functor, so $T
abla(w\cdot\lambda)=\operatorname{pr}_{\chi_\mu}(E\otimes
abla(w\cdot\lambda))\cong D(\operatorname{pr}_{\chi_\mu}(E\otimes\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)))\cong D\Delta(w\cdot\mu)=
abla(w\cdot\mu)$ by step 1.1. [F1, F6, step 1.1, algebra]

Let $F(X,Y)$ be a rational expression in two variables, and assume that after
the substitution

$X=\frac{z+z^{-1}}{2},\qquad Y=\frac{z-z^{-1}}{2i}$

the resulting rational function

$G(z):=\frac{1}{iz}F\!\left(\frac{z+z^{-1}}{2},\frac{z-z^{-1}}{2i}\right)$

has no pole on $|z|=1$. Then

$\int_0^{2\pi}F(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)\,d\theta =\int_{|z|=1}G(z)\,dz,$

where the right-hand side is taken on the positively oriented unit circle.

Assume countable choice.

For each integer $m\ge1$,

$$\zeta(-2m)=0.$$

These are the only zeros of $\zeta$ on the nonpositive real axis. Every other
zero $\rho$ of $\zeta$ satisfies $0<\operatorname{Re}\rho<1$. Moreover, if
$\rho$ is a nontrivial zero, then so are $1-\rho$ and $\overline{\rho}$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) and the actual type-$A$
tableau parabolic data of
[[def-integral-parabolic-category-o-block-for-higher-level-schur-weyl-duality]].
Let $\bar{\mathfrak p}$ have the reversed Levi block order, conjugate to the
opposite parabolic, with reverse-column labels, and let
$F=D\Psi$ be the exact **covariant** equivalence constructed by
[[lem-the-parabolic-semi-regular-duality-and-reverse-column-label-map]].
Then
$$F:\mathcal F(\bar\Delta)\simeq\mathcal F(\nabla),\qquad F(\bar M(A))=\nabla(A),\qquad F(\bar P(A))=T(A),$$
and the explicit highest-weight shifts cancel to the original column reading, so
labels $A$ and the matching central-character blocks are preserved. Therefore the
full-block Ringel dual is the opposite-parabolic block, and
$$(T(A):M(B))=[\bar M(B):\bar L(A)] .$$
For a proper original lower ideal $\Gamma$, its Ringel dual is the matching
opposite **highest-weight Serre quotient** by the complementary labels (an upper
ideal in the opposite order), not the same Serre down-set subcategory. The
filtered equivalence and the projective/tilting corner construction give this
compatible finite-ideal transport. No unchanged underived full-longest Borel
twisting and no equivalence on arbitrary category-$\mathcal O$ objects is
asserted.

proof_uses: 2.1 **Actual projective-to-tilting transport.** Put $X(A)=\Psi(\bar P(A))$. Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator with spectral
projection valued measure $E$ on $\mathbb R$ acting on a complex Hilbert space $H$
([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]) and let
$f,g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be Borel. Write $u(T)=u(E)$, with the truncation definition below. If $H=\{0\}$, use its unique PVM and unique full-domain operator directly. Then:

1. $f(T)^*=\overline f(T)$;
2. $f(T)g(T)$ has domain $D(g(T))\cap D((fg)(T))$ and equals the restriction of
   $(fg)(T)$ to that domain, and its closure is $(fg)(T)$;
3. on $D(f(T))\cap D(g(T))$ the sum $f(T)+g(T)$ equals the restriction of
   $(f+g)(T)$, and the closure of $f(T)+g(T)$ is $(f+g)(T)$;
4. the spectrum of $f(T)$ is the essential range
   $\{z\in\mathbb C:E(f^{-1}(B_\varepsilon(z)))\ne0$ for every
   $\varepsilon>0\}$ of $f$ with respect to $E$;
5. if $f$ is continuous then that essential range is the closure of
   $f(\sigma(T))$, with the closure redundant when $f(\sigma(T))$ is closed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator with spectral
projection valued measure $E$ on $\mathbb R$ acting on a complex Hilbert space $H$
([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]) and let
$f,g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be Borel. Write $u(T)=u(E)$, with the truncation definition below. If $H=\{0\}$, use its unique PVM and unique full-domain operator directly. Then:

[A4] A spectral PVM represents $T$ as the integral of the identity function with its exact squared-integrability domain; the cited spectral theorem assumes nonzero $H$ and AC ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). The resolvent convention is $(zI-S)^{-1}$, required bounded and everywhere defined ([[def-resolvent-and-spectrum-of-a-closed-unbounded-operator]]).
proof_uses: 1.1 For $H=\{0\}$ all integrals are the unique full-domain operator by [A1]. Sums, products, adjoints and closures are that operator; its resolvent is all $\mathbb C$ and its spectrum is empty. Every spectral projection is zero, so every essential range here is empty, as is $f(\sigma(T))$. Thus all claims hold. Henceforth $H\ne\{0\}$, and all bounded calculus uses have the hypothesis required by [A2]. [A1, A2, A4, A5]

4.2 Suppose $E(\{|f-z|<\varepsilon\})=0$ for some $\varepsilon>0$. Define the Borel function $w$ piecewise: $w(\lambda)=1/(z-f(\lambda))$ when $|f(\lambda)-z|\ge\varepsilon$, and $w(\lambda)=0$ otherwise. It is bounded by $1/\varepsilon$, and $(z-f)w=1$ off an $E$-null set. By the domain and value identities of step 3.1, $(z-f)(E)w(E)$ has domain all $H$ and equals $I$; $w(E)(z-f)(E)$ has domain $D_{z-f}$ and equals the identity there. Null-set invariance is supplied by [A1]. By step 2.1, $D_{z-f}=D_f$ and $(z-f)(E)=zI-f(E)$ (linearity with constants, or multiplication by $-1$ in step 2.2). Thus $w(E)$ is its bounded inverse and $z\in\rho(f(E))$ in the convention of [A4]. Only the inverse is asserted bounded. [A1, A2, A4, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 3.1]

5.1 Conversely suppose $E(\{|f-z|<\varepsilon\})\ne0$ for every $\varepsilon>0$. Using AC in [A4], choose unit $x_n$ in the range of $E(\{|f-z|<1/n\})$ for each $n\ge1$. The scalar measure of $x_n$ is supported there by [A5], and $|f|\le|z|+1/n$ there, so $x_n\in D_f$. Hence $\|(zI-f(E))x_n\|^2=\int|z-f|^2\,dE_{x_n}\le1/n^2$ by [A1] and step 2.1. A bounded inverse with bound $C$ would give $1\le C/n$ for every $n$, impossible. This proves the essential-range formula. [A1, A4, A5, step 2.1, step 4.2]

6.1 Apply steps 4.2 and 5.1 to $u(\lambda)=\lambda$, which represents $T$ by [A4]. Nonreal $z$ have a ball disjoint from $\mathbb R$, so $\sigma(T)\subseteq\mathbb R$; for real $\lambda$, membership in $\sigma(T)$ is equivalent to every interval about $\lambda$ having nonzero projection. The union $U$ of all rational intervals with zero projection is exactly $\mathbb R\setminus\sigma(T)$, by the rational base in [A5] and projection monotonicity from $E(B\cap C)=E(B)E(C)$. Enumerate pairs of a fixed rational enumeration by increasing sums of their indices, giving an enumeration of rational intervals. In that enumeration retain such intervals and replace the rest by the empty set. Disjointify this sequence by subtracting previous intervals. Each resulting set has zero projection, and their union is $U$, so strong countable additivity gives $E(U)=0$. In particular $U$ is open and measurable. [A4, A5, step 4.2, step 5.1]

[F1] Riemann surfaces and biholomorphy ([[def-riemann-surface-and-holomorphic-atlas]], [[def-biholomorphic-map]]): a Riemann surface is nonempty, connected, Hausdorff and second countable with a holomorphic atlas; a biholomorphism of Riemann surfaces is a bijective holomorphic map whose inverse is holomorphic, and the relation "$X$ is biholomorphic to $Y$" is symmetric and transitive because composites and inverses of biholomorphisms are again of that kind.

Since the Axiom of Choice [A1] supplies the Countable Choice required by [F3], the dichotomy applies to the pole $p_0$: either $g_X(q,p_0)=+\infty$ for every $q\in X\setminus\{p_0\}$, or $g_X(\cdot,p_0)$ is finite on $X\setminus\{p_0\}$, which by [F2] says exactly that $X$ admits a finite canonical Green kernel at $p_0$. $\sigma:H\to U(K)$ and $\sigma':H\to U(K')$ are strongly continuous unitary
representations, then the canonical transitive systems of
$\operatorname{Ind}_H^G\sigma$ and $\operatorname{Ind}_H^G\sigma'$ on $G/H$

between unitary equivalence classes of transitive systems on $G/H$ and unitary
equivalence classes of strongly continuous unitary representations of $H$.

rows.consumer_statement_or_definition:
Suppose $f\in\mathcal O_{m,0}$ is regular in $z_m$ of order $d$ and

$$f=uW=vP$$

with $u,v$ units and $W,P$ Weierstrass polynomials of degree $d$. Then
$W=P$ and $u=v$.

cited_passages: [L1] Units are exactly the germs with nonzero value at $0$ ([[prop-units-in-the-holomorphic-germ-ring]]).
proof_uses: 1.1 By [L1], after shrinking to a common neighbourhood the unit factors $u$ and $v$ are nowhere zero. Therefore for each fixed nearby parameter $z'$, the slice zeros of $f(z',\cdot)$ coincide, with multiplicity, with the slice zeros of $W(z',\cdot)$ and also with those of $P(z',\cdot)$. [given, L1]

cited_passages: [L3] A holomorphic function on a domain that vanishes on a nonempty open subset vanishes identically ([[thm-identity-theorem-in-several-complex-variables]]).
proof_uses: 3.1 With $W=P$, the two preparations give $(u-v)W=0$. On the nonempty open set where $W\ne0$ one therefore has $u=v$. Applying [L3] to the holomorphic function $u-v$ on the connected neighbourhood shows $u=v$ everywhere there, and hence as germs. [step 2.1, L3, algebra] ∎

rows.consumer_statement_or_definition:
Let $\gamma:[0,1]\to\Omega$ be a path and let $\xi_0$ be a holomorphic germ at
$\gamma(0)$. If $\xi_0$ admits analytic continuation along $\gamma$, then the
terminal germ at $\gamma(1)$ is unique.

cited_passages: [L1] Admitting analytic continuation along $\gamma$ means admitting at least one admissible continuation chain along $\gamma$ ([[def-analytic-continuation-along-a-path]]).
proof_uses: 1.1 By [L1], any analytic continuation of $\xi_0$ along $\gamma$ is represented by an admissible continuation chain whose successive representatives agree at the joining points of the subdivision. [L1, given]

cited_passages: [L2] Any two admissible continuation chains along the same path have the same terminal germ ([[thm-end-germ-of-path-continuation-is-independent-of-the-chain]]).
proof_uses: 2.1 If two such continuations existed with different terminal germs, their underlying admissible chains would contradict [L2]. Therefore the terminal germ is unique whenever continuation along $\gamma$ exists. [step 1.1, L2] ∎

rows.consumer_statement_or_definition:
Let $f:\mathbb D\to\mathbb D$ be holomorphic and satisfy $f(0)=0$. Then

$$|f(z)|\le|z|\qquad(z\in\mathbb D),\qquad |f'(0)|\le1.$$

Moreover, if either $|f(z_0)|=|z_0|$ for some $z_0\in\mathbb D\setminus\{0\}$
or $|f'(0)|=1$, then

$$f(z)=e^{i\theta}z$$

for some real $\theta$; conversely every rotation $z\mapsto e^{i\theta}z$
satisfies equality in both conclusions.

cited_passages: [F4] If the modulus of a holomorphic function has an interior local maximum, then the function is constant ([[thm-local-maximum-modulus-principle]]).

Thus in either equality case $g(z)\equiv e^{i\theta}$ for some real $\theta$, so $f(z)=e^{i\theta}z$ on $\mathbb D$. [F4, step 2.1, step 4.1, cases, algebra]

cited_passages: [F3] Boundary modulus control on a bounded domain bounds the modulus throughout the domain ([[thm-maximum-modulus-principle-with-boundary-and-infinity-control]]).

rows.consumer_statement_or_definition:
Assume AC. Let $T$ be a bounded normal operator on a nonzero separable complex
Hilbert space $H$ and let $T'$ be a bounded normal operator on a nonzero
separable complex Hilbert space $H'$, with multiplicity data $(\mu,m)$ and
$(\nu,m')$ obtained from countable cyclic decompositions as in
[[def-spectral-multiplicity-function-in-the-separable-case]]. Then $T$ and
$T'$ are **unitarily equivalent** — there is a unitary $V:H\to H'$ with
$VTV^*=T'$ — if and only if

1. $\sigma(T)=\sigma(T')$ as subsets of $\mathbb C$, and on this common compact
   set the scalar measures are in the same class, $[\mu]=[\nu]$ (mutual absolute
   continuity);
2. the multiplicity functions agree almost everywhere for that class,
   $m=m'$ $\mu$-almost everywhere, equivalently $\nu$-almost everywhere.

No change of spectral coordinate is allowed: the identification of the two
scalar measure classes is an equality of measures on the common set
$\sigma(T)=\sigma(T')$, not an identification after a homeomorphism of spectra.
The zero Hilbert space is a separate trivial class: it carries the zero
operator, whose spectrum is empty, and no regular projection valued measure on
the empty set is used anywhere above.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $G$ be an LCH group. The assignment
$\pi\mapsto\sigma_\pi$, $\sigma_\pi(f):=\pi(f)$, from strongly continuous
unitary representations of $G$ to star-representations of the Banach
$\ast$-algebra $L^1(G)$

[[def-integrated-form-of-a-unitary-representation]],
[[def-nondegenerate-star-representation-of-a-banach-star-algebra]]) is a
bijection, respecting unitary equivalence, between unitary representations of
$G$ up to unitary equivalence and nondegenerate star-representations of
$L^1(G)$ up to equivalence: every unitary representation has a nondegenerate
integrated form, every nondegenerate star-representation is the integrated
form of a unique unitary representation, and a unitary intertwines two
representations if and only if it intertwines their integrated forms.

Let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty family of subharmonic functions on a complex domain
$\Omega$, and suppose that for every compact set $K\subseteq\Omega$ there is a
real number $M_K$ with $v\le M_K$ on $K$ for every $v\in\mathcal F$. Define
$$u(z)=\sup_{v\in\mathcal F}v(z),\qquad U=u^*.$$
Then $U$ is subharmonic on $\Omega$.

A map $f:\mathbb H\to\mathbb H$ is an automorphism of the upper half-plane if
and only if

$$f(z)=\frac{az+b}{cz+d}$$

for real numbers $a,b,c,d$ with $ad-bc>0$.

rows.consumer_statement_or_definition:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. For a regular integral block and simple reflection
$s$, with $C=\operatorname{End}(P(w_0\cdot\lambda))$, there is a natural
isomorphism of functors to left $C$-modules
$$V\theta_s\cong C\otimes_{C^s}V.$$
Equivalently the functor is tensoring by the $(C,C)$-bimodule
$C\otimes_{C^s}C$, with left action on the first factor and right action on the
second. In type A over $\mathbb C$, its polynomial lift is tensoring on the
left by $B_s=S\otimes_{S^s}S(1)$; read up to the auxiliary suspension
normalisation fixed by the rank-one case, the right origin reduction of $B_s$
is the two-dimensional module of centered degrees $-1,1$, for $M=S$ the
coinvariant reduction satisfies
$B_s\otimes_SC\cong(C\otimes_{C^s}C)(1)$ in the same normalisation, and
$B_s\otimes_S\mathbb C$ itself is not the bimodule $C\otimes_{C^s}C$: the
former has vector-space dimension two, whereas the latter has dimension
$2|W|$. Forgetting the grading gives the displayed category-$\mathcal O$
formula, and no grading on arbitrary category-$\mathcal O$ objects is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $n\ge2$, $n<p<\infty$, and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded $C^{2,\alpha}$ domain for some $0<\alpha<1$. If $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ is a weak solution of $-\Delta u=f$ with $f\in L^p(\Omega)$, then $u\in W^{2,p}(\Omega)\cap W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)$ and
$$\|u\|_{W^{2,p}(\Omega)}\le C\bigl(\|f\|_{L^p(\Omega)}+\|u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\bigr),$$
where $C=C(n,p,\Omega)$. This is a weak-to-strong regularity theorem; the estimate applies to the weak solution only after its $W^{2,p}$ membership has been established, and the assumption $p>n$ is the range in which the bootstrap of Sobolev exponents terminates at $p$.

cited_passages: [F3] Higher-order Sobolev embedding ([[thm-higher-order-sobolev-embedding]]): on a bounded extension domain, with $k\ge1$ and $1\le q<\infty$, (a) if $kq<n$ then $W^{k,q}\hookrightarrow L^r$ for every $1\le r\le nq/(n-kq)$; (b) if $kq=n$ then $W^{k,q}\hookrightarrow L^r$ for every finite $r$; (c) if $kq>n$ then $W^{k,q}$ embeds into $L^\infty$ and into $C^{0,\beta}(\bar\Omega)$ for $0<\beta<\min\{1,k-n/q\}$.
proof_uses: 1.1 Initial integrability and the exponent list. Since $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)=W^{1,2}_0(\Omega)$ and $\Omega$ is a bounded extension domain for $W^{1,2}$ by [F4], the embedding [F3] with $k=1$, $q=2$ gives $u\in L^r(\Omega)$ for every $2\le r\le\frac{2n}{n-2}$ if $n>2$, and for every finite $r$ if $n=2$. invertible complex-linear change of these centered coordinates $T$ supplied

some degree $d\ge1$ in the new last variable, and a product neighbourhood

zero sets agree:

$$Z(\widetilde f\circ T)=Z(W)\quad\text{on }V\times D .$$

The resulting local projection in the original coordinates is transported by
the affine coordinate map $z\mapsto p+Tz$.

For this $W$ on the chosen product representative, put $X_W:=Z(W)\cap(V\times D)$. Then:

1. the projection $\pi:X_W\to V$, $(z',T)\mapsto z'$, is proper, surjective
   and has finite fibres;
2. the quotient algebra $\mathcal O_{n,0}/(W)$ is a finitely generated
   $\mathcal O_{n-1,0}$-module;
3. with $D_W:=\operatorname{Disc}_T(W)$, the restriction of $\pi$ over
   $V\setminus\{D_W=0\}$ is a $d$-sheeted holomorphic covering.

When $n=1$ the base $V$ is a point.

rows.consumer_statement_or_definition:
Let $\Lambda=\mathbb Z\omega_1+\mathbb Z\omega_2$ be a full complex lattice with
oriented basis and let $\wp=\wp_\Lambda$ be its Weierstrass function
([[def-weierstrass-elliptic-p-function]]). Then the identity
$$\wp(z+w)=-\wp(z)-\wp(w)+\frac14\left(\frac{\wp'(z)-\wp'(w)}{\wp(z)-\wp(w)}\right)^{2}$$
holds meromorphically in $(z,w)$: it holds as an equality of values wherever
the displayed quotient is defined, and all apparent exceptional cases — the
apparent singularity where $\wp(z)=\wp(w)$ with $z\equiv w$, the double pole
where $\wp(z)=\wp(w)$ with $z\equiv-w$, and the degenerate choices of $w$ —
are interpreted by meromorphic continuation, without asserting a finite value
at a genuine pole. Concretely, for every $w\in\mathbb C$ the identity is an
identity of meromorphic functions of $z$ on $\mathbb C$, and symmetrically it
is an identity of meromorphic functions of $w$ for every $z$.

A holomorphic function equals its Taylor series on a disc around each point and has complex derivatives of all orders there ([[thm-taylor-expansion-holomorphic-function]], [[thm-cauchy-integral-formula-higher-derivatives]]). A holomorphic function is continuous ([[cor-complex-differentiability-implies-continuity]]).

Let $\Lambda=\mathbb Z\omega_1+\mathbb Z\omega_2$ be a full complex lattice with
oriented basis $(\omega_1,\omega_2)$
([[def-complex-lattice-and-complex-torus]]), let $\wp=\wp_\Lambda$ be its
Weierstrass function ([[def-weierstrass-elliptic-p-function]]) and let

$$G_4:=G_4(\Lambda)=\sum_{\omega\in\Lambda\setminus\{0\}}\omega^{-4},\qquad G_6:=G_6(\Lambda)=\sum_{\omega\in\Lambda\setminus\{0\}}\omega^{-6},$$

where the sums are the unordered finite-subset sums over the lattice. Then:

1. both families $(\omega^{-4})_{\omega\ne0}$ and $(\omega^{-6})_{\omega\ne0}$
   are absolutely summable, so $G_4$ and $G_6$ are well defined complex numbers;
2. with the invariants
   $$g_2:=60\,G_4,\qquad g_3:=140\,G_6,$$
   the $\Lambda$-elliptic meromorphic functions $(\wp')^2$ and
   $4\wp^3-g_2\wp-g_3$ agree on $\mathbb C\setminus\Lambda$:
   $$(\wp')^2=4\wp^3-g_2\wp-g_3 .$$

rows.consumer_statement_or_definition:
Let $\Lambda=\mathbb Z\omega_1+\mathbb Z\omega_2\subseteq\mathbb C$ be a full
complex lattice with oriented basis $(\omega_1,\omega_2)$, and let

$$\wp_\Lambda(z)=\frac{1}{z^{2}}+\sum_{\omega\in\Lambda\setminus\{0\}}\left(\frac{1}{(z-\omega)^{2}}-\frac{1}{\omega^{2}}\right)$$

be the Weierstrass $\wp$-function of
[[def-weierstrass-elliptic-p-function]]. Then:

1. the sum converges absolutely at every $z\in\mathbb C\setminus\Lambda$ and
   uniformly on every compact subset of $\mathbb C\setminus\Lambda$, so it is
   normally convergent there and independent of any enumeration of $\Lambda$;
2. $\wp_\Lambda$ is holomorphic on $\mathbb C\setminus\Lambda$, is even
   ($\wp_\Lambda(-z)=\wp_\Lambda(z)$) and is $\Lambda$-periodic
   ($\wp_\Lambda(z+\lambda)=\wp_\Lambda(z)$ for every $\lambda\in\Lambda$ and
   every $z\in\mathbb C$, with poles matched), so it is a $\Lambda$-elliptic
   function;
3. at each lattice point $\lambda\in\Lambda$ the function $\wp_\Lambda$ has a
   double pole with principal part $(z-\lambda)^{-2}$, and it has no other
   poles;
4. $\wp_\Lambda'(z)=-2\sum_{\omega\in\Lambda}(z-\omega)^{-3}$ on
   $\mathbb C\setminus\Lambda$, this series being normally convergent there,
   and the derivative $\wp_\Lambda'$ is odd and $\Lambda$-elliptic as well.

Then $g$ is holomorphic, and $g^{(k)}=\sum_j g_j^{(k)}$ for every natural $k$, the derivative series converging locally uniformly ([[cor-locally-uniformly-convergent-holomorphic-series]], [[thm-weierstrass-convergence-holomorphic-functions]]).

For each lattice point retain only its least preimage, $j(\omega)=\min\{k:s(k)=\omega\}$, as in [F6]. The image of $j$ is an infinite subset of $\mathbb N$ (the distinct points $n\omega_1$, $n\ge1$, already form an infinite subset of the target); list that image in increasing order, recursively taking its least unused element. This list exhausts the image because every natural number has only finitely many predecessors. Applying $s$ gives a repetition-free enumeration $(\omega_j)_{j\ge0}$ of $\Lambda\setminus\{0\}$. Every finite subset is contained in a sufficiently long initial segment of this enumeration; the partial sums $S_N(z):=z^{-2}+\sum_{j<N}h_{\omega_j}(z)$ are holomorphic on $\mathbb C\setminus\Lambda$, and step 3.1 makes them converge locally uniformly to $\wp$. rows.consumer_statement_or_definition:
Let $f\in\mathcal O_{m,0}$ be regular in $z_m$ of order $d$. Then there are a
unit $u\in\mathcal O_{m,0}$ and a Weierstrass polynomial $W$ of degree $d$ such
that

$$f=uW.$$

cited_passages: [L3] The power sums of those slice zeros are holomorphic, and Newton's recurrences convert them into holomorphic elementary symmetric functions ([[lem-holomorphic-power-sums-of-slice-zeros]], [[lem-newton-identities-for-slice-roots]]).
proof_uses: 1.1 Choose a representative of $f$ on a neighbourhood of the closed cylinder $V\times\{|\zeta|\le r\}$ given by [L2]. For each $z'\in V$, let $\lambda_1(z'),\dots,\lambda_d(z')$ be the slice zeros in $|\zeta|<r$, counted with multiplicity. By [L3], the elementary symmetric functions $e_1(z'),\dots,e_d(z')$ of those roots are holomorphic in $z'$. Define $$W(z',\zeta):=\zeta^d-e_1(z')\zeta^{d-1}+\cdots+(-1)^d e_d(z').$$ At $z'=0$ all slice roots equal $0$, so $e_j(0)=0$ for every $j$; therefore $W$ is a degree-$d$ Weierstrass polynomial by [L4]. [given, L2, L3, L4, construct]

proof_uses: 4.1 On the central slice, regularity gives $f(0,\zeta)=\zeta^d h(\zeta)$ with $h(0)\ne0$, while step 1.1 gives $W(0,\zeta)=\zeta^d$. Hence step 3.1 yields $u(0,0)=h(0)\ne0$. proof_uses: 3.1 Define $$u(z',z_m):=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{|\zeta|=r} \frac{f(z',\zeta)}{W(z',\zeta)(\zeta-z_m)}\,d\zeta.$$ Because $W(z',\zeta)\ne0$ on $|\zeta|=r$, the integrand is continuous on $V\times\{|\zeta|=r\}\times\{|z_m|<r\}$ and holomorphic in each parameter variable. By [L6], the resulting function $u$ is separately holomorphic and locally bounded, hence holomorphic on $V\times\{|z_m|<r\}$. For fixed $z'$, the one-variable Cauchy formula [L7] applied to the holomorphic slice quotient $q_{z'}$ from step 2.1 gives $$u(z',z_m)=q_{z'}(z_m),$$ so $$f(z',z_m)=u(z',z_m)W(z',z_m).$$ [step 2.1, L6, L7]

rows.consumer_statement_or_definition:
Let $m\ge0$ be an integer, and let $(a_n)_{n\ge1}$ be a sequence of nonzero
complex numbers with no finite accumulation point, where each value may repeat
according to its intended multiplicity. Then there are integers $p_n\ge0$ such
that

$$P(z):=z^m\prod_{n\ge1}E_{p_n}(z/a_n)$$

converges normally on $\mathbb C$ and is entire, with zero set exactly
$\{0\}$ of order $m$ together with the nonzero zeros $a_n$ counted with
multiplicity.

cited_passages: [F2] For every integer $p\ge0$ and $|w|\le1$, the elementary factor satisfies $|1-E_p(w)|\le|w|^{p+1}$ ([[lem-unit-disc-estimate-for-weierstrass-elementary-factors]]).
proof_uses: 2.1 For $|z|\le R$ and $n\ge N$, one has $|z/a_n|\le R/|a_n|<1/2\le1$, and $E_n(z/a_n)\ne0$ because its unique zero occurs at $z=a_n$, outside the closed disc $|z|\le R$. Using [F2] with $p=n$ gives $$|1-E_n(z/a_n)|\le|z/a_n|^{n+1}\le(R/|a_n|)^{n+1}\le2^{-n-1}.$$ Therefore $$\sum_{n\ge N}\sup_{|z|\le R}|1-E_n(z/a_n)|$$ converges. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

cited_passages: [F3] A normally convergent holomorphic product defines an entire function whose zeros on each compact set are exactly those contributed by the finitely many exceptional factors ([[thm-normal-convergence-of-holomorphic-products]]).
proof_uses: 3.1 Step 2.1 is exactly the normal-convergence condition on the closed disc $|z|\le R$, and $R$ was arbitrary. Hence [F3] makes $$\prod_{n\ge1}E_n(z/a_n)$$ an entire function whose zeros are exactly the points $a_n$, counted with multiplicity. Multiplying by $z^m$ contributes precisely the order-$m$ zero at $0$ and no other zeros, so $$P(z)=z^m\prod_{n\ge1}E_n(z/a_n)$$ has exactly the stated zero divisor. Since $p_n=n\ge0$, this is a Weierstrass product in the sense of [F1]. [F1, F3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

rows.consumer_statement_or_definition:
Let $\Lambda=\mathbb Z\omega_1+\mathbb Z\omega_2\subseteq\mathbb C$ be a full
complex lattice with oriented basis $(\omega_1,\omega_2)$
([[def-complex-lattice-and-complex-torus]]), let
$\wp=\wp_\Lambda$, $\zeta=\zeta_\Lambda$ and $\sigma=\sigma_\Lambda$ be its
Weierstrass functions
([[def-weierstrass-elliptic-p-function]],
[[def-weierstrass-zeta-and-sigma-functions]]), and put
$\eta_j:=2\zeta(\omega_j/2)$ for $j=1,2$, so that $\omega_1,\omega_2$ are
primitive and $\eta_j=\eta_{\omega_j}$. Then:

1. the finite-subset net defining $\zeta$ converges normally on
   $\mathbb C\setminus\Lambda$ (uniformly on every compact subset), the
   unordered limit being independent of the exhaustion of
   $\Lambda\setminus\{0\}$ by finite subsets; the function $\zeta$ is meromorphic on $\mathbb C$,
   holomorphic exactly on $\mathbb C\setminus\Lambda$, odd, and has at each
   lattice point $\lambda\in\Lambda$ a simple pole with principal part
   $(z-\lambda)^{-1}$ and residue $1$, with no other poles; moreover
   $$\zeta_\Lambda'(z)=-\wp_\Lambda(z)\qquad(z\in\mathbb C\setminus\Lambda);$$
2. the finite-subset net defining the product of the elementary factors
   $E_2(z/\omega)$ over $\omega\in\Lambda\setminus\{0\}$ converges normally on
   $\mathbb C$, independently of the exhaustion, so that $\sigma$ is entire; $\sigma$ is odd, its zero set is
   exactly $\Lambda$ and every zero is simple, $\sigma'(0)=1$, and
   $$\frac{\sigma_\Lambda'(z)}{\sigma_\Lambda(z)}=\zeta_\Lambda(z)\qquad(z\in\mathbb C\setminus\Lambda);$$
3. the **quasi-period laws** hold, for $j=1,2$ and all
   $z\in\mathbb C$ (with poles matched),
   $$\zeta_\Lambda(z+\omega_j)=\zeta_\Lambda(z)+\eta_j,\qquad \sigma_\Lambda(z+\omega_j)=-\exp\!\left(\eta_j\Bigl(z+\frac{\omega_j}{2}\Bigr)\right)\sigma_\Lambda(z),$$
   and the **Legendre relation** holds:
   $$\eta_1\omega_2-\eta_2\omega_1=2\pi i .$$

cited_passages: [F2] For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$: $|z|\ge0$ with $|z|=0$ exactly for $z=0$, $|zw|=|z|\,|w|$ and $|z+w|\le|z|+|w|$ ([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]); continuity and convergence on $\mathbb C$ are the metric notions for $d_{\mathbb C}(z,w)=|z-w|$ ([[def-complex-metric-convergence-and-continuity]]); a complex differentiable function is continuous ([[cor-complex-differentiability-implies-continuity]]).
proof_uses: 1.1 (Uniform gap and finiteness in discs.) Put $A:=|\omega_1|^2$, $B:=\operatorname{Re}(\omega_1\overline{\omega_2})$, $C:=|\omega_2|^2$ and $M:=\max(A,C)$. Expanding with [F2] gives $|s\omega_1+t\omega_2|^2=As^2+2Bst+Ct^2$ for real $s,t$, and $AC-B^2=(\operatorname{Im}(\omega_1\overline{\omega_2}))^2>0$ because real-linear independence forbids $\operatorname{Im}(\omega_1\overline{\omega_2})=0$. If $|s|\ge|t|$, write $x:=|s|$ and $\tau:=|t|\le x$: then $As^2-2|B||s||t|+Ct^2$ is a convex quadratic in $\tau$ whose values at $\tau=0$, at its vertex $\tau=|B|x/C$ and at $\tau=x$ are $Ax^2$, $x^2(AC-B^2)/C$ and $(A-2|B|+C)x^2$, all at least $x^2(AC-B^2)/C\ge x^2(AC-B^2)/M$; the case $|t|\ge|s|$ is symmetric with $A$ and $C$ interchanged. Hence $|s\omega_1+t\omega_2|\ge\delta\max(|s|,|t|)$ with $\delta:=\sqrt{(AC-B^2)/M}>0$: every nonzero lattice point has modulus at least $\delta$, while a lattice point $\lambda=m\omega_1+n\omega_2$ with $|\lambda|\le R$ has $|m|,|n|\le R/\delta$ by [F1] and the displayed inequality. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open, let $f$ be meromorphic on $\Omega$, let
$\Gamma$ be admissible for the residue theorem in $\Omega$, suppose
$f(z)\ne0$ for every $z\in\Gamma^\ast$, and let $g$ be holomorphic on
$\Omega$. Then

$$\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_\Gamma g(z)\frac{f'(z)}{f(z)}\,dz=\sum_{a\in Z(f)} n(\Gamma,a)\operatorname{ord}_a(f)\,g(a)-\sum_{b\in P(f)} n(\Gamma,b)\operatorname{ord}^{\mathrm{pole}}_b(f)\,g(b),$$

and only finitely many terms are nonzero.

cited_passages: [L1] The logarithmic derivative has residue $m$ at a zero of order $m$ and residue $-m$ at a pole of order $m$ ([[lem-logarithmic-derivative-order-residue]]).
proof_uses: 1.1 Put $h(z):=g(z)f'(z)/f(z)$. Away from the zeros and poles of $f$, the function $f'/f$ is holomorphic, so $h$ is holomorphic there as well. At a zero or pole $c$ of $f$, the function $g$ is holomorphic and therefore admits the expansion $g(z)=g(c)+(z-c)u(z)$ near $c$ for some holomorphic $u$. Multiplying that by the principal-part decomposition from [L1] shows $$\operatorname{Res}(h,c)=g(c)\operatorname{Res}\!\left(\frac{f'}{f},c\right).$$ [given, L1, algebra]

2.1 Step 1.1 and [L1] therefore give $$\operatorname{Res}(h,a)=g(a)\operatorname{ord}_a(f)$$ at each zero $a$ of $f$, and $$\operatorname{Res}(h,b)=-g(b)\operatorname{ord}^{\mathrm{pole}}_b(f)$$ at each pole $b$ of $f$. By [L2], only finitely many such points have nonzero index with respect to $\Gamma$. [step 1.1, L1, L2]

cited_passages: [L2] The unweighted argument principle already shows that only finitely many zeros and poles of $f$ have nonzero index with respect to $\Gamma$ ([[thm-argument-principle-null-homologous-cycle]]).
proof_uses: 2.1 Step 1.1 and [L1] therefore give $$\operatorname{Res}(h,a)=g(a)\operatorname{ord}_a(f)$$ at each zero $a$ of $f$, and $$\operatorname{Res}(h,b)=-g(b)\operatorname{ord}^{\mathrm{pole}}_b(f)$$ at each pole $b$ of $f$. By [L2], only finitely many such points have nonzero index with respect to $\Gamma$. [step 1.1, L1, L2]

cited_passages: [L3] The residue theorem sums the indexed residues of an admissible meromorphic function over $\Gamma$ ([[thm-residue-theorem-null-homologous-cycle]]).
proof_uses: 3.1 Applying [L3] to $h$ and substituting the residue values from step 2.1 gives the displayed weighted sum formula. [step 2.1, L3] ∎

rows.consumer_statement_or_definition:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $h:\mathbb S^1\to\mathbb S^1$ be an orientation-preserving homeomorphism, and let $(\Gamma,f,g)$ and $(\Gamma',f',g')$ be two conformal weldings of $h$ in the convention $h=f^{-1}\circ g$ of [[def-conformal-welding-of-a-jordan-curve]].

(a) If $\Gamma$ is globally conformally removable, then there is a Möbius transformation $A$ such that $f'=A\circ f$ and $g'=A\circ g$. In particular, $\Gamma'=A(\Gamma)$.

(b) If $h$ is quasisymmetric, then a welding with a quasicircle curve exists ([[thm-quasiconformal-welding-existence]]). Every other welding of $h$ has curve Möbius-equivalent to that quasicircle, so the welding curve is unique up to Möbius postcomposition.

cited_passages: [F3] A compact set is globally CH-removable when every sphere homeomorphism conformal off it is Möbius ([[def-conformal-removable-compact-set]]). Its neighborhood-local formulation is recorded separately; this theorem uses only the global definition.
proof_uses: 4.1 On $\Omega_0$ and $\Omega_1$, respectively, $F$ is the conformal composition $f'\circ f^{-1}$ and $g'\circ g^{-1}$; hence it is conformal on $\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus\Gamma$. If $\Gamma$ is globally conformally removable, [F3] makes $F$ a Möbius transformation $A$. Restricting to each component gives $f'=A\circ f$ and $g'=A\circ g$, so $\Gamma'=A(\Gamma)$. Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $A$ be a self-adjoint operator on a complex Hilbert space H and let
$\lambda\in\mathbb R$. Then $\lambda\in\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A)$ if and only if
there is a sequence $x_n\in D(A)$ with $\|x_n\|=1$, $x_n\rightharpoonup0$ weakly
([[def-weak-convergence-of-nets-and-sequences]]) and
$\|(A-\lambda)x_n\|\to0$. The sequence may be chosen orthonormal; such a
sequence is called a singular Weyl sequence for $\lambda$.

Sequences below are indexed by all n in N={0,1,2,...}; the shrinking radii are 1/(n+1). Inner products are linear in the first variable.

cited_passages: [A1] For every real lambda, membership in the essential spectrum is equivalent to infinite rank of every projection $P_\varepsilon=E((\lambda-\varepsilon,\lambda+\varepsilon))$, epsilon>0. This equivalence includes real resolvent points and isolated finite-multiplicity eigenvalues. On the zero Hilbert space the essential spectrum is empty. [[def-discrete-and-essential-spectrum-of-a-self-adjoint-operator]]
proof_uses: 1.1 If H={0}, there is no unit vector and the essential spectrum is empty, so both sides are false. Otherwise use the PVM of [A2]. For any bounded interval J and x in ran E(J), the projection identity gives E_x(R\J)=0 and $\int v^2dE_x\le(\sup_{v\in J}|v|)^2\|x\|^2<\infty$, hence x belongs to D(A). For any x in D(A) and epsilon>0, [A2] gives $\|(I-P_\varepsilon)x\|^2=E_x(\{|v-\lambda|\ge\varepsilon\})\le\varepsilon^{-2}\int|v-\lambda|^2dE_x=\varepsilon^{-2}\|(A-\lambda)x\|^2$. The closed complement includes both interval endpoints. [A1, A2]

2.1 Suppose a singular Weyl sequence exists. If any P_epsilon had finite rank, step 1.2 would give P_epsilon x_n to zero, while step 1.1 and the residual hypothesis would give (I-P_epsilon)x_n to zero. The triangle inequality would contradict norm x_n=1. Thus every P_epsilon has infinite rank, and [A1] proves lambda belongs to the essential spectrum. This proves the implication for all real lambda, including exclusion of real resolvent points, rather than merely excluding the discrete spectrum. [A1, step 1.1, step 1.2]

2.2 Suppose lambda is in the essential spectrum. For n>=0 write V_n=ran E((lambda-1/(n+1),lambda+1/(n+1))), infinite dimensional by [A1]. Given a finite list of n previously chosen orthonormal vectors x_0,...,x_(n-1), there is a nonzero vector in V_n orthogonal to them: choose n+1 linearly independent vectors in V_n and solve the n homogeneous linear equations for their pairings with the preceding vectors; a nonzero coefficient solution exists by finite-dimensional elimination, and independence makes its vector nonzero. Normalize it. For n=0 choose any nonzero vector in V_0 and normalize; there are no orthogonality equations. On the set of finite lists meeting these conditions, the relation of adjoining such a vector is entire. Apply DC from [A4] with the empty list as initial point; the compatible lists define x_n for every n>=0. The sequence is orthonormal and lies in D(A) by step 1.1. Its scalar measure is carried by the stated interval, so $\|(A-\lambda)x_n\|^2=\int|v-\lambda|^2dE_{x_n}\le(n+1)^{-2}\|x_n\|^2=(n+1)^{-2}$. Step 1.3 gives weak nullity. This constructs the required sequence and proves the converse. [A1, A2, A4, step 1.1, step 1.3]

3.1 The two implications are steps 2.1 and 2.2. Finite-dimensional H (including dimension one) has only finite-rank interval projections, so neither side holds there. Infinite multiplicity at an isolated point and spectral accumulation points are both covered by the same infinite-rank construction. Lambda=0 is allowed, since only the positive radii n+1 and epsilon are inverted. The empty initial list and the index-zero vector are included in step 2.2; the Choice use is [A4] and the spectral/Riesz interfaces, with no separability assumption. [A1, A4, step 2.1, step 2.2] ∎

rows.consumer_statement_or_definition:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). In the completed
character ring $\mathcal R$ of
[[def-completed-formal-character-ring-for-downward-cones]],
$$A(\rho)=e^{\rho}\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}(1-e^{-\alpha});$$
equivalently
$$\sum_{w\in W}(-1)^{\ell(w)}e^{w\rho}=e^{\rho}\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}(1-e^{-\alpha})\qquad\text{and}\qquad\sum_{w\in W}(-1)^{\ell(w)}e^{w\rho}=\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}\bigl(e^{\alpha/2}-e^{-\alpha/2}\bigr),$$
where $\rho=\tfrac12\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}\alpha$ is the Weyl vector
([[def-weyl-vector-rho-for-a-chosen-positive-system]]) and $A(\rho)$ is the
alternant of [[def-weyl-alternation-operator]]. Both sides are finite
expressions: the left side is a finite sum and the right side is a finite
product, and the identity holds in the group ring $\mathbb Z[P]$.
Consequently $A(\rho)$ is invertible, with
$$A(\rho)^{-1}=e^{-\rho}\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}(1-e^{-\alpha})^{-1}.$$

cited_passages:
[F1] For every $\lambda\in\Lambda^+$ the BGG Euler identity gives
$\operatorname{ch}L(\lambda)=\sum_{w\in W}(-1)^{\ell(w)}e^{w\circ\lambda}\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}(1-e^{-\alpha})^{-1}$
in $\mathcal R$, where the dot action is $w\circ\lambda=w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho$;
in particular $w\circ0=w\rho-\rho$
([[cor-bgg-euler-character-identity]],
[[def-grothendieck-group-and-character-of-category-o]]).
proof_uses: 1.1 The Euler identity [F1] at the dominant integral weight $\lambda=0$ reads $\operatorname{ch}L(0)=\sum_{w\in W}(-1)^{\ell(w)}e^{w\rho-\rho}\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}(1-e^{-\alpha})^{-1}$, and [F2] gives $\operatorname{ch}L(0)=1=e^0$. [F1, F2, algebra, A1]

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). For every dominant
integral weight $\lambda\in\Lambda^+$,
$$\dim L(\lambda)=\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}\frac{(\lambda+\rho,\alpha)}{(\rho,\alpha)}=\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}\frac{\langle\lambda+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle}{\langle\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle};$$
the denominators are nonzero because $\langle\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle>0$ for
every positive root
([[lem-positive-root-pairings-of-a-dominant-integral-weight]]).

cited_passages:
[F1] For every $t>0$ one has
$\sum_\mu m_\lambda(\mu)e^{2t(\mu,\rho)}=\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}\bigl(e^{t(\lambda+\rho,\alpha)}-e^{-t(\lambda+\rho,\alpha)}\bigr)\big/\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}\bigl(e^{t(\rho,\alpha)}-e^{-t(\rho,\alpha)}\bigr)$;
the left side is a finite sum of exponentials, continuous at $t=0$ with value
$\sum_\mu m_\lambda(\mu)=\dim L(\lambda)$, and the right side has the finite
limit $\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}(\lambda+\rho,\alpha)/(\rho,\alpha)$ as
$t\to0+$ ([[lem-regularized-evaluation-of-the-weyl-character-quotient-at-one]]).
proof_uses: 1.1 By [F1] the identity of the two functions of $t>0$ holds for every $t>0$, the left side extends continuously to $t=0$ with value $\dim L(\lambda)$, and the right side has the finite limit $\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}(\lambda+\rho,\alpha)/(\rho,\alpha)$ as $t\to0+$; since limits are unique by [F2] and a continuous extension is the limit of its values, $\dim L(\lambda)=\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}(\lambda+\rho,\alpha)/(\rho,\alpha)$. [F1, F2, algebra, A1]

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $A,C$ be self-adjoint operators such that
$R_A(z)-R_C(z)$ is compact for one nonreal $z$ (equivalently, for every
$z\in\rho(A)\cap\rho(C)$). Then
$\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A)=\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(C)$. In particular a bounded
self-adjoint compact perturbation preserves the essential spectrum, and if $K$
is symmetric and $A$-compact, then
$\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A+K)=\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A)$ with
$D(A+K)=D(A)$.

cited_passages: [A1] $\lambda\in\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(S)$ exactly when $S$ has an orthonormal singular Weyl sequence at $\lambda$ ([[thm-weyl-criterion-for-essential-spectrum]], [[def-discrete-and-essential-spectrum-of-a-self-adjoint-operator]]).
proof_uses: 1.1 Let $\lambda\in\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A)$ and let $(x_n)$ be the orthonormal Weyl sequence of [A1]. By [A2] and $\|(A-\lambda)x_n\|\to0$ one has $(R_A(z)+\frac1{\lambda-z})x_n\to0$; since $R_A(z)-R_C(z)$ is compact and $x_n\rightharpoonup0$, [A3] gives $(R_C(z)+\frac1{\lambda-z})x_n\to0$ as well. [A1, A2, A3]

2.1 Then $(C-\lambda)R_C(z)x_n=(z-\lambda)R_C(z)x_n-x_n\to0$ by [A2] and step 1.1, and $\|R_C(z)x_n\|\to|\lambda-z|^{-1}>0$; the normalized vectors $y_n:=\|R_C(z)x_n\|^{-1}R_C(z)x_n$ lie in $D(C)$, have unit norm, converge weakly to $0$ and satisfy $(C-\lambda)y_n\to0$, so they form a singular Weyl sequence and $\lambda\in\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(C)$ by [A1]. Interchanging the roles of $A$ and $C$ gives equality. [A1, A2, step 1.1]

rows.consumer_statement_or_definition:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $f,g:S^1\to\mathbb R^2$ be oriented immersions of the circle (regular
closed curves). Then $f$ and $g$ are regularly homotopic through immersions if
and only if their rotation numbers agree, $\operatorname{rot}(f)=\operatorname{rot}(g)$.
Equivalently, the rotation number induces a bijection
$\pi_0\operatorname{Imm}(S^1,\mathbb R^2)\cong\mathbb Z$; every integer is
realised by a $k$-fold round circle for $k\ne0$, and by the Gerono
lemniscate for $k=0$. Reversing the domain negates the rotation number, so
the once-traversed round circle cannot be turned inside out in the plane
through immersions. A zero-rotation immersed circle is regularly homotopic
to its reversal.

cited_passages: [F1] A regular homotopy is a smooth family of immersions with prescribed ends; the rotation number is $\deg(\tau_f)$ for the normalised velocity, is invariant under regular reparametrisation and negates under reversal of the orientation of the domain. [[def-regular-homotopy-of-immersions]], [[def-rotation-number-of-an-immersed-oriented-circle-in-the-plane]]
proof_uses: 3.1 Consequently rotation number gives a bijection $\pi_0\operatorname{Imm}(S^1,\mathbb R^2)\cong\mathbb Z$: necessity and sufficiency give well-definedness and injectivity. For $k\ne0$, $f_k(\theta)=(\cos k\theta,\sin k\theta)$ has velocity of norm $|k|$ and unit tangent $\operatorname{sgn}(k)(-\sin k\theta,\cos k\theta)$, a constant rotation of $e^{ik\theta}$, hence degree $k$. For $k=0$, take $\delta(\theta)=(\cos\theta,\sin2\theta)$. Its velocity is $p(\sin\theta)$, where $p(u)=(-u,2-4u^2)$ never vanishes for real $u$: if its first coordinate is zero its second is $2$. The homotopy $p((1-t)\sin\theta)$ contracts this velocity loop to $(0,2)$ through nonzero vectors, so its degree is zero. Thus every integer occurs. [F1, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 Reversing the domain gives $\tau_{f\circ a}(\theta)=-\tau_f(-\theta)$ for $a(\theta)=-\theta$. The constant target rotation by $\pi$ preserves degree and domain reversal negates it, so the reverse of a curve of rotation number $k$ has rotation number $-k$. rows.consumer_statement_or_definition:
Let $\Gamma$, $\Gamma_1$, $\Gamma_2$ be complex chains
([[def-complex-chain-and-cycle]]). Then:

1. $(\Gamma_1+\Gamma_2)^\ast=\Gamma_1^\ast\cup\Gamma_2^\ast$,
   $(-\Gamma)^\ast=\Gamma^\ast$ and $(\Gamma^-)^\ast=\Gamma^\ast$;
2. $\partial(\Gamma_1+\Gamma_2)=\partial\Gamma_1+\partial\Gamma_2$,
   $\partial(-\Gamma)=-\partial\Gamma$ and $\partial(\Gamma^-)=-\partial\Gamma$
   as functions on $\mathbb C$; consequently a sum of cycles is a cycle, and the
   negative and the reversal of a cycle are cycles;
3. for $f$ continuous on $\Gamma_1^\ast\cup\Gamma_2^\ast$,
   $$\int_{\Gamma_1+\Gamma_2}f\,dz=\int_{\Gamma_1}f\,dz+\int_{\Gamma_2}f\,dz,$$
   and for $f$ continuous on $\Gamma^\ast$,
   $$\int_{-\Gamma}f\,dz=-\int_\Gamma f\,dz,\qquad \int_{\Gamma^-}f\,dz=-\int_\Gamma f\,dz;$$
4. for $p\notin\Gamma_1^\ast\cup\Gamma_2^\ast$,
   $n(\Gamma_1+\Gamma_2,p)=n(\Gamma_1,p)+n(\Gamma_2,p)$, and for
   $p\notin\Gamma^\ast$, $n(-\Gamma,p)=-n(\Gamma,p)=n(\Gamma^-,p)$;
5. the empty chain is a cycle, its integral of every function is $0$, and its
   index is $0$ at every point of $\mathbb C$.

proof_uses: 1.1 The list $\Gamma_1+\Gamma_2$ has as its terms exactly the terms of $\Gamma_1$ followed by those of $\Gamma_2$, so the set of indices with nonzero coefficient splits as a disjoint union and [L2] gives $(\Gamma_1+\Gamma_2)^\ast=\Gamma_1^\ast\cup\Gamma_2^\ast$. Negating a coefficient does not change whether it is zero, and reversing a contour does not change its trace by [L8], so $(-\Gamma)^\ast=(\Gamma^-)^\ast=\Gamma^\ast$. This is claim 1. [given, L2, L8]

1.2 For each $q$, the two defining sums of $\partial(\Gamma_1+\Gamma_2)(q)$ run over the disjoint union of the corresponding index sets for $\Gamma_1$ and $\Gamma_2$, so [L6] splits each of them and gives $\partial(\Gamma_1+\Gamma_2)(q)=\partial\Gamma_1(q)+\partial\Gamma_2(q)$. Replacing every $m_k$ by $-m_k$ multiplies both sums by $-1$ by [L5], giving $\partial(-\Gamma)=-\partial\Gamma$; and by [L8] the reversal exchanges the roles of the two endpoint sums, giving $\partial(\Gamma^-)=-\partial\Gamma$. Hence if $\partial\Gamma_1$ and $\partial\Gamma_2$ vanish identically so does $\partial(\Gamma_1+\Gamma_2)$, and likewise for $-\Gamma$ and $\Gamma^-$; this is claim 2. [given, L2, L5, L6, L8]

Let $a\in\mathbb C$, let $r>0$, let $k\in\mathbb Z$ and put

$$\gamma_k(t)=a+r\exp(ikt),\qquad t\in[0,2\pi].$$

Then $\gamma_k$ is a closed complex contour and

$$n(\gamma_k,z)=k\quad\text{for }|z-a|<r,\qquad n(\gamma_k,z)=0\quad\text{for }|z-a|>r.$$

For $k\ne0$ the trace of $\gamma_k$ is the circle $\{z:|z-a|=r\}$. For $k=0$ the
contour is the constant path at $a+r$ and its trace is $\{a+r\}$; the two
displayed formulas still hold, both values being $0$, and both regions still lie
off the trace.

rows.consumer_statement_or_definition:
Let $f$ be a nonzero entire function of finite order $\rho$. For a finite
multiset of nonzero zeros, use the convention that its exponent of convergence
is $0$. If the nonzero zero multiset is infinite, let $(a_n)_{n\ge1}$ list it
with multiplicity and without finite accumulation point. In either case the
exponent of convergence satisfies

$$\lambda\le\rho.$$

Equivalently, for every real $s>\rho$ the reciprocal power sum over all nonzero
zeros, counted with multiplicity, is finite; in the infinite case this is

$$\sum_{n\ge1}|a_n|^{-s}<\infty.$$

cited_passages: [F2] Jensen's counting corollary bounds the number $n(r)$ of zeros in $|z|\le r$ in terms of the boundary growth on a larger circle ([[cor-jensen-zero-counting-bound]]).
proof_uses: 4.1 Fix real numbers $\sigma,s$ with $\rho<\sigma<s$. By [F1] and step 3.1, for all sufficiently large $r$ one has $\log M_g(2r)\le(2r)^\sigma$. Applying [F2] to $g$, whose value at $0$ is nonzero by step 1.1, yields $$n(r)\log2\le\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\log|g(2re^{it})|\,dt-\log|g(0)|\le(2r)^\sigma-\log|g(0)|,$$ where $n(r)$ counts the nonzero zeros of $f$ in $|z|\le r$. Thus $n(r)\le Cr^\sigma$ for all large $r$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 3.1, choose, algebra]

rows.consumer_statement_or_definition:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $S$ be holomorphic and zero-free on $\mathbb D$ with $|S|\le1$, and suppose
that its boundary function satisfies $|S^*|=1$ $m$-almost everywhere
(equivalently, $S$ is an inner function without zeros). Then there are a unique
$\lambda\in\mathbb T$ and a unique finite positive measure $\mu\perp m$ with
$$S=\lambda\,S_\mu,\qquad S_\mu(z)=\exp\Bigl(-\int_{\mathbb T}K(z,\zeta)\,d\mu(\zeta)\Bigr).$$
With the normalizations $S_\mu(0)=e^{-\mu(\mathbb T)}>0$ and
$\lambda=S(0)/S_\mu(0)$, the pair $(\lambda,\mu)$ is unique. In particular
$S_\mu$ is the singular inner function of $\mu$, and every inner function is,
up to a unimodular constant, the product of a Blaschke product and a singular
inner function.

Every compact set $K\subseteq\widehat{\mathbb C}$ with $\mathcal H^1_\chi(K)=0$ is globally conformally removable; the same proof shows this for every compact $K$ with $\mathcal H^1_\chi(K)<\infty$ ([[def-conformal-removable-compact-set]]).

Every quasicircle is globally conformally removable ([[def-quasicircle]]).

cited_passages: [F1] [[lem-zeta-horizontal-logarithmic-derivative-comparison]]: There are absolute $d>0,C>0$, with $d<c_0$, such that for $|t|\ge3$ and $\sigma\ge1-d/\log(|t|+2)$, $\left|\frac{\zeta'(\sigma+it)}{\zeta(\sigma+it)}\right|\le C\log(|t|+2).$
proof_uses: 1.1 Under countable choice, choose $c_1$ smaller than the constant in the horizontal comparison. This gives the stated derivative bound throughout the high-height region. [F1]

cited_passages: [F2] [[thm-riemann-zeta-classical-zero-free-region]]: There is an absolute $c_0>0$ such that $\zeta$ has no zeros in $\sigma\ge1-c_0/\log(|t|+2)$. The pole at $s=1$ is not a zero.
proof_uses: 3.1 On the compact low-height portion choose $c_2<c_1$ sufficiently small that $h(s)=(s-1)\zeta(s)$ is holomorphic and nonvanishing on a neighborhood, including $h(1)=1$. Then $h'/h$ and $1/h$ are bounded there. The identities $\zeta'/\zeta+1/(s-1)=h'/h$ and $1/\zeta=(s-1)/h$ prove both low-height estimates and their removable interpretations. [F2, F4] ∎
